The table in question is the “Contents” (table of contents) from the SOFiSTiK CSM (Construction Stage Manager) Manual, Service Pack 2025-4 Build 146. Its primary purpose is to document all chapters, major sections, sub‐sections and their associated starting page numbers. When ingested into a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store, each row can serve as a retrieval unit keyed by section ID, title and page location. Below is a breakdown of its structure and major content blocks:

1. Header and Metadata (not strictly tabular but important context)  
   • Product name: “CSM Construction Stage Manager”  
   • Version: “CSM Manual, Service Pack 2025-4 Build 146”  
   • Copyright notice and legal disclaimers  
   • Publisher and contact information: SOFiSTiK AG, Nuremberg & Garching offices, email, phone, web  

2. Top-Level Chapters  
   The Contents are organized into four top-level chapters, each with a Roman or Arabic chapter number and title:  
   • Chapter 1: General  
   • Chapter 2: Theoretical Background  
   • Chapter 3: Input Description  
   • Chapter 4: Examples  

3. Column Layout  
   From left to right the table spans:  
   • Section ID (e.g. “2.1”, “3.14”, “4.5”) – hierarchical decimal numbering  
   • Section Title (indented according to level)  
   • Page Number where the section begins (e.g. “2-1”, “3-28”, “4-2”)  

4. Chapter 1 – General  
   • Section 1.1 “General” starts on 1-1  

5. Chapter 2 – Theoretical Background  
   • Sections 2.1 through 2.12.12 cover all aspects of the theoretical underpinnings:  
     – 2.1 General  
     – 2.2 Activation of new elements  
     – 2.3 Numbering  
     – 2.4 Construction Stages to be Computed  
     – 2.5 Load Cases (Primary, Difference)  
     – 2.6 Analysis of Creep and Shrinkage (with sub-subsections 2.6.1–2.6.9)  
     – 2.7 Comparison with Cast-in-one System  
     – 2.8 Check-Print and Control-plots of the Calculation  
     – 2.9 Precambler Analysis (sub-heads 2.9.1–2.9.6)  
     – 2.10 Shape and Force Optimization (2.10.1–2.10.3)  
     – 2.11 Incremental Launching (2.11.1–2.11.2)  
     – 2.12 CSM Design (2.12.1–2.12.12: Superposition, Dataflow, Design Tasks, Fatigue Checks, etc.)  

6. Chapter 3 – Input Description  
   • Sections 3.1–3.40 present every input keyword or block that the user can specify, for example:  
     – 3.1 INPUT LANGUAGE  
     – 3.2 CTRL – Control parameters  
     – 3.3 LAUN – Launching  
     – 3.4 CS – Construction Stages  
     – 3.5 GRP – Groups  
     – 3.6 GRCS – Group-Stage Special Settings  
     – 3.7 TXCS – Text Input for Special CS  
     – …  
     – 3.11 CREP – Creep Parameters  
     – 3.15 DESI – Design  
     – 3.16 GRPD – Group Selection for the Design  
     – …  
     – 3.19 GAMT – Temporary Gamma Values  
     – 3.20 LCCS – Design of Construction Stages – Additional Loadcases  
     – 3.21 DECS – Design Construction Stage  
     – 3.22 COPY – Copy of Construction Stage Design Results  
     – 3.23 SUMA – Sum of CSM Stage Actions  
     – …  
     – 3.29 EXPO – Export  
     – 3.30 EQLC – Equation Load Cases  
     – 3.31 EQUU – Displacement Restriction  
     – 3.32 EQPP – Reaction Restriction  
     – 3.33 EQBE – Beam Force Restriction  
     – 3.34 EQIT – Construction Stage Iteration  
     – 3.35 KINK – Add New Segment with a Kink  
     – …  
     – 3.40 ECHO – Output Control  

7. Chapter 4 – Examples  
   • Demonstrative workflows and case studies, each with its own page:  
     – 4.1 Four-span Bridge with Stepwise Construction (4-1)  
     – 4.2 Two-Span Girder Creeping (4-1)  
     – 4.3 Precast Girder Bridge with Cast In Situ Deck (4-1)  
     – 4.4 Prestressed FE Slab – Test System (4-2)  
     – 4.5 Free Cantilever Erection – Small Test Bridge (4-2)  
     – 4.6 Free Cantilever Erection – Big Bridge (4-2)  
     – 4.7 Multistorey – Incremental Erection (4-2)  

8. Indexing Recommendations for RAG  
   • Treat each distinct section or sub-section row as a separate document chunk, embedding:  
     – “section_id” (e.g. “3.15”)  
     – “title” (e.g. “DESI – Design”)  
     – “page_start” (e.g. “3-30”)  
     – “chapter” grouping (e.g. “Input Description”)  
   • Use the hierarchical ID to support “find me all subsections under 2.6” or “list all input keywords in Chapter 3.”  
   • Include the manual’s metadata (version, copyright, publisher) at the root level of your vector index for context.  

This structured description ensures that queries such as “where is the Creep Parameters input block?” or “list all design-related input keywords” can be directly answered by retrieving the corresponding section ID, title and page number.

 With the Construction Stage Manager, shortly called CSM, construction stages and creep analysis problems can be defined and controlled in an easy way.
 The CSM program produces an input file for the common SOFiSTiK programs ASE and AQB that finally do the analysis. The program does not require further licences. For ASE at lease ASE1 is needed, for creep analysis in AQB, AQBS is needed.

With the CSM (Construction Stage Manager) a construction sequence can be defined and analyzed.
 The construction stages are controlled with the following tables:
 the table CS defines the used construction stages
 the group table GRP defines, when a group is activated
 -
 the load case table LC defines additional loads (g_2)
 Tendons are automatically activated starting from the ICS1 number defined in TENDON. From ICS2 on they are bonded.
 With a few input to variable actions then an automatic design can be started with CSM DESI.

The provided illustration is divided into two main parts: a series of schematic strip‐diagrams on the left and a real‐world photograph of a tower crane on the right. Together they document the “CTRL CANT 1” procedure for activating a new girder segment in a multispan post‐tensioned bridge model, highlighting four key sub‐stages: formwork placement, concrete placement, concrete hardening, and formwork removal (or dead‐load activation).  

Left–hand schematics (three small diagrams stacked vertically plus an inset block)  
  • Each of the three strip‐diagrams shows a simplified multispan girder composed of light-blue rectangular segments joined end to end. Two permanent supports are shown as solid red triangles beneath the continuity spans. At the free (cantilever) end of the first erected span, a new segment (span 2) is about to be added. A rectangular cyan “formwork” block is depicted under the cantilever tip, spanning horizontally back toward the last fixed support.  
  • Top diagram (Stages 1+2+3):  
      – The cyan formwork rests directly on the ground (or temporary falsework) beneath the cantilever nose; no additional load is yet transferred to the existing structure.  
      – A thin black line above the cyan block suggests the level of fresh concrete that will be cast.  
      – The girder itself remains in the geometry induced by the dead-load and prestress of span 1 only; there is a slight downward curve at the cantilever tip.  
  • Middle diagram (still Stages 1+2+3):  
      – Visually almost identical to the top sketch, indicating that pouring the concrete (liquid state) and its subsequent hardening introduce no incremental load to the already activated finite‐element model.  
      – The newly cast volume is “activated” in the software as a stress‐free element, matching the current deformed shape of the cantilever.  
  • Bottom diagram (Stage 4):  
      – The formwork has been removed (or, equivalently, the element is “unloaded” from its crane support) so that the dead load of the hardened concrete now transfers onto the girder.  
      – As a result, the cantilever tip deflects further downward under its own weight, and the newly added span adopts a slightly steeper downward slope.  
  • Small inset rectangle at upper right of the strip-diagrams shows the cyan block in isolation, emphasizing its purely horizontal, ground‐supported position.  

Caption below these sketches (“Figure 2.1: CTRL CANT 0-1-2 activation of a new group…”) refers to the fact that all four of these conditions are typically combined into a single numerical construction stage in the CSM (Construction Stage Model) software. The new element is first “activated” as if hanging stress‐free, then its self-weight is applied immediately, producing the deflection shown in the bottom view.  

Right–hand photograph (tower crane at a real bridge site)  
  • A bright-red tower crane mast rises into a clear blue sky. Its long horizontal jib (painted in alternating black-and-white lattice sections) extends to the left, with a trolley and hoist line supporting a slender beam segment beneath.  
  • The counter-jib to the right carries concrete counterweights marked “EIOSA.” The operator’s cabin is perched just below the main horizontal boom.  
  • The suspended beam, tinted pale green, mimics the shape of the cyan formwork in the left sketches—it represents the new span awaiting welding (or concreting) to the cantilever tip.  
  • Small red hooks and rigging lines connect the beam to the trolley, illustrating the “stress‐free hanging” condition of the new element before dead‐load activation.  

Overall, the image pair juxtaposes an abstract modeling workflow (left) with the physical reality (right) of adding a new girder span via formwork and crane support. The four conceptual steps—placement of formwork, pouring and hardening of concrete, then formwork removal and full dead-load transfer—are visualized in the CAD‐style diagrams, while the photograph grounds the process on an actual construction site. This dual representation underscores how the CSM software simulates each stage, first as a stress‐free activation (mimicking a crane) and then as a loaded element in the continuous multispan structure.

The image consists of two horizontally oriented line‐drawings, one above the other, each showing a multi‐span, segmental girder rendered as a chain of lightly shaded blue rectangular elements. Both drawings sit against a pale blue background and share the same overall geometry—a left‐hand cantilever “nose” of several small, connected elements, followed by a longer, nearly straight mid‐span, then continuing into further spans toward the right edge. Below the lower drawing is the caption “Figure 2.2: Activation of a new group, formwork stands on ground.”  

Top Drawing (Stages 1 + 2 + 3)  
• The left portion of the chain curves downward in a smooth, continuous deflection; individual segment boundaries are indicated by narrow darker lines. At the far left, the cantilever tip slopes slightly downward.  
• Moving rightward, the beam gradually straightens and rises toward the first support zone.  
• Immediately beneath the mid‐span straight run sits a large, flat, gray rectangular block representing the formwork platform. This block is drawn just below the bottom flange of the beam, with no visible gap, indicating direct contact.  
• Under the gray block are five small red solid triangles—icons for ground‐borne supports—spaced evenly along the length of the formwork. Each red triangle has a black outline.  
• Further to the right, beyond the formwork, a row of six additional red triangles supports the straight portion of the girder; these indicate the permanent supports or piers of spans 2 and beyond.  
• No special symbols or load arrows appear, emphasizing that in this combined stage the formwork and liquid concrete are present but impose no load on the structure because they bear on the ground.

Bottom Drawing (Stage 4)  
• The same chain of blue segments is redrawn in a slightly different deflected shape: the left‐hand cantilever nose now shows a deeper sag, and the mid‐span portion between supports is more noticeably curved downward. This reflects the sudden application of the dead load once the formwork is removed.  
• The gray formwork block is absent. Only the red triangular supports remain under the mid‐span and right‐hand sections, carrying the beam’s self‐weight.  
• Two of these triangles—one just right of center, another near the far right—are drawn with an additional small black rectangle beneath them, perhaps indicating adjusted support reactions or a temporary shoring arrangement.  
• The contrast between the two drawings highlights the key difference: above, formwork standing on the ground prevents any load transfer to the girder; below, removal of that support instantly applies the concrete dead load and produces the new deflected shape.

General Notes  
• The segmented beam is depicted as a series of equal‐length, lightly shaded blue elements to emphasize that each segment can be activated (added) in the construction simulation as a separate group.  
• The red triangles universally symbolize supports: those under the formwork represent temporary ground support; those under the girder beyond the formwork represent permanent supports or piers.  
• The gray rectangular formwork is shown only in the top view, positioned horizontally under the cantilever nose and over several supports, to reflect “CTRL CANT 1” formwork placement.  
• Visually, the illustrations serve to explain four discrete actions in one construction stage: placing the formwork (no load on girder), filling it with concrete (load transmitted to formwork onto ground), concrete curing (no additional load change), and finally removing formwork (dead load transferred to girder).  
• By comparing the nearly straight mid‐span in the top drawing to the sagging curve in the bottom one, the viewer can immediately grasp how activating the dead load in the same stage generates the characteristic deflections and internal forces that the Construction Stage Method (CSM) must simulate.

The figure is a side-by-side illustration of a free cantilever erection stage in a multi-span girder, combining a simplified numerical model on the left with an on-site crane photograph on the right.  

Left half (FE model sketch):  
• A continuous girder is shown in plan-view elevation, divided into several precast segments (each segment tinted a slightly different shade of cyan/blue). Two red support symbols mark the first pier at the far left (fixed‐end) and an intermediate support about one span in. Beyond that support the beam “cantilevers” freely.  
• Superimposed on the straight baseline is the deformed shape of the cantilever portion, drawn in wireframe and exaggerated for clarity: the tip of the cantilever has sagged vertically, producing a curved bending profile.  
• At the free end (cantilever nose) a small horizontal slab or platform is sketched in solid turquoise. This represents the temporary formwork or seating used to support the next segment during casting or erection. It is explicitly drawn horizontal—even though the cantilever (without formwork) deflects downward—because under CTRL_CANT1 the formwork bears on the ground (or falsework) and remains level.  
• A thin vertical line divides this schematic from the photograph on the right.  

Right half (site photograph):  
• A lattice-boom tower crane looms against a pale sky. The crane’s horizontal jib extends into frame from the right, its hook block lowering on steel wire ropes.  
• Suspended from the hook by four slings is a fresh precast concrete beam segment, rectangular in cross-section and painted a uniform teal. The bottom face of the segment is visible, with cast-in lifting anchors and slinging points at each corner.  
• No formwork is attached to the segment at this moment—the slab is still hanging freely on the crane, mirroring “situations 1–3” in the construction stage: (1) formwork/platform in place on the cantilever; (2) concrete cast into that formwork (no structural load on the main girder, since the formwork transfers weight to ground); (3) concrete hardens (still no additional load). The actual dead load of the new segment will only be activated when the formwork is removed (“situation 4”).  

Context in CSM‐type simulation:  
Under the CTRL_CANT1 strategy, new elements are first introduced as stress-free in the deflected geometry of the existing structure (primary load case). Only after formwork removal (or “unloading from the crane”) is the self-weight of the segment applied in the same construction stage, triggering permanent deformations and internal forces. This avoids artificial load spikes and correctly captures the time-sequence of support, casting, hardening, and load transfer in cantilevered segmental bridge erection.

Main task of the CSM is the simulation of a construction sequence. A main part is the activation of a new element.
 Lets consider a multispan girder where we start with erection and loading of span 1. The cantilever nose gets a vertical deformation. In the following, span 2 shall be activated and this leads to the problem how to position the formwork. For this we have three possibilities, see CTRL CANT ??:
 We choose CTRL CANT 1 and place the formwork horizontally at the cantilever nose. Four important actions or situations follow:
 - 1. the formwork is placed. This does not create a new load as the formwork stands on the ground, see following figure.
 -
 2. the concrete is filled in. This also does not create a new load as the concrete load goes directly over the formwork in the ground.
 -
 3. concrete hardens. This also does not create a new load as the concrete only goes from state liquid to a stressfree hardened state.
 4. the formwork is removed. Now the dead load of the concrete loads out structure.
 The following figure shows situation 1+2+3 on top and situation 4 on bottom:
 All these four situations are often calculated in one construction stage. It is important to imagine that the new elements are first activated as stressfree elements in the displacement situation of the previous construction stage (primary loadcase). The activation of the dead load in the same construction stage then immediately causes deformations and forces in the actual construction stage, see example csm1_4span_centering.dat.
 Alternatively you can think that the new elements hang stressfree on a crane and are so welded to the cantilever (situation 1+2+3). The activation of dead load then acts first with the unloading from the crane (situation 4).
 To also show the formwork position in a separate stage it is possible to insert a second con- struction stage. In the first the element is activated without dead load - this gives the formwork position. In the second, the dead load is activated - that represents the removal of formwork or unloading from the crane, see example csm26_precamber_spanbyspan.dat.

To also show the formwork position in a separate stage it is possible to insert a second con- struction stage. In the first the element is activated without dead load - this gives the formwork position. In the second, the dead load is activated - that represents the removal of formwork or unloading from the crane, see example csm26_precamber_spanbyspan.dat..
 In case you do not want to precamber your segments BUT you want to add (weld) them tan- gentially (CTRL CANT 2) AND you want to have the beams placed on the supports in the architectural position:
 csm26_tangential_without_precamber.dat
 That needs lifting or lowering of supports because when you add the segment tangentially you will NOT reach the next support with displacement zero when you add the segment ’stress- free without deadload’ (’stressfree without deadload’ means that the segment still hangs on the
 crane in this stage),

A very concise calculation can be done, if the numbering of groups, construction stages and prestressing stages match together in ascending order with respect to time.
 Due to the fact that intermediate construction steps (e.g.: prestressing, grouting, moving of temporary loads, creep..) are carried out between two main construction stages (CS) it is useful to store these main stages in every 10th construction stage number. So there are enough numbers in between to stor re the intermediate steps properly without shifting the numbers of the main stages, even if the intermediate steps are inserted subsequently.
 Proposed Numeration:
 - 10th : Activation of a new group
 - 11th : Prestressing
 - 12th : Grouting / extrusion
 - 13th : Loads of construction stages (e.g.: cantilever carriage..)
 - 15th : Creep-step
 For example: Group 50 is activated in construction stage 50 (hardening of concrete in CS 50) then the corresponding tendon is prestressed in CS 51 and grouted / extruded in CS 52.Hence the tendon has to be defined in TENDON...CS with ICS1=51 and ICS2=52.

All construction stages that cause changes of stresses have to be considered. Therefore construction stage grouting / extrusion (CS: x2) is not necessarily to be computed, due to the fact that the grouting mortar causes no changes in stresses.
 The change of a support-condition does not introduce new loads but leads to deformations and resulting stresses and has to be taken into account as a load case in an own stage.

A list over the loadcases used by CSM is printed at the end of this chapter.
 The TYPE (LC TYPE) of a loadcase has no longer an effect. Importand is the TYPE in CS.
 The load cases of additional loads should be advantageously defined with the same load case- and construction stage number, e.g.: Load case 43: loads of cantilever carriage for construction stage 43.
 Initially the calculation is performed with the complete loading resulting in complete internal forces for the end of the computed construction stage. This is necessary, because with a change of the support conditions the complete active support-force has to be shifted accord- ingly. Hence ASE is taking all loads activated for this construction stage into account. The load case numbers of these complete load cases are stored within the 4000 numbers, e.g. CS 40 with all loads in load case 4040.
 For the further design with AQB only the difference in internal forces between the load cases is required, AQB for instance has to consider different safety-factors for design at the ultimate
 limit state. Thus, in addition to the internal forces of the complete load case, the difference in internal forces refering to the last load case is stored as well within the 5000 numbers (e.g.: CS 40 in load case 5040). Load case 5040 stores the difference in internal forces between load case 4040 and 4035 (assuming load case 4035 is the construction stage before 4040).
 Load cases with creep are stored by AQB within the 6000 load cases and contain the change of internal forces due to creep and shrinkage of the cross-section, the corresponding load cases with numbers 5000 of the creep analysis with ASE only store the internal forces due to the redistribution of forces caused by creep and shrinkage.
 Please refer also to ASE...CTRL DIFF 2000 and ASE...LCC PLC YES/NEW and AQB...COMB LCST.

content:
From the effective width of the elements see AQUA (for quad elements the 1.4 times quad thick- ness is taken due to a considered covering on top), the CSM calculates creep and shrinkage values in dependence of T0 and TS, the creep duration, the temperature and the air humidity. The CSM uses code based functiions that are also used in AQB.
 See also YOUTUBE Video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=taaBfPlIRGA
 All workshop YOUTUBE videos are listed in the command GRP, search there for ’Overview workshop YOUTUBE videos’

For shrinkage an age TS of 3 days is set by default, With the input GRP...TS this can be changed in CSM. We assume/calculate that physically shrinkage starts at this age TS. The analysis creep and shrinkage intervals start at T0 (loading age). So in the first creep and shrinkage interval T0 to T0+T the shrinkage part from TS to T0 is not applied! This is correct for the standard case prestress with subsequent bond where prestress C+S loss starts at T0. With the same reason also the total shrinkage value does not include this first shrinkage part from TS to T0!
 In steel composite sections it is necessary to take into account the first shrinkage part from TS up to the start of loading. To do this you must input T0=TS= 1 day, see example steel_composite_orto.dat .
 For in situ concrete slab on a prerefabricated beam T0 may not be input too small because then the concrete wounld be too weak for first dead load G_1 or prestressing. Thus in example csm3_composite_beam.dat T0=3 and TS=1 is set for group 10. Completely correct could also be to input T0=TS= 1 day, calculate the first activation of the beams without dead load (GRP FACD), then add a creep step with e.g. 7 days and then activate dead load G_1 and following prestress P.

metadata.sections: 2.6.1 Loading start T0 and shrinkage start TS

content:
The table “Creep Values” lays out the key input and output parameters for a one-span girder creep analysis using the CTRL CREP RCRE (real creep) algorithm. It is structured in eight columns and six rows (excluding the header), and it captures both staging information (times, humidity, temperature) and the resulting creep coefficients for different load parts. Below is a detailed breakdown:

1. Column Headers  
   • Grp – Material group number in the model (integer).  
   • Mat – Material identifier (integer).  
   • h-0 [mm] – Initial gross section height of the member in millimeters.  
   • t0 [d] – Reference loading age (time zero for that load part) in days.  
   • CS 15, CS 25, CS 35 – Creep stages numbered 15, 25, 35, corresponding to the time intervals between key construction or loading events.  
   • total φ-eff – The effective total creep coefficient (dimensionless sum across all creep stages for that load part).

2. Staging Information Rows  
   • Row “t[d] →” (staging times):  
     – CS 15 begins at t1–t0 = 93 days (i.e. 100 d minus stripping age 7 d).  
     – CS 25 spans t2–t1 = 200 days (i.e. 300 d minus 100 d).  
     – CS 35 covers t∞–t2 = 10 950 days (i.e. 30 years minus 300 d).  
     – The final number 11 243 is the total time from initial age t0=7 d to t∞.  
   • Row “RH[%] →” – Constant relative humidity assumed in all three stages: 80 %.  
   • Row “T[°C] →” – Constant ambient temperature in all stages: 20 °C.

3. Creep Coefficients for the Dead-Load Part (Group 1, Material 1)  
   • Grp=1, Mat=1, h-0=400.0 mm, t0=7 d.  
   • φ at CS 15 (first creep interval under load from day 7 to day 100): 0.82  
   • φ at CS 25 (second interval from day 100 to day 300): 0.28  
   • φ at CS 35 (long-term interval from day 300 to 30 years): 0.61  
   • Total effective creep coefficient φ-eff = 0.82 + 0.28 + 0.61 = 1.71

4. Real-Creep Contributions (RCRE) for Successive Load Increments  
   The table then separates out two “real creep” (RCRE) sub-parts, each introduced at different ages and therefore having their own delayed-elastic and viscous parts:  
   a. Load part introduced at t0 = 100 d (start of load A):  
      – No creep during CS 15 (this load does not exist until after stage 15)  
      – φRCRE in CS 25 (from day 100 to day 300): 0.61  
      – φRCRE in CS 35 (from day 300 to 30 years): 0.43  
      – Total φRCRE = 0.61 + 0.43 = 1.03  
   b. Load part introduced at t0 = 300 d (end of load A):  
      – No creep during CS 15 or CS 25 (load not yet applied)  
      – φRCRE in CS 35 (from day 300 to 30 years): 0.83  
      – Total φRCRE = 0.83

5. Interpretation and Context  
   • The dead-load (permanent) part and each subsequent load increment (“positive load A” at day 100, then its removal at day 300) are assigned independent creep functions.  
   • Because each load part is shifted in time, backward creep (negative creep) can occur when load is removed: the two real-creep parts superimpose.  
   • The sum of all φ values for each part produces the net long-term deformation prediction at 30 years.  
   • This detailed breakdown is only available when using CTRL CREP RCRE, which assigns its own delayed-elastic and viscous parameters to each new load event.

The behavior of function CTRL CREP RCRE (real creep) can be best demonstrated on a simple one span girder with a temporary load -> real_creep_creepparameter.dat.
 A girder will be stripped after t0=7 days. To keepn it simple dead load is switched off (or you imagine the load to be horizontally). After further 93 days a loading A occurs. After further 200 days the load is taken away again:
 - t0 = 7 days : Stripping construction stage CS 10
 - t1=100 days : Start loading load A construction stage CS 20
 - t2=300 days : End of load construction stage CS 30
 - t∞ =30 years : final stage
 As the two creep parts have own time shifted delayed elastic parts, the backward creeping occurs.
 In example real_creep_creepparameter.dat we get the following output (first CSM run):
 In creep stage 25 from t1 up to t2 the system creeps under load with a delta-phi of 0.61 (last but one line RCRE für t0=100). In creep stage 35 from t2 up to t∞ the positive load part 5020 creeps with a delta-phi of 0.43, the negative load part 5020 (t0=300) creeps with 0.83. This results in the backward creeping.
 For an exact creep analysis on time varying loading CTRL CREP RCRE should be used be- cause only then a later load part will get an own creep function.

The table is a side‐by‐side comparison of how creep‐strain increments (Δφ) accumulate over a series of construction stages (CS) when using the “RCRE” creep‐control option.  It is organized into seven columns of interest—one for each stage CS 15, 25, 35, 45, 46, 47 and 48—plus a final column showing the total creep factor φ_eff.  Common header information (given once at the top) applies to all groups:

• h-0 [mm]: 400.0 mm (notional member size)  
• t₀ [d]: 7 days (age at which loading begins)  
• RH [%]: 80 % (relative humidity during all intervals)  
• T [°C]: 20 °C (temperature during all intervals)  
• t_eff [d]: the effective duration of each creep interval, namely  
  – CS 15 → 28 d  
  – CS 25 → 28 d  
  – CS 35 → 100 d  
  – CS 45 → 468 d  
  – CS 46 → 1 814 d  
  – CS 47 → 7 022 d  
  – CS 48 → 27 196 d  
  (cumulative total = 36 656 d)

Below this header, each row is one “load‐part group” (Grp 1–3).  All three groups share the same material (Mat 1), geometry (h-0 = 400 mm) and start‐of‐creep age (t₀ = 7 days), but differ in when they first become active in the creep analysis:

1. Grp 1 (active from CS 15)  
2. Grp 2 (active from CS 25)  
3. Grp 3 (active from CS 35)

For each group, the table lists the incremental creep factor Δφ that is “accrued” during each construction stage.  A dash (–) indicates the group was not yet active and so contributes no creep increment in that interval.  At the end of the row, the sum of all Δφ values is shown as “total φ_eff.”  

Detailed numbers:

Group 1 (starts at CS 15)  
• Δφ@15 = 0.63  
• Δφ@25 = 0.14  
• Δφ@35 = 0.25  
• Δφ@45 = 0.39  
• Δφ@46 = 0.30  
• Δφ@47 = 0.14  
• Δφ@48 = 0.05  
→ total φ_eff = 1.91  

Group 2 (starts at CS 25)  
• Δφ@15 = –  
• Δφ@25 = 0.63  
• Δφ@35 = 0.34  
• Δφ@45 = 0.43  
• Δφ@46 = 0.31  
• Δφ@47 = 0.14  
• Δφ@48 = 0.05  
→ total φ_eff = 1.91  

Group 3 (starts at CS 35)  
• Δφ@15 = –  
• Δφ@25 = –  
• Δφ@35 = 0.91  
• Δφ@45 = 0.48  
• Δφ@46 = 0.33  
• Δφ@47 = 0.15  
• Δφ@48 = 0.05  
→ total φ_eff = 1.91  

Key takeaways:  
- Under CTRL CREP RCRE each load group receives its own reference age T₀ and its own sequence of Δφ increments.  
- Although the onset of creep differs (CS 15, 25 or 35), all groups accumulate the same overall creep factor (1.91).  
- Environmental conditions remain constant (RH 80 %, T 20 °C).  
- The table fully defines the temporal partitioning of creep intervals and quantifies the contribution of each stage to the total long‐term creep.  

This level of detail ensures that a retrieval‐augmented system can answer queries about stage‐by‐stage creep developments, group‐specific activation, and total creep factors under the RCRE creep model.

With CTRL CREP STAN this load part depending analysis of creep values is not performed. In every creep step all loadparts are treated with the same delta-phi, analyzed with the T0 value defined in GRP.

In case of real creep via AQB the individual creep values are always calculated in AQB. So they cannot be manipulated via CSM. Then the input CREP...PHI and DEPS...DPHI can not be used. Furthermore AQB calcualtes the values depending on the actual effective member thickness of each beam. CSM makes this only with an average effective member thicknesss within a group.
 Please notice that you can define different degrees of air contact for every edge of a cross section in AQUA to adjust the analysis of the effective member thickness (compare to csm3_composite_beam.dat AQUA...VERT...EXP).
 Also the shinkage values are calculaed in AQB depending on the actual thickness. Only if you input final shrinkage values in CREP...EPS or delta values in DEPS...DEPS. Then CSM would pass the manipulated shrinkage values to AQB. AQB would take these values but then ignoring a possible individual effective member thickness e.g. in haunches.
 So it is better to change material parameter in AQUA to adjust creep and shrinkage. Then both CSM and AQB can use them.
 For concrete you can input more parameter for creep and shrinkage in AQUA MEXT EIGE according EN 1992-1. See example real_creep_creepparameter.dat.
 Often only the final creep or shrinkage value shall be adjusted. Then you can just use the following major parameter:
 - MEXT ... VAL1 = value beta-bc1 = factor on final creep value
 - MEXT ... VAL3 = value beta-cd1 = factor on drying shrinkage
 - MEXT ... VAL5 = value beta-ca1 = factor on chemical shrinkage
 e.g. for 1.2 times creep and 1.4 times shrinkage:
 CONC 1 C 40 ; MEXT 1 TYPE EIGE VAL1 1.20 VAL3 1.40 VAL5 1.40

content:
Prestressed beams and composite cross sections require the analysis of creep and shrinkage via AQB due to the fact that only AQB differentiates the internal stresses of a cross section.
 Beams without prestress or bond can be computed with ASE directly without AQB. Prestressed slabs can be computed as well using CSM+ASE without AQB.

metadata.sections: 2.6.5 Systems Consisting of Beams with AQB

content:
QUAD, BRIC and Truss elements can be computed with ASE directly without AQB. Prestressed slabs can be computed as well using the CSM.
 For QUAD elements the effective member thickness can be entered with CREP...DEFQ. With- out any input for the effective thickness CSM computes an averaged value over all QUAD elements of one group and multiplies this thickness with 1.4 to get the effective member thick- ness.
 For BRIC elements the effective member thickness must be input in CREP...DEFQ for the BRIC groups.

metadata.sections: 2.6.6 Creep and Shrinkage of quad- and bric- and truss elements

content:
Springs, elastic boundaries, quad bedding, FLEX- and HASE- halfspace elements do not have a concrete material number and are treated separate.
 Please notice: in case spring elements represent concrete elements, e.g. an abutment, they should creep as well. Otherwise spurious restraints can occur. E.g. a single span girder is fixed with rotations springs right and left, the restraint moment will increase if only the girder creeps and the springs not. But this is not the case if all is mase of concrete and creeps simultanious. Only in case the springs are really made of steel and do not creep this can be input with CSM GRP PHIF 0.
 Elastic boundaries, quad bedding, FLEX- and HASE- halfspace elements often represent soil. But soil also creates long term deflections what is similar to creep. CSM+ASE can simulate these long term deflections by using a concrete creep behavior also for these elements.
 - Springs have a group number and react on GRP-PHIF. They use the creep curves of a concrete beam or quad in the same group. If this does not exist, ASE uses the creep curves of a reference element - see below.
 - Quad beddings have a group number and react on GRP-PHIF. As the quad-material is used for the quad concrete, the bedding uses a creep curve of a reference element - see below.
 - Elastic boundaries (BOUN) and FLEX elements use the group number for GRP-PHIF and PHIP-PHI only in case of CTRL CREP STAN. In the real creep (RCRE) however GRP-PHIF is taken from group 0, PHIP-PHI can not be used, the creep function of a reference element is used - see below.
 - HASE halfspace elements always use the reference element.
 - Pile element with a bore profile bedding however use the concrete creep value also for the bedding!

In the real creep (RCRE) however GRP-PHIF is taken from group 0, PHIP-PHI can not be used, the creep function of a reference element is used - see below.. - HASE halfspace elements always use the reference element.. - Pile element with a bore profile bedding however use the concrete creep value also for the bedding!.
 If a reference element is needed you best define a dummy concrete element in group 0. That material will then be used for the creep curves of these elements, see example hase3_hase3_variable_surface_level.dat. In case in group 0 no element is found ASE takes the first concrete element (beam or quad).
 In the real creep (RCRE) in GRP 0 PHIF only the input 1 and 0 is allowed for creep YES and NO. Best input GRP-PHIF with the same value for all groups.

Without input, CSM works on 20 degree celsius. Via CS...TEMP for each creep step an in- dividual temperature can be definied. The effective age on first loading in GRP...T0 is always related to 20 degrees!
 In case of a heat treatment we recommend to not calculate the heat treatment in CSM directly but to start with the analysis at the time when the tendons are cut in the factory. So we recommend to not input a higher temperature but to stretch the time in the heat treatment manually and to insert a higher value for T0 (first loading), e.g.
 for a first heat treatment on 2 days with 50 degree (dt-eff=2*3.547 = 7.094d)
 you must input T0=7.1 days.
 The above used factor 3.547 is analyzed using EN 1992-1-1 annex C equation (B.10).
 As the tendon usually also expands due to the heat treatment, the effective prestress is lower according EN 1992-1-1 10.5.2. So in TENDON a prestress reduced by the temperature dif- ference must be input! See example csm3_casting_bed_method.dat comments after PROG CSM.

Whenever two quad groups with different element thickness meet together, the different phi and eps values will result in additional stresses! This schould be considered in the arrangement of the groups or via the manual input of an average effective member thickness. On problem temperature on quad superstructure see also example temp_load_tbeam.dat.
 Weak concrete E modulus of young concrete is already included in the creep values.

With CTRL CAST 1 the following load cases are computed for the means of a comparison:
 Load cases for cast-in-one system (with the last group setting!)

For beam structures a printout of internal forces and stresses for a certain cut is also gen- erated automatically. This tabular AQB output should be checked in any case especially for prestressed structures. The results can be found in the report file (NAME_csm.plb) in chapter ”Considered Section BEAM...”.
 After the tabular AQB output mentioned above, a plot of the overall stresses of all construction stages is generated. These results are stored in AQB with COMB...LCST in the load cases 6000 and following, these results are only stored in the Database for this very beam section.
 You can also enforce a separate Check-Print and Controll-Plot, see ’Check print construction stages for another beam’ in csm31_design.dat.
 If these stresses should be computed and stored for all beam sections CTRL STOR +1 can be input (default for prestressed bridges).
 At the end of the input file CSM can also generate input data for plots of the results. In case of a system consisting of beams, internal forces My, N and displacements are plotted for every construction stage for instance. Please refer to input SCAL.
 A visual check using the animator is essential in any case (setting of a con stant magnitude for all load cases and disabling the load case animation - freeze image v=0). Please mention that you see the total displacement and the total forces in the 4000-loadcases, as you would see it in reality no site!
 The real inner stresses including the inner creep effects are only found in the 7000... loadcases (see check print)!
 There is also a check print in the CSM DESI - see chapter design - check print.

The provided illustration (Figure 2.4) consists of four small, schematic beam‐bending diagrams arranged in a two‐by‐two grid. Each diagram shows a single‐span girder simply supported at its ends (red triangles) and rendered in a uniform light‐blue color against a pale blue background. The purpose of the four panels is to compare the deflected shapes of a straight (“no‐precamber”) girder and a purposely cambered (“with‐precamber”) girder under the same loading sequence, such that in service (at traffic opening) both beams arrive at almost perfectly straight profiles.

Top Row: “Without precamber”  
  • Top‐Left (“system”): A perfectly straight, horizontal girder, divided into equal segments by faint vertical gridlines. At each end sits a red triangular support symbol. No visible curvature is present, indicating the initial, unloaded geometry.  
  • Top‐Right (“deformation g₁ + g₂”): The same beam after self‐weight (g₁), superimposed construction loads (g₂), and time‐dependent creep have acted but without any built‐in camber. The beam now sags into a smooth, downward‐curving arc. Although still discretized into the same gridlines, the geometry clearly shows deflection toward the midpoint. Red support symbols remain at the ends to underline the simple‐span boundary conditions.

Bottom Row: “With precamber”  
  • Bottom‐Left (“formwork”): Here the beam is cast with an initial, upward curvature that is essentially the mirror image of the anticipated service deflection. The illustration is a schematic comparison of two “moving‐spring” contact definitions used in a CSM construction-stage model. Both diagrams live on a pale‐blue field and share a thick horizontal line at the top (representing a rigid beam or rail reference). Below that line, each sketch shows a single spring element (in green zigzag) and its kinematic coupling to a blue vertical reference line (the superstructure or pier head) and, in the left sketch, to a red rigid block (a support or sliding shoe).

1. Left half (“z-spring”):  
   - A green zigzag spring hangs vertically between the red block at bottom and the blue reference line at mid-height.  
   - A red arrow, labeled “springdirection,” points straight upward from the spring, indicating the direction in which the spring force develops (the z-axis).  
   - A blue arrow, labeled “searchdirection,” is drawn collinear with the red arrow, also pointing upward. This shows that the spring’s search direction (the axis along which the program seeks a contact partner) coincides with the mechanical spring direction.  
   - A text label reads:  
     “z–spring :  
      searchdirection = springdirection, L0 = distance”  
     implying that the initial free length L0 is simply the spatial distance between the two attachment points along that common axis.  

2. Right half (“x-spring”):  
   - The same green zigzag spring is attached horizontally to the vertical blue reference line. Its main coil axis runs left–right (the x-axis).  
   - A red arrow labeled “springdirection” points to the right (along the spring’s axis).  
   - A blue arrow labeled “searchdirection” points upward (perpendicular to the spring coil). This indicates that, unlike the vertical spring, the program searches for contact partners in a direction transverse to the spring’s line of action.  
   - The accompanying text reads:  
     “x–spring :  
      searchdirection(blue) = transverse to springdirection(red) → L0 = TRAN”  
     indicating that the initial length parameter L0 is not the straight distance along the spring axis but is set to a special “TRAN” value to denote a transverse search constraint.  

3. Caption:  
   Underneath the two sketches is a brief caption (“2.15: Search direction (blue): on top: main vertical spring, right: longitudinal spring with L0=TRAN”), reiterating that the left image illustrates a vertical (z-axis) spring whose search direction equals its load direction, while the right shows a horizontal (x-axis) spring whose search direction is orthogonal, invoking the TRAN‐type initial length.

Overall, the figure visually contrasts how CSM’s moving springs can be defined either with coincident force and search directions (yielding a simple “distance” initial length) or with a transverse search direction (requiring the special TRAN flag for L0), an essential distinction when modeling contact between rails, beams, or moving elements in staged construction.

The image is a schematic flow-chart titled “Figure 2.16: YOUTUBE video -> https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zoCshbOx5q0.” It visually summarizes how construction-stage load components and variable actions are assembled into design combinations for beam checks (AQB) in SOFiSTiK’s CSM environment.

1. Left-hand side: CSM Construction Stages  
   • Five stacked colored blocks labeled G_1, P, C_1, G_2 and C_2 represent successive construction-stage load groups.  
     – G_1 and G_2 denote dead-load stages on the statically determined system.  
     – P is the initial prestress stage (P₀).  
     – C_1 and C_2 are creep-and-shrinkage stages (C₀ and redistribution C).  
   • A downward arrow feeds these five stages into a blue box labeled “GPC.”  
     – GPC stands for the aggregate container of dead loads (G), prestress (P), and creep (C).  
     – Internally this “GPC” record holds primary and secondary effects (G₀+G, P₀+P, C₀+C) for later combination.

2. Right-hand side: Variable Actions and MAXIMA  
   • Under the heading “Variable actions:” a small SOFiSTiK logo appears at top right.  
   • A table lists action codes (ACT) and their meanings, for use in SLS and ULS:  
     – L_U: uniformly distributed load (UDL) base load (SLS, ULS)  
     – L_T: tandem axle (SLS, ULS)  
     – T: temperature (SLS, ULS)  
     – ZF: true settlement (SLS)  
     – SF: possible settlement (ULS)  
   • Red arrows point from these variable actions toward a box labeled “MAXIMA,” indicating the procedure that extracts peak values of each action type.

3. Central assembly: AQB Beam Design  
   • Two bold arrows—from “GPC” on the left and “MAXIMA” on the right—converge on a central box labeled “AQB Beam Design.”  
     – This signifies that both the stored construction-stage results (dead load, prestress, creep) and the envelope of variable loads are required inputs to the AQB beam design module.  
     – Under Eurocode principles, the primary and secondary parts of prestress (P₀ and P) and creep/shrinkage (C₀ and C) are combined with imposed actions to form design load cases.

4. Bottom: Combination “COMB MAXD”  
   • A horizontal strip at the bottom shows a sample combination command:  
     “COMB MAXD LC1 G LC2 P LC3 C” followed by “LC4 Y_D 1.0.”  
   • Below this line, load-factor values appear:  
     – 1.35 for G (dead loads)  
     – 1.0 for P (prestress)  
     – 1.0 for the variable action group Y_D (ultimate limit state container of variable actions).  
   • Three red rings highlight the identifiers “LC1,” “LC3,” and “Y_D,” emphasizing the load-case numbers selected for maxima extraction and combination.

5. Contextual linkage  
   • The slide ties back to the ability of CSM to compute consistent load-case factors (e.g. EQBE bending-moment targets) and to store primary load histories in GPC.  
   • The video reference suggests a deeper dive into how force-target equations (EQLC/EQBE) and variable-action envelopes are implemented in a step-by-step example file (csm23_cable_stay_optimisation_2.dat).  
   • By aligning the construction-stage store (GPC) with the maxima of live and environmental actions, AQB can generate the required design checks for bending, shear and other limit states.

Overall, the diagram abstracts SOFiSTiK’s process: accumulate staged dead and prestress effects in GPC, identify peak live-load or settlement actions via MAXIMA, and merge them under Eurocode-based factors in the AQB Beam Design module. It underlines the workflow for creating combined load cases (COMB MAXD) and enforcing target bending-moment or deformation criteria in a consistent construction-staging context.

Why AQB: because forces can act on different cross section stages:
 1. Post-tensioned prestress P and structural dead load G_1 act on a partial cross sec- tion with the ungrouted duct and do not create an additional stress change in the tendon (still unbonded). (We assume that while stressing the tendon, the girder lifts from the formwork and simultaneously activates G_1)
 2. Additional dead load G_2 acts on the grouted cross section ( with tendon in bond) and creates a stress change in the tendon. Therefore we should not mix G_1 and G_2 before the design! After a pre-superposition it is not possible to separate those effects!
 3. Moreover in composite sections, the dead load G_1 usually acts on the steel part of the section and the dead load G_2 acts on the composite steel and concrete.
 4. Creep and shrinkage C create internal stress stages that cannot be taken into ac- count in MAXIMA. In a composite section, shrinkage creates tension in the concrete and compression in the steel while the external forces N and MY are zero. In pre- stressed sections the loss of prestress due to creep and shrinkage is only an internal stress state, the external forces N and MY are zero as well (without secondary ef- fects). See also figure dataflow in chapter loadcases.
 5. All the variable load cases, that act on the final section can be pre-superimposed in a MAXIMA container e.g. Y_D (CSM-DESI Eurocode design - see csm31_design.dat).
 Why MAXIMA: because AQB only works on beams:
 1. All other elements like springs, cables or quads and support reactions do not have
 internal section stages and can be superimposed in MAXIMA completely. Quads can directly be designed with the MAXIMA result forces (tendons in quad elements work in a different way than tendons in beam elements).

The image presents a three-dimensional finite‐element rendering of a prestressed concrete slab, discretized into a regular grid of quadrilateral elements. The top surface of the slab is colored in a deep azure blue and shows a uniform mesh pattern of small rectangular panels. The underside of the slab is depicted in a lighter turquoise tone, also subdivided into matching quadrilateral elements. Through the bottom face of selected elements run slender, red‐brown lines representing prestressing tendon ducts. These tendons are shown at a slight angle, sloping from left to right, and penetrate the underside of the slab at regular intervals.  

Superimposed on the image are two black annotation arrows, each pointing to a different element on the underside:  
• The left arrow identifies “element 15 with tendon,” highlighting one of the turquoise underside panels through which a red‐brown tendon duct passes.  
• The right arrow identifies “element 17 without tendon,” marking an adjacent underside panel that lacks any tendon representation.  

Beneath the graphic appears the caption  
   Figure 2.18: Tendons in a prestressed slab  

Key visual features and their significance:  
• Finite‐Element Mesh – Both top and bottom faces are meshed into small quadrilaterals, indicating the slab has been modeled element‐by‐element for structural analysis.  
• Tendon Paths – The red‐brown slanted lines represent the trajectory of prestressing tendons (unbonded or bonded) within the slab. Their angled orientation suggests how prestress forces are introduced into the concrete.  
• Missing Tendon Element – Element 17 is deliberately shown without a tendon path, calling attention to a modeling limitation: the BEMESS design module cannot assign or extract prestress internal forces (NV0, MV0) for elements that lack an explicitly defined tendon.  
• Context of Prestress Effects – In the broader workflow of SOFiSTiK software, prestress can be broken into primary (P₀ or PB) and secondary (P₁ or ZP) components. This image underscores the difficulty of separating those components on an element‐by‐element basis when a tendon is omitted.  

Overall, the figure visually communicates the geometry of tendon placement in a prestressed slab and highlights the challenge of analyzing individual elements (specifically element 17) when prestress tendons are not modeled in every finite element.

 2. ACT P_1 : for post-tensioning with bonded tendons: rsup = 1.10 and rinf = 0.90
 Usage B: Separation of primary and secondary (hyperstatic) effect of prestress (only beam design)
 1. ACT PB : primary effect of prestress
 2. ACT ZP : secondary (hyperstatic) effect of prestress (redistribution)
 Due to the complexity only these literal shall be used!
 The CSM can handle these 2 sets of actions in a beam design and uses them in AQB combi- nations automatically:
 in usage A CSM uses Set P_0 and P_1 CSM writes for AQB e.g. COMB ... LC1 P_0 0.95 LC2 P_1 0.90 see csm3_P_0_P_1.dat -> first PROG CSM -> CTRL PKIN 0.95 V2 0.90 (decompression check)
 in usage B CSM uses Set PB and ZP
 CSM writes for AQB e.g. COMB ... LC1 PB 0.90 LC2 ZP 1.00
 see csm31_design.dat -> last CSM -> DESI FAT PAR3 0.9 PAR4 1.00
 (fatigue check according EN1992-1-1 5.10.9)
 So it is not allowed to mix usage A and B. For manual input it is not allowed to mix P_0 and P_1 with PB and ZP (only beam design).

 Primary and secondary (hyperstatic) effect of prestress : quad design
 The issue is depicted in the image above, highlighting the absence of a tendon in element 17. Module BEMESS, tackles the design of each element individually. Consequently, it faces a limitation in receiving NV0 and MV0 for element 17, even though this element is part of the overall superstructure.
 The only way to separate the internal force components would be to determine the statically determinate components by supporting the superstructure in a statically determinate manner and applying the prestress.
 The moments in all members (including member 17) would then be MV0. The total moment MV=MV0+MV’ is obtained using the normal statically indeterminate type of calculation. The MV’ portion alone could then be obtained by subtracting the MV0 portion from the total MV portion, as explained in the example secondary_effect_of_prestress.dat
 Since this is usually extremely complicated, CSM and BEMESS only use the total MV compo- nent. There is no separation between primary and secondary part in the quad design.

In case settlement or temperature actions are defined in the CSM DESI MAXI run, the induced MAXIMA creates a container Y_8 (combination TEMP_SETZ) that combines the most unfa- vorable forces of settlement and temperature. In the AQB run then in a loop in a time one of these Y_8 loadcases (LC 1841...) is used as permanent part and the stress range is calculated with the fatigue acting FAT loadcases. With DESI FAT PAR1 0 no temperature or settlement loadcases are taken into account.
 If necessary and possible, the reinforcement is increased in the fatigue design. An additional loop performs the check one time for pk-inf and one time for pk-sup.
 As for different span and support locations different axle load factors (1.40 und 1.75) must be applied, three AQB design runs are started: - In a first run with axle load factor 1.40 (span) for all elements the reinforcement fatigue check is done. The used or increased reinforcement is stored in design case 23. The maximum stresses can be plotted in Wingraf under the AQB LCST loadcase storage number. See "Overview result access beam elements in WINGRAF" in the CSM DESI report.
 - With the possible increased reinforcement then the concrete check with axle load factor 1.0 is done. The results of this run can be plotted in Wingraf under the AQB LCST loadcase storage number. This block runs after the span run with factor 1.40 to use the may be increased reinforcement!
 - Finally the design for support regions is done with axle load factor 1.75 for all elements. The used or increased reinforcement is stored in design case 25. The user then has to decide manually, if a beam must be assigned to span or support region and if for this beam either design case 23 or 25 is relevant.
 Generally the used or increased reinforcement is always stored in a new design case. This is also done in case no reinforcement is increased e.g. in a stress check. That allows the user to check the reinforcement that has really been used for this design.
