The input is made in the CADINP language (see general manual SOFiSTiK: ’FEA / STRUC- TURAL Installation and Basics’).
 Three categories of units are distinguished:
 mm Fixed unit. Input is always required in the specified unit.
 [mm] Explicit unit. Input defaults to the specified unit. Alternatively, an explicit as- signment of a related unit is possible (eg. 2.5[m] ).
 [mm]1011 Implicit unit. Implicit units are categorised semantically and denoted by a cor- responding identity number (shown in green). Valid categories referring to the unit ”length” are, for example, geodetic elevation, section length and thickness. The default unit for each category is defined by the currently active (design code specific) unit set. This input default can be overridden as described above. The specified unit in square brackets corresponds to the default for unit set 5 (Eu- rocodes, NORM UNIT 5).

The table you provided is the master list of “CTRL” (control) parameters for CSM‐based construction‐stage, creep‐shrinkage and prestress analyses in SOFiSTiK.  Each row of the table defines:

• The keyword (Item) that you place in your CSM input  
• A concise Description of what that keyword controls  
• Any allowable Options (OPT) or flags  
• The precise syntax for the control statement  
• Default values or behaviors if you omit the control  

Below is a structured walkthrough of each major parameter block, with its purpose, options and defaults.

1.  DL  – Dead‐Load Activation  
    • AUTO = automatic dead‐load activation at each stage  
    • NO or 0 = do not apply self‐weight automatically (you must load it explicitly)  
    • Default: AUTO  

2.  BEAM  – Creep+Shrink Philosophy for Beam Elements  
    • AQB = use AQB (classic) creep+shrink module  
    • DSLN = use Design Structural Lines  
    • ASE = compute creep+shrink inside ASE (affects T‐beam stiffness)  
    • TBEA = SOFiSTiK T‐beam philosophy (embedded beams in slabs)  
    • Default: system‐dependent (usually AQB for simple tasks, ASE or TBEA for composite/t‐beam)  

3.  GPCS  – GPC‐Load Separation for Construction Stages  
    • 1 = separate G and PC loads per stage (removing temporary supports produces its own load part)  
    • 0 = treat “removal of temporary support” as G‐load only (no extra stage)  
    • Default: 0  

4.  CREP  – Creep Representation  
    • STAN = standard creep (single load‐part, fixed creep coefficient)  
    • RCRE = “real” creep (creep coefficients computed per load part)  
    • Optionally define EIGE model variant (EN10, MC90, MC10 or SUM)  
    • Default: STAN  

5.  EIGE  – Analysis of Creep Values  
    • Varies by material: EN10, MC90, MC10, SUM (see AQB manual under CTRL EIGE)  
    • SAFE V2 / V3 = safety levels for creep application  
    • Default: per material prescription  

6.  RELZ  – Tendon Relaxation  
    • AUTO = automatic relaxation calculation  
    • NO or 0 = no relaxation considered  
    • Default: AUTO  

7.  CANT  – Adding New Prefabricated Elements (Cantilever Erection)  
    Code determines how the new element is positioned and matched to existing geometry:  
    • 0 = place at system coordinates  
    • 1 = original inclination, but moved into extension  
    • 2 = tangential (free‐cantilever) erection  
    • 3/4 = block‐insertion with pre‐deformation to match joint (only on individual CS…CANT stages)  
    • 5,6,7 = like 1–3 but lock XY position  
    • 8 = internal for nonlinear precamber (not user‐set)  
    • 11/12 = element‐by‐element (node‐by‐node) insertion for in‐situ slabs  
    • 21/22 = as 11/12 but ignore couplings  
    • Note: CANT 3/4 must be set per‐stage, not as a global default  

8.  DESI / BEMESS  – Design / Verification Controls  
    – MAXI (Superposition per EN 1990):  
      • 0 = use Table A2.4(B) variant 6.10ab (Norway/Sweden/Finland/Denmark)  
      • 1 = same table for all other countries  
      • 2 = variant with country‐specific partial factors (GAMF)  
      • V2 = also create non‐frequent combinations  
      • V3 = exact handling of nonlinear temperature effects (V3 1 ignores temperature as controlling action)  
      • RSET =0 skip superposition of RSET load parts (default RSET=1)  

    – PKIN / PKSU (Prestress Inputs):  
      • CTRL PKIN 0.95 = set Pk,nƒ for tendons (immediate bond)  
      • CTRL PKSU = override Pk,sp (secondary prestress)  
      • Default: PKIN=0.90, PKSU=1.05·PKIN  

    – STOR (Storage Options – bit‐coded):  
      +1 store all AQB‐LCST results (up to 7 000 loadcases)  
      +2 store ASE group settings (e.g. for eigenfrequency studies)  
      +4 write per‐combination _desi.dat files (MAXIMA runs)  
      +8 use generated _csmlf.dat load‐case list  
      +64 retain old loadcases (do not delete unused stage data)  
      • V2=0 skip primary/secondary prestress storage  
      • V3=skip full 7 000 stress storage (see csm5_free_cantilever.dat)  

    – LCEQ = load‐case number for equation solver (default 1)  
    – ADDF =1 add optimization factor to last one (default 0)  

9.  CTRL EMOD  – Concrete‐Stiffness Development  
    • Uses CEB‐FIP 1990 temperature‐adjusted age T₁, writes to ASE GRP.  
    • ASE then applies code‐specified stiffness growth, and can plot stiffness‐age curves.  

10.  CTRL B_G1  – Save Construction Stages as Type G_1  
    • YES (default) = treat all B‐stages as G_1 for superposition (avoids MAXIMA conflicts)  
    • NO = keep type B  

11.  CTRL GAMC  – Support‐Moment Factor for Creep Redistribution  
    • Sets secondary creep factor GAMU (ULS factor, default 1.35 or 1.40 BS)  
    • V2 allows input of GAMF (secondary creep ratio, e.g. 0.95)  
    • Use this to limit or amplify dead‐load moment redistribution due to creep/shrinkage  

12.  CTRL PROB NONL  – Nonlinear Analysis Iterations  
    • V2 nnn = set number of iterations (e.g. V2 120 for 120 loops)  

13.  PROG CSM ctrl ase text …  – Dynamic ASE‐CTRL over Construction Stages  
    • Insert arbitrary ASE control lines based on the stage counter #cs_csm  
    • Example:  
        PROG CSM  
          ctrl ase text ’if xxx_cs_csm<25 ; CTRL CONC V4 0.80 ; endif’  
    • Allows you to vary, for example, tensile strength or other ASE‐CTRL options stage by stage.  

Every parameter above can be mixed and matched in your CSM input deck.  Where an option is not set, the default behavior (listed) will apply.  See the example data files referenced (e.g. csm36_gpc_separated.dat, csm7_cant_3.dat, csm37_composite_nonlin_temp.dat, etc.) and the AQB/ASE manuals for full worked examples.

The table below summarizes the user‐selectable CSM control keywords (the “Item” column), a brief description of what each keyword does, its input unit or format, and the default value applied when the keyword is omitted. These directives are used to steer how SOFiSTiK’s Construction Stage Manager (CSM) writes commands for the underlying ASE (structural analysis) and AQB (prestress/creep) modules.

1. CAST  
   • Description: “Cast‐in‐one” load‐case generation.  
     – 1: generate cast-in-one load cases.  
     – 0: suppress them to reduce output volume.  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: 0  

2. PROB  
   • Description: Selects the ASE solver type.  
     – LINE: linear analysis (default).  
     – NONL: material nonlinearity.  
     – TH3: geometric nonlinearity.  
     – TH3B, NONB: ASE variants without TH2.  
     – V2: specify iteration count.  
     – V3: convergence tolerance (TOL).  
     – V4: FMAX parameter.  
     (Example: “CTRL PROB TH3 V2 120 V3 –0.5 $ kN”)  
   • Unit: literal (LIT)  
   • Default: LINE  

3. NMAT  
   • Description: Activate ASE’s material‐update routine (SYST NMAT).  
     – YES or NO.  
   • Unit: literal (LIT)  
   • Default: NO  

4. ASE  
   • Description: Pass arbitrary text lines directly into ASE input.  
     (E.g. “CTRL ASE TEXT ‘CTRL ITER 3’”)  
   • Unit: text  
   • Default: –  

5. ASE2  
   • Description: Additional free text inserted after ASE-GRP header.  
   • Unit: text  
   • Default: –  

6. AQB  
   • Description: Pass arbitrary text lines to the prestress/creep module AQB.  
   • Unit: text  
   • Default: –  

7. BEME  
   • Description: Pass control text to the BEMESS design module.  
   • Unit: text  
   • Default: –  

8. FILE  
   • Description: Specify output file name for the generated CSM input.  
   • Unit: text  
   • Default: –  

9. HEAD  
   • Description: Custom header line(s) for ASE+AQB input files.  
   • Unit: text  
   • Default: –  

10. EMOD  
    • Description: Time‐dependent stiffness of concrete elements.  
      – AUTO: apply age‐adjusted E-modulus (default).  
      – 0 or NO: switch off time dependence.  
    • Unit: literal (LIT)  
    • Default: AUTO  

11. SVRF  
    • Description: Enables reinforcement effects in creep and shrinkage calculations per AQB’s CTRL SVRF record.  
    • Unit: none  
    • Default: 1.0  

12. B_G1  
    • Description: Treat B‐type construction stages as G_1 type for load‐case superposition (avoids MAXIMA conflicts).  
    • Unit: literal (LIT4)  
    • Default: YES  

13. GAMC  
    • Description: Factor applied to the “parasitic” (statically indeterminate) part of creep and shrinkage in ultimate‐limit‐state design.  
    • V2: secondary creep factor (GAMF) may also be specified.  
    • Unit: none  
    • Default: 1.35 (1.40 for British Standard)  

14. PLC  
    • Description: Initial load‐case index for the first construction‐stage load case.  
    • Unit: none  
    • Default: 0  

15. LCRI  
    • Description: Reinforcement distribution identifier for CSM‐generated ASE groups.  
    • Unit: none  
    • Default: –  

These CSM controls give the user fine‐grained command over how construction stages are modeled, how nonlinearity and prestress effects are handled, and what output files and load‐case formats are generated for subsequent ASE/AQB runs.

The input table is a catalog of CSM-DESI (“Construction Stage Method – Design”) control parameters for SOFiSTiK’s CSM–AQB–ASE workflow. It is structured into five logical columns (Item, Description, Control Option, Permissible Values, Default) and groups together all the low-level switches that govern creep & shrinkage, prestress losses, load superposition, construction stage releases, element insertion, storage options, nonlinear solution settings and ASE‐side overrides. Below is a row-by-row breakdown.

1. BEAM  
   • Description: Selects how creep & shrinkage (C+S) are treated in composite slab systems with embedded beams.  
   • Options:  
     – AQB: C+S computed in AQB  
     – DSLN: “with Design Structural Lines”  
     – ASE: C+S computed in ASE  
     – TBEA: T-beam philosophy (cross‐sectional prestress losses in AQB; curvature in ASE)  
   • Default: system‐dependent  

2. GPCS  
   • Description: Separates Gpc (permanent) loads during construction stages.  
   • Values:  
     – 1: treat temporary‐support removal as separate G part  
     – 0: do not separate (all dead‐load parts lumped)  
   • Default: 0  

3. CREP  
   • Description: Creep‐load partitioning.  
   • Options:  
     – STAN: standard creep (no separate load part)  
     – RCRE: real creep (each load part treated individually)  
   • EIGE Analysis Modes (EN10, MC90, MC10 or SUM) via CTRL EIGE  
   • Default: material‐dependent  

4. CTRL EIGE  
   • Description: chooses EIGE creep‐analysis mode for AQB.  
   • Versions: V2, SAFE, V3  
   • Values: 0…3 (per AQB manual)  

5. RELZ  
   • Description: tendon‐relaxation activation.  
   • Values:  
     – AUTO: automatic relaxation  
     – NO / 0: no relaxation  
   • Default: NO  

6. CANT  
   • Description: rules for adding new elements in construction‐stage sequence.  
   • Values:  
     – 0: system‐position  
     – 1: original inclination  
     – 2: tangential erection  
     – 3/4: free-cantilever pre-deformation (block)  
     – 5–7: same as 1–3 but retain XY position  
     – 8: internal precamber (nonlinear)  
     – 11/12: node-by-node insertion  
   • Default: 0  

7. CTRL MAXI  
   • Description: load superposition for limit‐state combinations.  
   • Values:  
     – 0: per EN 1990 table A2.4(B)  
     – 1: same for other countries  
     – 2: Norway variant with FAKF/GAMF  
   • V2: ALL (include non-frequent COMBs)  
   • V3:  
     – 1: exclude temperature as controlling action  
     – 2: exact treatment of nonlinear temperature  
     – 3: prepare ULS superposition  
   • Default: 0  

8. RSET  
   • Description: superposition of prestress load sets.  
   • Values: 0 = no superposition, 1 = yes  
   • Default: 1  

9. PKIN / PKSU  
   • Description: input characteristic prestress levels for bonded tendons.  
   • PKIN: Pk,n ƒ for general prestress (default 0.90; V2 allows P_1)  
   • PKSU: Pk,sp for supplementary prestress (auto‐set from PKIN unless overridden)  

10. STOR  
   • Description: bitmask to control result storage.  
   • Bits:  
     +1 = store all AQB‐LCST stresses (up to 7000 load cases)  
     +2 = store ASE group (DYNA) settings  
     +4 = write individual MAXIMA runs (_desi.dat)  
     +8 = use generated _csmlf.dat AQB loadcase list  
     +64 = preserve old unused loadcases  
   • V2: suppress primary/secondary prestress effects  
   • V3: selective stress storage  

11. LCEQ  
   • Description: load‐case number for linear equation solution.  
   • Range: 1…1999  
   • Default: 1  

12. ADDF  
   • Description: add optimization factor to previous factor (ADDF = 1 to activate)  

13. CTRL EMOD  
   • Description: development of stiffness of concrete elements.  
   • CSM computes temperature‐adjusted concrete age T1 (CEB-FIP 1990), passed to ASE for graphical plotting and stiffness evolution  

14. CTRL B_G1  
   • Description: tag construction‐stage loadcases as type G_1 for superposition.  
   • Values: YES (default), NO  

15. CTRL GAMC  
   • Description: factor for support moments induced by creep at stage closures.  
   • V1 (single factor) or V2 (GAMU = dead‐load factor, GAMF = secondary creep factor).  
   • Default GAMU = 1.35 (1.40 BS), GAMF = 1.00.  

16. CTRL PROB NONL  
   • Description: nonlinear analysis iteration limit.  
   • V2: number of iterations (e.g. 120)  

17. Change of ASE CTRL values  
   • Via PROG CSM ctrl ase text: inject arbitrary CTRL lines into ASE input, using the variable #cs_csm to branch by stage number  

All of these commands must appear before any loadcase definitions in the CSM input file. Together they allow fine-grained control over construction-stage sequencing, prestress loss models, creep/shrinkage activation, superposition rules, nonlinear solution parameters and ASE‐side parameter overrides.

The table is a catalogue of “CTRL” options used by the SOFiSTiK Construction-Stage Method (CSM) together with ASE (Analysis & Structural Engineering) and AQB (pre- and post-processor for prestress, creep & shrinkage).  It defines every switch, flag and parameter you can feed into a CSM sequence.  Below is a structured, detailed description of the main entries, grouped by functional category.  Wherever relevant, unit, default value and an illustrative example or reference file are given.

1. Dead-Load Activation  
   • Code:   DL  
   • Description:  Automatic (“AUTO”) or manual (“NO” or 0) insertion of self-weight into the load cases.  
   • Default: AUTO  
   • Example:   DL NO to suppress dead load in the first run.

2. Beam Design Philosophy  
   • Code:   BEAM  
   • Options:  
     – AQB   – concrete + steel design via AQB  
     – DSLN  – “with” Design Structural Lines  
     – ASE   – C+S design inside ASE  
     – TBEA  – SOFiSTiK T-beam philosophy (cross-sectional losses handled by AQB, creep curvature by ASE)  
   • Default: depends on system  
   • Note:  T-beam mode requires CTRL CANT settings for composite slabs.

3. General Primary & Construction-Stage Loads  
   • Code:   GPCS  
   • Options:  
     – 1 = separate GPC (permanent) loads by stage (temporary supports removed as G-parts)  
     – 0 = do not separate; treat removal stages as G only  
   • Default: 1  
   • Example File:  csm36_gpc_separated.dat

4. Creep Representation  
   • Code:   CREP  
   • Options:  
     – STAN = standard creep (no separate part)  
     – RCRE = real creep, computed per load‐part  
   • Default: STAN  

5. Creep Analysis Standard  
   • Code:   EIGE  
   • Options: EN10, MC90, MC10 or SUM (see AQB manual)  
   • Versioning:   CTRL EIGE V2 or SAFE V3 exist to refine/enforce checks  
   • Default: based on material class  

6. Tendon Relaxation  
   • Code:   RELZ  
   • Options:  
     – AUTO = let AQB compute relaxation automatically  
     – NO or 0 = ignore relaxation losses  
   • Default: AUTO  

7. Cantilever Element Insertion  
   • Code:   CANT  
   • Options (values 0–12):  
     – 0 = place new element in system (as if in global coordinates)  
     – 1 = original inclination & position  
     – 2 = tangential (free-cantilever) erection  
     – 3,4 = special block-fit modes (pre-deform/cap insertion; see csm7_cant_3.dat)  
     – 5–7 = like 1–3 but XY‐position retained  
     – 8 = internal for nonlinear precamber  
     – 11,12 = node‐by‐node insertion (better for in-situ slabs)  
   • Default: 0  

8. Time‐Step / Creep Time‐Integration  
   • Code:   LT  
   • Options:  
     – AUTO = automatic time stepping  
     – RCRE = uses real creep part (–)  
   • Default: AUTO  

9. Ultimate Limit State & Combination Settings  
   • Code:   DESI (BEMESS)  
   • Sub-code: MAXI = superposition variant (EN 1990 Table A2.4)  
     – 0/1 = standard EN1990 superposition  
     – 2 = as 1 but include unfavorable factor FAKF/GAMF for creep maxima  
   • CTRL MAXI V2,V3 refine nonlinear‐temp handling and ULS vs. SLS preparation  
   • RSET =0/1 to disable/enable superposition of RSET groups  
   • Example: csm37_composite_nonlin_temp.dat  

10. Prestress Input  
    • Codes: PKIN, PKSU  
    • PKIN = factor Pk,nƒ for tendon pre-stress (default 0.90 for later grouting, 0.95 for immediate bond)  
    • With CTRL PKIN V2 you may define P_1 separately  
    • PKSU = input Pk,sp for secondary losses if special usage required  

11. Results Storage Flags  
    • Code:   STOR  
    • Bitwise options:  
      +1 = store AQB-LCST (all 7000 stress cases)  
      +2 = store ASE group settings (e.g. for DYNA eigenfrequencies)  
      +4 = output individual MAXIMA runs (_desi.dat)  
      +8 = use custom _csmlf.dat load-case list  
      +64= keep old load cases (do not delete by default)  
    • CTRL STOR V2,V3 allow finer control over which stress sets to keep  
    • Example: see csm5_free_cantilever.dat  

12. Equation Run Load-Case Number  
    • Code:   LCEQ  
    • Description: select which load case (LC) number triggers a special equation‐run.  
    • Default: 1  
    • Max Value: 1999  
    • Example: csm37_composite_nonlin_temp.dat sets LCEQ = 1999  

13. Additional Optimization Factor  
    • Code:   ADDF  
    • Description: adds an extra optimization factor to the last defined factor set  
    • Options: 0 or 1  
    • Default: 0  

14. Concrete Modulus Development  
    • Code:   CTRL EMOD  
    • Description: calculates temperature-adjusted concrete age (T1) per CEB-FIP 1990, passes it to ASE for stiffness evolution plots.  

15. Stage-Type Assignment  
    • Code:   CTRL B_G1  
    • Options: YES/NO  
    • Description: stores “B” (construction) stages as group type G_1 (YES, default) or leaves them as B (NO). Avoids later MAXIMA conflicts.  

16. Creep Redistribution Factor  
    • Code:   CTRL GAMC (and GAMU, GAMF via V2)  
    • Description: sets factor for support moments induced by creep/shrinkage in indeterminate beams.  
    • Defaults: GAMU = 1.35 (1.40 for BS), GAMF = 1.00  
    • Example: CTRL GAMC 1.25 0.95 overrides for secondary creep factor = 0.95. Must be given in first CSM run.  

17. Nonlinear Iteration Control  
    • Code:   CTRL PROB NONL  
    • V2: specify max iterations (e.g. V2 120 for 120 passes)  
    • See csm34_stage_design.dat for usage in CS-stage design.  

18. Dynamic Updates of ASE Controls in a CSM Sequence  
    • Method: use PROG CSM ctrl ase text ‘…’ blocks, referencing the auto-incremented variable #cs_csm.  
    • Example:  
         PROG CSM  
           ctrl ase text ’CTRL CONC V4 2.50’  
           ctrl ase text ’if xxx_cs_csm<25; CTRL CONC V4 0.80; endif’  
      → applies tensile‐strength V4=2.50 in stages 1–24, then V4=0.80 thereafter.  

This structured outline should allow a Retrieval-Augmented-Generation (RAG) system to index and retrieve any specific parameter, its possible values, defaults and examples, enabling automated snippet generation or direct lookup in documentation.

The screenshot shows part of a four-column “CTRL” input table used by the CSM/ASE interface.  Each row in the table defines one input parameter (or a sub-parameter) that can be passed via a “CTRL” command.  The columns are:

• Item  
  – The name of the control parameter or a placeholder (e.g. VAL, V2, V3, V4, TEXT).  
• Description  
  – A human-readable explanation of what the parameter does and any sub-values or switches it accepts.  
• Unit  
  – The expected unit or data‐type for the field (often “–” if it’s a pure option, “LIT” if it’s a literal text string).  
• Default  
  – The default value used if this parameter is omitted.

Below is a row-by-row breakdown of what appears in the screenshot:

1. TEST  
   • Description:  
     – Restricts the CSM run to a subset of construction stages (“calculate only stage from-to”).  
     – Usage: CTRL TEST VAL V2 [V3]  
       • VAL = starting stage index  
       • V2 = ending stage index  
       • V3 = include creep‐step subdivisions? (1=yes, 0=no)  
     – Additional switches:  
       • CTRL TEST ANI  
         • Performs a “dry run” of the construction sequence—load cases are generated with group metadata but no numerical results.  
       • CTRL TEST STEP  
         • If the sequence suffers numerical instability, this option adds a dynamic stiffness term and applies damping to test deformations.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: –  

2. VAL  
   • Description: “Value of the option”  
     – In the context of TEST, this is the “from” stage index.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: –  

3. V2  
   • Description: “Possible 2nd value of the option”  
     – For TEST, this is the “to” stage index.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: –  

4. V3  
   • Description: “Possible 3rd value of the option”  
     – For TEST, toggles creep‐step subdivision (1 or 0).  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: –  

5. V4  
   • Description: “Possible 4th value of the option”  
     – Reserved for future expansions or additional switches.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: –  

6. TEXT  
   • Description:  
     – A literal text string (up to 64 characters) that is passed verbatim after “CTRL ASE,” or “CTRL ASE,ASE”.  
     – Used to send arbitrary ASE control commands within a CSM sequence.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: –  

Notes on usage pattern:  
• All of these appear as keywords following a “CTRL” directive in the CSM input file.  
• The absence of a “Default” entry means the option is simply not activated unless explicitly provided.  
• Unit “–” indicates the parameter is not numerical in a physical‐unit sense but rather a pure logical/integer switch.  

In practice, you might write in your CSM deck:  
   CTRL TEST 10 120 1  
to run only stages 10 through 120 and include creep subdivisions, or  
   CTRL TEST ANI  
to perform the sequence check without full analysis.

The image is a five‐panel technical illustration, shown in planar view, that demonstrates three different “CANT” methods for inserting the final cap or cantilever segment of a curved precast beam. All panels depict the same overall bridge or beam geometry—a gently arcing line of contiguous finite‐element beam segments—color‐mapped from green (low bending moment or stress) through yellow to red (high bending moment or stress). Small red triangular icons mark existing supports or bearings at key nodes.  

Panel 1 (top) is captioned “situation before insertion of last segment.” It shows a continuous, slightly curved beam spanning two supports: one at the left end, one just left of midspan. The beam is discretized into rectangular elements. The right end is truncated, leaving a visible gap to the next, yet‐to‐be‐inserted segment. The color map is mostly green with a yellow‐orange region near mid‐span, indicating the highest bending moment in the existing structure.  

Panel 2, directly below, is labeled “insertion with CANT 1.” Here a straight new beam block has been dropped into the gap at the right end in its original, unbent orientation. The newly inserted segment aligns only approximately with the curvature; the joints on the left and right of the newly placed block remain offset. The overall color pattern is unchanged except for the fresh elements, which also display a stress gradient.  

Panel 3, captioned “bending last segment before insertion on CANT 3,” returns to the single‐block element shown in isolation at the right end. Red curved arrows highlight the process of applying a pre-bend or deformation to that piece. The illustration shows the beam segment deflecting upward and rotated slightly so its end nodes match the curved profile of the existing structure.  

Panel 4, labeled “insertion of bended segment with CANT 3,” presents the same sequence as panel 1–2 but now with the previously bent block placed into the gap. Because it was pre-deformed, it fits seamlessly into the curved geometry, and the color contours show a smooth continuation of the stress distribution across the joint. Red arrows at the insertion point emphasize the matching of curvature.  

Panel 5 (bottom) is titled “insertion with CANT 4.” In this scenario, the last cap segment is adjusted on both sides: two red curved arrows indicate bending at each end of the new block, and the piece is then inserted in a single operation that simultaneously aligns both ends to the existing grid. The discretized beam chain is now fully continuous, and the color map shows a uniform gradient across all elements.  

Beneath the panels is the caption “Figure 3.1: Insertion of last cap segment: CANT 1‐3‐4.” The figure visually contrasts three erection philosophies for precast curved beams: CANT 1 (straight placement), CANT 3 (pre-bend single block), and CANT 4 (dual-end adjustment), illustrating how each affects geometry and stress continuity at the joint.

The input table defines the parameters of the LAUN command used in the CSM incremental-launching procedure. It has four columns—Item, Description, Unit, Default—and lists ten parameters that control which elements move, how they move, and whether they rotate or launch from one or both ends. Below is a detailed breakdown of each column and parameter:

1. Columns  
   • Item: Name of the parameter as it appears on the LAUN command line.  
   • Description: What the parameter controls or how it is used.  
   • Unit: The physical unit expected (if any). Units appear in square brackets; “[–]” signifies a dimensionless quantity, while “—” means no unit applies.  
   • Default: The value assumed if you omit the parameter.

2. Parameters

   • GRP  
     – Description: Specifies the group number whose elements are to be displaced or launched.  
     – Unit: none.  
     – Default: none (mandatory).

   • DX, DY, DZ  
     – Description: Components of the launch direction expressed as a unit vector. Before launching, you must normalize (DX, DY, DZ) so its magnitude equals 1.0.  
     – Unit: none.  
     – Default: none (mandatory together).

   • XM, YM, ZM  
     – Description: Coordinates of the centre of rotation for circular launches (only used when PHI=1). XM/YM/ZM define the global axis about which the group rotates in the XY-plane.  
     – Unit: meters [m] (unit code 1001).  
     – Default: none (required if circular rotation is used).

   • NR1, NR2  
     – Description: Reference node numbers defining a free axis for rotation. If you supply PHI=1 (circular launch), the line through nodes NR1→NR2 becomes the rotation axis.  
     – Unit: none.  
     – Default: none.

   • PHI  
     – Description: Set PHI = 1 to enable rotation instead of linear translation. When activated, the subsequent CS-LAUN value is interpreted in radians.  
     – Unit: dimensionless [–] (unit code 3).  
     – Default: 0 (linear displacement mode unless overridden).

   • NO_L  
     – Description: Chooses which side(s) perform the launch.  
       1: Launch elements from one side only  
       2: Launch elements from the opposite side  
     – Unit: none.  
     – Default: 1.

3. Usage Notes and Context  
   – After defining a launch direction with DX, DY, DZ, the actual travel distance per construction stage is set via the CS LAUN command, where you specify a distance in meters.  
   – For pure circular launching in the XY-plane, set PHI = 1 and supply centre coordinates (XM, YM).  
   – To run two concurrent, opposite-side launches, invoke LAUN twice with NO_L=1 and NO_L=2. Then define separate CS LAUN distances for each run (CS LAUN and CS LAU2).  
   – If you omit GRP, LAUN still computes the current distance internally and writes it into the CADIMP variable #laun_csm. You can then reference that in an ASE-TEXT or similar control command.  
   – Full theoretical background, examples, and advanced instructions are in the CSM manual section “Theoretical background – Incremental Launching Training” and in sample dat files (e.g. csm48_spiral_ani.dat).

The input table defines a small catalog of worked examples for the LAUN (launching) command in the context of incremental launching analysis (CSM). It maps a human‐readable description of each example (“Examples to LAUN:”) directly to the name of the corresponding input data file (“Input file”). Below is a breakdown of its structure, contents and naming conventions:

1. Table Structure  
   • Two columns  
     – Column 1 (Examples to LAUN:)  
       • A concise, descriptive title for each launching example or scenario.  
       • Rows are sorted by their example index (41 through 47), plus one “Introduction ASE launching” that uses a different prefix.  
     – Column 2 (Input file)  
       • The filename of the .dat file that implements that example in the CSM software.  
       • All standard CSM examples use the prefix “csm” followed by a two-digit example number and a short descriptor, then “.dat.” One uses “movs_” as a prefix.  

2. Entries (Rows)  
   1. Introduction launching  
      – csm41_launching_principle.dat  
      – A basic primer demonstrating the principal use of LAUN.  
   2. Big example  
      – csm42_incremental_launching.dat  
      – A more involved case covering a full incremental launch sequence.  
   3. Circle supports lauched  
      – csm43_incremental_launching_circle.dat  
      – Circular launching in the XY plane with support definition.  
   4. Circle superstructure lauched  
      – csm44_incremental_launching_circle_2.dat  
      – A second variation of circular launching, now including superstructure elements.  
   5. Launching precambered beam  
      – csm45_launching_precamber.dat  
      – Illustrates how to combine LAUN with precamber definitions.  
   6. Nonlinear contact  
      – csm46_launching_nose_nonlinear.dat  
      – Demonstrates a non-linear contact model at the launching nose.  
   7. Nonlinear test  
      – csm47_nonlinear_test.dat  
      – A general nonlinear material/contact test case.  
   8. Introduction ASE launching  
      – movs_incremental_launching_principle.dat  
      – ASE version of the introductory launching example, showing how to control animations/movements.  
   9. -> Example overviews  
      – -> Summary of example overviews  
      – A pointer to a consolidated summary page listing all examples.  

3. Naming Patterns & Conventions  
   • Prefix “csmXX_”  
     – “csm” denotes CSM (Incremental Launching) module examples.  
     – “XX” is the two-digit example number, which aligns with sections in the CSM manual’s training and theoretical background.  
   • Prefix “movs_”  
     – Used for ASE (Animation & SEquence) specific example to distinguish from pure CSM.  
   • Descriptor text  
     – SNAKE_CASE style with keywords for quick retrieval (“incremental_launching,” “circle,” “nonlinear,” “precamber,” etc.).  
   • Extension “.dat”  
     – Standard input file format for the solver.

4. Relationships & Usage  
   • Each descriptive title can serve as a query key in a vector database, returning the exact filename needed to reproduce or inspect that scenario.  
   • Filenames embed both the example number (for ordering) and the technical focus (for semantic search).  
   • The final row’s “Summary of example overviews” provides a high-level entry point when a user wants to browse all available LAUN examples.

5. Integration with RAG Workflow  
   • Metadata fields for ingestion:  
     – example_id (integer 41–47 plus “ASE”),

The input table defines the schema for one record of a “construction stage” (CSM) in a prestressed‐concrete analysis model.  Every row (field) in the table corresponds to one input parameter.  The four columns are:

• Item: the keyword used in the input file.  
• Description: an English label plus extended notes.  
• Unit: the measurement unit or data type.  
• Default: the value assumed when the field is omitted.

Below is a detailed walkthrough of each field:

1. NO  
   – Construction stage number (integer from 1 to 9 998).  
   – You may use offsets relative to the current stage:  
     • ACT1 = current stage + 1, …, ACT9 = current + 9.  
   – Unit: “—/LIT” (literal integer).  
   – Default: required (no default).

2. TYPE  
   – Type of stage, entered as a literal string (LIT).  
   – Common codes (see “Theoretical background – Numeration”):  
     • G_1 or D_1 (new concrete placement, dead‐load activation)  
     • C, C_1, C_2, CR_1…CR_4 (creep steps; AASHTO uses CR; NCRE splits long durations)  
     • P, P_0…P_4 or PS_0…PS_4 (prestress stages, immediate vs. post‐bond)  
     • SL (short‐term live load without creep)  
     • ZC (creep‐active live load only for creep/shrinkage calculation)  
     • B (temporary support or load change)  
     • R, R_1… (earth pressure, treated as variable action unless forced to G_3/G_4)  
   – Default: “B” (temporary load or support change).

3. T  
   – Effective duration of the period, in days.  
   – Used for creep/shrinkage computation.  
   – Unit: days.  
   – Default: 0.0

4. RH  
   – Relative humidity in percent.  
   – Typical presets:  
     • ARID = 30% (dry)  
     • INTE = 50% (interior)  
     • TEMP = 70% (moderate)  
     • TROP = 90% (tropical)  
   – Unit: %.  
   – Default: 80

5. TEMP  
   – Concrete temperature during the stage.  
   – Influences creep and shrinkage rates.  
   – Unit: degrees (°C).  
   – Default: 20

6. NCRE  
   – Number of subdivisions for a long creep period, to limit strain increments.  
   – Unit: dimensionless.  
   – Default: 1

7. PROB  
   – Controls whether this stage is solved by linear analysis (“LINE”) or uses any globally set non‐linear settings (ASE – SYST PROB).  
   – Unit: literal.  
   – Default: “–” (inherits global setting).

8. LAUN  
   – Launching distance for this stage on the first girder line (LAUN NO_L 1).  
   – Unit: meters.  
   – Default: not set.

9. LAU2  
   – Same as LAUN but for the second girder line (LAUN NO_L 2).  
   – Unit: meters.  
   – Default: not set.

10. FACV  
   – “Start deformation”: overrides all prior deformations at stage start.  
   – Used, for example, to model a perfectly horizontal launching bed (CS…FACV 0).  
   – Unit: dimensionless flag.  
   – Default: not set.

11. CANT  
   – Temporary cantilever or support setting for this stage (CSM CTRL).  
   – Can be used to ignore displacements/deformations of supports.  
   – Unit: dimensionless.  
   – Default: not set.

12. ICS1  
   – Marks this stage as the prestress stage for a partial prestress defined later (FACP).  
   – Unit: literal flag.  
   – Default: NO

13. FACP  
   – Magnitude of the partial prestress to be applied at ICS1.  
   – For details see the example “csm31_partial_prestress.dat.”  
   – Unit: none.  
   – Default: not set.

14. TITL  
   – Free‐text title (up to 24 characters) for identifying the stage in reports.  
   – Unit: LIT24 (string).  
   – Default: not set.

Notes / Cross‐References  
– Every “TYPE ZC” stage must align with a corresponding LC…TYPE ZC load case, since ZC loads are only used in creep/shrinkage and are excluded from strength design.  
– B‐type cases are treated as G_1 for maxima/AQB calculations and design checks.  
– If earth pressure R is large and its favorable effect must be captured, it should be defined under a G_3 or G_4 stage with proper safety factors (SOFILOAD).  
– CS…PROB LINE forces linear analysis even if non‐linear is selected elsewhere.  
– CS…FACV 0 zeroes existing deformations—useful when modeling incremental launches over a leveled bed.

Below is a detailed, field-by-field description of the “GRP” input table.  This table controls how individual “groups” (portions of your structure, e.g. slab segments, prefabricated beams, cable sets, etc.) are activated, carry loads, and interact with time-dependent effects (creep, shrinkage) during a staged construction analysis (CSM).

Columns  
• Item: the keyword you place on a GRP record.  
• Description: what the keyword means and how it affects group behavior.  
• Unit: the data type or units you supply.  
• Default: the value assumed if you omit the keyword.

1) NO  
• Description: identification number of the group to which this line applies.  
  – Use “ALL” (or “–”) to set global defaults for every group before you start defining numbered groups.  
• Unit: none  
• Default: ALL  

2) ICS1  
• Description: the construction‐stage at which the group’s stiffness “comes alive.”  
  – You can give an absolute stage number (e.g. 10, 21, …), or use special tokens:  
     • ACTU = the current stage number when the GRP line is read  
     • ACT1 = current stage + 1  
     • ACT9 = current stage + 9  
  – 99999 = never activate.  
• Unit: integer stage number or literal (LIT) token  
• Default: ACTU  

3) ATIL  
• Description: “active until” stage. After this stage, the group is no longer considered in the stiffness matrix.  
• Unit: integer stage number  
• Default: infinite (never de-activate)  

4) VAL  
• Description: toggles load‐value interpolation or stepwise application for this group. See ASE-GRP-VAL YES/LIN for details.  
• Unit: literal  
• Default: YES  

5) ASTI  
• Description: “active stiffness until” – often used for cable systems, up until EQIT (cable removal) occurs.  
• Unit: integer stage number  
• Default: infinite  

6) HFIX  
• Description: stage at which modeled hinges or releases within this group become “fixed” (locked).  
• Unit: integer stage number  
• Default: always fixed (no hinges open)  

7) BEDD  
• Description: stage at which bedding (quadratic springs under the group) is activated.  
• Unit: integer stage number  
• Default: 0 (bed springs always active)  

8) SITU  
• Description: for in-situ concrete parts within a composite section (AQUA framework), this forces activation of that part’s dead load independently of the stiffness activation (ICS1).  
  – If SITU ≥ ICS1, load and stiffness come in together.  
  – SITU < ICS1 (e.g. SITU –1) brings in the dead load one stage before stiffness, useful for pre-loading prior to composite action.  
  – SITU > ICS1+10000 delays dead load by n stages beyond stiffness.  
• Unit: integer stage offset  
• Default: * (i.e. immediate with ICS1)  

9) T0  
• Description: the “effective age” of the concrete at form-stripping (in days, at 20 °C).  
• Unit: days (d)  
• Default: 7  

10) TS  
• Description: age when shrinkage formally “starts.”  Shrinkage from TS – T0 to T0 is not applied in the very first creep/shrinkage interval.  
  – Choose TS carefully if you want to capture early shrinkage prior to loading.  
  – TS > 3 days usually is not recommended.  If TS needs to equal T0 to get initial shrinkage loads, set T0 = TS.  
• Unit: days (d)  
• Default: min(3, T0)  

11) FAC1  
• Description: global stiffness scaling factor applied the moment the group is first activated (useful for simulating reduced rigidity at early ages, staged pre-stress, etc.).  
• Unit: none  
• Default: 1.0  

12) ICSD  
• Description: the stage from which the group’s **dead load** is brought into the model (must satisfy ICSD ≥ ICS1).  You can use ACTU/ACT1/ACT9 here as well.  
• Unit: integer stage number or literal (LIT) token  
• Default: = ICS1  

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
Notes from context:  
– A “first” GRP record (with NO=ALL) sets these defaults globally; subsequent numbered GRP lines override them.  
– Use ACTU/ACT1/ACT9 to reference the simulation stage at the time the GRP line is read in.  
– Carefully choose T0 and TS when modeling time‐dependent material behavior (creep, shrinkage) to ensure the un-loaded shrinkage portion is—or is not—applied prior to prestressing or dead-load introduction.  
– For staged composite beams or slabs, SITU can decouple the load activation sequence of precast and cast‐in‐place concrete.  
– FAC1 may help avoid instabilities when mixing creeping elements (concrete) with non-creeping ones (springs, steel), by temporarily reducing the newly activated stiffness.  
– For sequential SLS/ULS runs, you can carry over groups and stages via CTRL PLC, CTRL STOR, define new primary stages (e.g. CS 4900), and re-scale loads (GRP … FACD, LC … FACT).

The input table you are ingesting is the “GRP‐table” used by the CSM (Construction Stage Model) pre-processor to define the sequence and properties of how loads, stiffnesses and time-dependent effects are activated or overridden in each construction stage.  Below is a field-by-field description of the table’s structure, data types and semantics, together with the key contextual rules from the additional text.

1. Record Type (always “GRP”)
   • Literal token “GRP” at the start of each row.  
   • Indicates that this row defines a “group” (construction stage) record.

2. Group Identifier (optional integer)
   • If omitted in the first GRP line → this row sets the default values for all groups.  
   • If present → applies only to the specified construction stage number (e.g. 10, 21, 51).  
   • Data type: integer ≥ 1.

3. Parameter Name (enumeration)
   Each GRP row may contain one or more of these keywords:
   – ACT9     : “actual CS construction stage number +9” (used internally for ACT9 indexing).  
   – FACD     : factor to scale dead loads (G) when the group activates. Default = 1.0.  
   – FACT     : factor to scale external non‐prestress loads (e.g. live, wind).  
   – TS       : “shrinkage age” (in days) at which shrinkage strains begin to accumulate. Default = 3.  
   – T0       : “loading age” (in days) at which the first creep+shrinkage interval starts.  
   – SITU     : controls activation stage of in-situ dead load for additional cast-in-place parts.  
   – (others occasionally used: e.g. “LAUN”, “EQLC” in specialized optimization sequences)

4. Parameter Value (integer or real)
   • For FACD, FACT: real number (e.g. 1.35, 1.50).  
   • For TS, T0: integer or real days.  
   • For SITU: integer; can be positive (absolute stage or stage‐offset as +10000+n), negative (activate n steps before stiffness), or plain stage number.  
   • For ACT9: integer offset, typically +9.

5. Implied Behavior and Units
   – TS defines the “zero‐point” for shrinkage. Shrinkage creep only applies for t ≥ TS.  
   – T0 defines the start of creep and shrinkage analysis intervals. If T0 > TS, the shrinkage portion from TS to T0 is not retroactively applied (standard prestress use).  
   – To include the missing shrinkage segment (TS → T0) in composite sections, set T0 = TS = 1 day.  
   – SITU > stage number: activates full weight at that stage; SITU –1 (etc.) → weight enters one stage early; SITU 10000+n → delayed by n stages.

6. Default vs. Override Rows
   • First “GRP” without a group number acts as the default template.  
   • Subsequent “GRP 10”, “GRP 21” lines override only the parameters explicitly listed; unspecified parameters inherit from the default.

7. Interactions with Other Commands
   – CTRL PLC: links a previous SLS run stage as primary stage for a follow-up ULS run.  
   – CTRL STOR +64: preserves existing stage definitions when appending new ones.  
   – CS 4900, LC … FACT …: new ultimate limit state definitions follow GRP blocks.  
   – PHIF: default 1.0 for steel springs representing creeping media; avoid unexpected redistributions.

8. Example Usage Patterns
   – Default row: “GRP   TS 3  T0 0  FACD 1.0  FACT 1.0”  
   – Composite beam, stage 10: “GRP 10  TS 1  T0 3  FACD 1.0”  
   – In-situ slab earlier weight: “GRP SITU -1”  
   – Delayed dead load: “GRP SITU 10005” (activates 5 stages after stiffness)

9. RAG-Store Considerations
   – Tokenize each row by fields: {recordType, groupId, parameter, value}.  
   – Store “TS” and “T0” with units (days), and “FACD/FACT” as dimensionless scale factors.  
   – Represent SITU offsets distinctly: flag negative vs. large offset (>10000).  
   – Maintain reference links to example files (e.g. csm3_composite_beam.dat, csm12_composite_activation.dat) as metadata.

Summary  
The GRP table is essentially a keyed parameter list per construction stage.  It defines when and how loads and time‐dependent effects come into action.  A no-number default entry establishes global values; numbered entries override selectively.  Understanding TS/T0 interplay is crucial for correct shrinkage and creep modeling in both prefabricated and in-situ composite elements, while SITU offers fine‐tuning of dead-load timing relative to stiffness activation.

The table shown defines a small set of dimensionless control parameters that can be supplied in a GRP-type input record of the CSM (construction stage) module.  It has four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and (in the excerpt) four rows, each naming one of the available controls.

1. Column headings  
   • Item: the mnemonic code you use in your input file (e.g. PHIF, QUEA, …)  
   • Description: a brief explanation of what that parameter does and, where relevant, pointers to more detailed theory or other input records  
   • Unit: the physical unit (if any). In this table all entries are “–” because they are pure multipliers or switches.  
   • Default: the value assumed when you do not override it explicitly.

2. Rows in detail  
   • PHIF  
     – “Factor for creep of springs, beddings, STEX and HASE”  
     – References the theoretical section “other elements.”  In actual practice you are only allowed to choose a binary option, 1 (creep enabled) or 0 (creep disabled), but a real-number multiplier >1 or <1 could be used to exaggerate or damp out the effect.  A value of 1.0 means that springs and bedding elements will participate in creep just like concrete or soil would.  
     – Unit: none (dimensionless)  
     – Default: 1.0  

   • QUEA  
     – An input control flag whose precise interpretation is defined in the ASE program’s GRP2 record (see the ASE manual).  In most workflows it is left blank and the program defaults govern.  
     – Unit: –  
     – Default: – (no preset)  

   • QEMX  
     – Similar to QUEA: another ASE record GRP2 control.  Often used in advanced workflows to alter the internal algorithm of how group sequences are formed or how extreme values get treated.  
     – Unit: –  
     – Default: –  

   • FACD  
     – “Factor dead load” – a multiplier that scales all dead-load actions when you perform a two-stage CSM run (for example, first an SLS load combination, then a separate ULS run).  By assigning FACD in your GRP input you can activate dead-load at a higher factor (say 1.35) in the second pass without changing your original model.  
     – Unit: –  
     – Default: –  

3. How this fits into a typical CSM workflow  
   – You invoke these keywords in a GRP (Group) section, which sequences construction‐stage activations (see also the CAMB, GRP, ACT9 discussion).  
   – If the first GRP line has no group number, the values given there become the defaults for all subsequent groups.  Any later GRP statement that repeats, say, “PHIF 0.0” will override for that group only.  
   – PHIF is important any time you mix creeping (concrete slabs, foundations, soil) and non-creeping (steel spring supports) elements, because unbalanced creep behavior can otherwise cause unexpected load redistributions.  
   – FACD is typically used when you run a two-step sequence: first serviceability (SLS) with LC-factors = 1.0; then ultimate (ULS) with dead load scaled by FACD and other live-load factors set in LC…FACT.  

In practice, you would see an input snippet like:

  GRP    10    PHIF  1.0    FACD 1.35  
  GRP    20    …  

This tells the solver: in construction stage 10 use standard creep participation of any bedding/spring element, and in the second CSM pass apply dead‐load at 1.35×. Any group that does not explicitly list PHIF or FACD inherits the defaults set on the first, unnumbered GRP line.

The table is a concise index that pairs ten illustrative “GRP” – group‐activation scenarios with their corresponding CSM (Construction Stage Modelling) input files. In a RAG (Retrieval‐Augmented Generation) context, this summary can be used as metadata for vector‐store lookups, letting downstream workflows quickly identify which example data set to pull when users ask about a particular GRP feature. Here is a breakdown of its structure and purpose:

1. Column headers  
   - “Examples to GRP”: A human‐readable label for each tutorial or demonstration scenario, emphasizing the particular construction‐stage activation concept being illustrated.  
   - “Input file”: The filename (with “.dat” extension) containing the actual CSM commands (including GRP entries) that implement the scenario.

2. Rows (ten example mappings)  
   1. Introduction → csm1_4span_centering.dat  
      • Covers basic GRP usage in a simple four‐span centering example.  
      • Demonstrates how a first GRP line without a group number establishes default parameters.  
   2. Creep → csm2_simplecreep.dat  
      • Shows incremental creep activation only (no shrinkage or prestress).  
      • Useful for understanding T0, TS, and the first creep interval beginning at loading age T0.  
   3. Prestressed bridge → csm31_design.dat  
      • Introduces prestressing losses (creep + shrinkage) starting at T0.  
      • Emphasizes that the first shrinkage part (from TS to T0) is omitted in the total shrinkage value.  
   4. Precast prestressed girder → csm3_composite_beam.dat  
      • Combines prefabricated beam activation with subsequent in‐situ slab.  
      • Illustrates setting T0 and TS separately (e.g. T0=3 days, TS=1 day) to ensure adequate early‐age strength.  
   5. Quad prestress → csm4_quad_singlespan.dat  
      • A single‐span quad‐cable prestress example.  
   6. QUAD prestressed bridge → csm32_slab_design.dat  
      • Extends quad prestress concepts to a full bridge slab.  
   7. Free cantilever erection → csm5_free_cantilever.dat  
      • Demonstrates sequential launch and cantilever balance procedures via GRP incrementing.  
   8. Building stepwise → csm9_multistorey1.dat  
      • Activates storeys one at a time, showing GRP FACD and load‐factor usage for dead loads.  
   9. Steel composite → csm12_composite_activation.dat  
      • Focuses on in situ additions to prefabricated elements.  
      • Uses “GRP SITU –1” to activate section‐part dead weight one stage before stiffness activation.  
   10. Quad in situ on beam girder → csm13_quad_weight_lar_activation.dat  
      • Illustrates delaying or advancing dead‐load activation relative to stiffness by applying offsets (e.g. SITU +10000 + n for later activation).

3. Contextual notes (drawn from the longer GRP description)  
   • GRP entries control the order and intensity (factored or unfactored) of activating stiffness, dead loads, prestress, creep, and shrinkage.  
   • Default creep/shrinkage age (TS=3 days) can be overridden per group.  
   • For composite sections, the first shrinkage interval may need special handling (e.g. T0=TS=1 day).  
   • The “SITU” keyword in a GRP line lets you decouple the activation of weight from stiffness, shifting it earlier (negative offset) or later (positive offset).  
   • In multi‐run workflows (first SLS, then ULS), the “CTRL PLC” and “CTRL STOR +64” commands preserve and extend stages for factored analyses.

By indexing these ten examples with their .dat filenames, the table makes it trivial to retrieve a concrete input script when a user requests guidance on any particular GRP use case—whether it’s simple creep, incremental launching, prestress sequencing, or advanced composite‐section activation strategies.

   • Embed each row as a separate document with metadata fields:  
     – “subject”: full title string  
     – “link”: URL string  
     – “category”: inferred from keyword (ASE, CSM, DESI, BEMESS, Teddy, Misc)  
   • Optionally enrich with context tags derived from your additional text (e.g., “creep‐shrinkage,” “GRP activation,” “SITU command”).  
   • Include the YouTube thumbnail or transcript snippet in the document body for richer retrieval.  

5. Potential Retrieval Use Cases  
   • A query on “incremental launching” would surface the CSM incremental launching row.  
   • Searching “tendon optimization” yields both the “Tendon Optimization” and the related eigenvalues video.  
   • “German layer design” would hit the BEMESS “deutsch” entry and the punching-shear (“Durchstanzen”) video.  

By capturing the table’s two‐column structure, thematic clusters, URL patterns and relationships, this description lays the groundwork for high‐precision retrieval and seamless integration into any vector‐based RAG pipeline.

 For shrinkage now an age TS of 3 days is set by default, With the new input GRP...TS this can be changed in CSM. Physically shrinkage starts at this age TS. The analyis creep and shrinkage intervals start at T0 (loading age). So in the first creep and shrinkage interval T0 to T0+T the shrinkage part from TS to T0 is not applied! This is correct for the standard case prestress with subsequent bond where prestress C+S loss starts at T0. With the same reason also the total shrinkage value does not include this first shrinkage part from TS to T0!
 In steel composite sections it is necessary to take into account the first shrinkage part from TS up to the start of loading. To do this you must input T0=TS= 1 day, see example steel_composite_orto.dat .

Completely correct could also be to input T0=TS= 1 day, calculate the first activation of the beams without dead load (GRP FACD), then add a creep step with e.g. 7 days and then activate dead load G_1 and following prestress P.

The table shown defines the five fields you must supply when you create or modify a “group” in a RAG‐style input (via GRP or GRCS), together with each field’s meaning, units, and default value.  In most workflows it is used to activate, deactivate or re‐activate sets of elements, to scale their stiffness or loads, or to impose prestress when they represent cables or spring supports.

1.  NO (Group number)  
    –  Description: an integer tag identifying which group you are addressing.  All elements you wish to control must have been assigned this same group number in their definition.  
    –  Unit: –  
    –  Default: Mandatory (“!”) – you must explicitly supply it.

2.  CS (Construction stage number)  
    –  Description: an integer stage at which the operation takes place.  Typical construction‐sequence analyses advance from stage 1 up through N.  At each stage, GRCS entries can switch groups on/off, change stiffness, apply prestress, etc.  
    –  Unit: –  
    –  Default: Mandatory (“!”).

3.  FACS (Factor of stiffness)  
    –  Description: scales the group’s stiffness relative to the base (100 %) value.  Set FACS = 0 to remove all stiffness (group effectively deleted from the model).  Values between 0 and 1 reduce stiffness; values > 1 increase it.  
    –  Unit: –  
    –  Default: 1 (no change).

4.  FACL (Factor of load from primary loadcase)  
    –  Description: scales the internal forces/tensions derived from the “primary” loadcase (see ASE‐GRP documentation) for every element in the group.  
       • FACL = 0 removes all primary‐load stress → the group is placed back in a stress‐free state.  
       • FACL = 1 applies the full original load.  
       • FACL > 1 would amplify it.  
    –  Unit: –  
    –  Default: 1.

5.  PREX (Prestress of a group)  
    –  Description: an additional axial‐force offset applied only to elements that can take prestress—typically cables or springs.  Use this when you want to impose a targeted cable force or to simulate “support lifting” via springs.  
    –  Unit: kN  
    –  Default: 0 (no added prestress).

—  
Illustrative Workflows (see “See also: TXCS / GRCS”)

A.  Removing and later re-activating a group  
   • Stage 40: “GRP 21 ICS1 40”  
     – shorthand for group 21, stiffness factor = 1, load factor = 1 at stage 40.  
   • Stage 60 → 69: “GRCS 21 CS (60 69 1) FACS 0”  
     – temporarily set FACS = 0 → group 21 removed.  
   • Stage 70 onward: by default group is once again active (no further GRCS entry needed, or you could explicitly reset FACS to 1).

B.  Re-stress a cable to a new predefined force  
   • “GRCS 31 CS 210 FACS 1E-9 FACL 0 ; LC 210 ICS1 210”  
     – group 31 (cable) has its stiffness nearly zero’d out (1E-9) to decouple geometry from force, FACL = 0 to throw away old cable force, then add the prestress from loadcase 210.  
     – (FACL = 0 means: discard old internal stress from the primary loadcase, then apply the new from LC 210.)

C.  Support lifting or lowering via springs  
   • If a coupling spring sits in group 7 with (original) stiffness 1 × 10^6 kN/m, you can request a 1 cm lift by writing:  
     “GRP 7 PREX –1.E4”  
     – because –1 × 10^4 kN over a 1 cm deformation corresponds to the stiffness times deflection.  
   • Alternatively, you can use the TXCS…ELEM…UX syntax to impose a direct displacement boundary condition on a node.

Important Note:  
– Avoid mixing GRCS‐FACL manipulations with the equation‐based cable system (EQLC).  If you do need to remove cables in an EQLC setup, the recommended workaround is to use 100 % stiffness cables and introduce a separate, scalable loadcase whose target cable force is set to zero at the removal stage (see csm25_equation_cable_removal.dat).

See also: TXCS
 GRCS
 Usage (without EQLC): removal of a group with later re-usage:
 GRP 21 ICS1 40
 GRCS 21 CS (60 69 1) FACS 0 $ removal
 From stage 70 on the group is again active.
 Usage (without EQLC): restress a cable to a new defined force:
 GRCS 31 CS 210 FACS 1E-9 FACL 0 ; LC 210 ICS1 210
 (cable in group 31, new cable prestress force in loadcase 210):
 (FACL 0 means: throw away old cable force and apply new from LC 210)
 Usage support lifting or support lowering:
 With springs you can use PREX to simulate a support lifting. E.g. you used a coupling spring in group 7 with stiffness 1.E6, you can achieve a support lifting by 1 cm with GRP 7 PREX -1.E4.
 An elegant possibility of support lifting can also be input with TXCS...ELEM...UX.
 Attention: do not use GRCS-FACL in combination with the equation system EQLC. Then better always use cables with 100 % stiffness and insert a scalable loadcase with target cableforce=0 for stage cable removal!
 see csm25_equation_cable_removal.dat

The table shown defines the three core parameters that govern how arbitrary text commands (“TEXT”) are applied over a range of construction stages in an ASE‐based workflow.  In practice you will see these parameters combined in a TXxCS record (e.g. TXBA, TXCS) to route user-supplied instructions into the numerical model for a specified stage interval.  Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown, followed by contextual notes and examples.  

1. Columns  
   • Item  
     – The name of the input field (ICS1, ATIL, TEXT).  
   • Description  
     – A short English description of that field’s purpose.  
   • Unit  
     – All three fields carry “–”, indicating they are dimensionless or purely index‐based.  
   • Default  
     – “!” means mandatory input, “–” means optional or empty by default.

2. Rows / Items  

   a. ICS1 (Construction stage number “from”)  
      • Description: Specifies the first (lowest) construction stage in which the TEXT commands become active.  
      • Unit: none (index only)  
      • Default: “!” (user must supply a value)  
      • Notes: Acts as the “start” marker.  Every TXxCS entry must define an ICS1 stage.  

   b. ATIL (Construction stage number “to”)  
      • Description: Specifies the final (highest) construction stage in which the TEXT commands remain active.  
      • Unit: none (index only)  
      • Default: “!” (user must supply a value)  
      • Notes: Acts as the “end” marker.  The TEXT string is applied in all stages ≥ ICS1 and ≤ ATIL.  

   c. TEXT (Input for these construction stages)  
      • Description: A free‐format character string containing one or more ASE directives—for example, element loads, stiffness adjustment commands, grouping instructions, spring elongations, hinge activation, etc.  
      • Unit: none (alphanumeric text)  
      • Default: “–” (if omitted, no additional text commands are sent)  
      • Notes: Can carry virtually any command syntax understood by the ASE preprocessing flow.  Because it is free text, this field supports very complex or multi-line instructions when used within a single TXxCS record.

3. Context and Usage Patterns  
   • These three inputs typically appear together under a TXxCS or TXBA keyword header.  For example,  
     TXCS 240 TEXT ’ELEM SPRI 5001,5002 UX 20[mm]’  
     implicitly uses ICS1 = 240 and ATIL = 240 (single‐stage activation) to impose a 20 mm lift in springs 5001+5002 precisely in CS 240.  
   • When multiple construction stages need identical text commands, set ICS1 to the first stage and ATIL to the last.  
   • If ATIL is omitted, the directive would remain active indefinitely—however, since ATIL is mandatory in this table, the user must explicitly bound the range.  

4. Cross-References  
   • See also:  
     – GRCS  (alternate syntax for stiffness or hinge manipulation)  
     – TXxCS / TXCS  (umbrella record types carrying ICS1, ATIL, TEXT)  
     – TXBA  (variant for stiffness or hinge activation over a range)  

By adhering to this schema, the ASE preprocessing layer can stage‐wise inject virtually any custom directive into the finite‐element model, supporting complex schedules for loading, restraint changes, stiffness updates or other specialized operations.

The table shown is the definition of the WAIT‐group record.  In the context of RAG/CSM (Construction Stage Method) analysis, WAIT allows you to designate certain construction groups as “inactive” (i.e. not undergoing creep or time‐dependent effects) in order to introduce an explicit time shift between different parts of the structure.  By doing so you can model, for instance, two piers that really are constructed at different calendar times but whose erection phases you wish to align structurally in the analysis to minimize the total number of stages and load cases.

Below is a detailed breakdown of the table’s columns and rows:

1.  Column Headings  
   •  Item  
      –  The keyword or parameter name that must appear in the input deck.  
   •  Description  
      –  A brief explanation of what the parameter controls.  
   •  Unit  
      – The physical unit (if any) associated with the parameter.  A dash (–) indicates a dimensionless value or integer.  
   •  Default  
      – The value assumed if the parameter is omitted.  An exclamation mark (!) signals that this parameter is mandatory.

2.  Rows (Parameters in the WAIT record)  
   •  NO  
      –  “Group number.”  An integer identifier for the particular construction group you are marking as inactive during the WAIT interval.  
      –  Unit: – (integer)  
      –  Default: !  (You must supply a group number.)  
   •  FROM  
      –  “Construction stage number of the inactive phase.”  Indicates at which construction stage this group first stops creeping (i.e. goes into a ‘wait’ or hold state).  
      –  Unit: – (integer stage index)  
      –  Default: !  (Mandatory: you must specify an initial stage index.)  
   •  TO  
      –  “Construction stage number at the end of the inactive phase.”  The stage index when the group resumes normal, time‐dependent behavior (creep, shrinkage, relaxation).  
      –  Unit: – (integer stage index)  
      –  Default: !  (Mandatory: you must specify an ending stage index.)

3.  How WAIT is used in practice  
   –  Suppose you have two piers to build:  
      •  Pier A takes 85 days (40 erection stages + 20 creep stages).  
      •  Pier B starts 100 days later, but itself needs 40 erection stages + 20 creep stages.  
   –  A naïve stage‐by‐stage simulation would produce 60 + 60 = 120 stages, doubling your load‐case count.  
   –  With WAIT, you:  
      1.  Erect both piers in parallel (60 stages).  
      2.  Insert a WAIT record for Pier B: it “waits” (no creep) for the 100 days while Pier A alone creeps.  
      3.  Resume normal behavior of Pier B after stage index = 60 (end of the hold).  
   –  The result: Pier A is effectively 85 + 100 days old at the time you connect the levers; Pier B is 85 days old.  You only need 60 + 1 stages, drastically reducing load cases, database size, and computation time.

By mapping each construction group’s idle interval via the NO/FROM/TO fields of the WAIT record, you maintain accurate age‐dependent material behavior while optimizing your CSM model’s size and performance.

WAIT
 With WAIT individual groups can be defined as not-creep-active. This can be used to introduce a time shift in the construction sequence.
 For example if in reality you build a pier in 85 days with 40 stages and 20 creep stages and 100 days later a 2. pier in 40 stages and 20 creep stages you need 60+60=120 stages.
 In the CSM analysis you can do: build both piers in parallel (60 stages) and then insert a creep step of 100 days where only the first pier creeps and the second pier waits. So you get the correct erection of both piers. If you then continue and connect the lever arms, the first pier is 85+100 days old, the second only 85 days old - as in reality - and you only need 60+1 stages -> less loadcases, smaller database, quicker analysis.

The table under consideration defines the key parameters that control how “additional” load cases are declared, activated and scaled within the Construction Stage Model (CSM).  It is intended to be read alongside the higher-level guidance on numbering conventions, relationships between load cases (LC) and construction stages (CS), and prestress load handling.  For clarity, most practitioners assign identical numbers to a load case and the construction stage at which it first appears; this alignment is neither enforced by the software but strongly recommended.  

Overview of Columns  
• Item: the mnemonic or keyword used in the input file.  
• Description: a free-text explanation of the item’s purpose and any special rules.  
• Unit: an indication of whether the item takes a literal (LIT) argument, a numeric factor, or has no unit.  
• Default: the value assumed if the item is omitted.  

Row-by-Row Description  

1. NO (Load case number)  
   – This integer uniquely identifies each additional load case.  
   – It must not collide with automatically generated prestress load case numbers (these are produced according to TENDON…CS ICS1 definitions).  
   – Default: 1  

2. TYPE  
   – Obsolete within the load case table itself; it does not influence activation or duration of the load.  
   – Retained solely for user reference, often used as a short textual title.  
   – Note: an item named TYPE in the CS definition (Construction Stage) is critical for distinguishing load types (e.g. dead, live, short-time).  
   – Unit: LIT  
   – Default: none  

3. ICS1 (First‐action construction stage)  
   – Specifies the construction stage at which this load case comes into effect.  
   – Can be given explicitly as an integer (CS number), or relative to the current stage via special codes:  
     • ACTU  – the current (actual) construction stage  
     • ACT1  – current stage + 1  
     • ACT9  – current stage + 9 (and so on up to ACT9)  
   – By aligning ICS1 with the CS index, you ensure that the software applies the load exactly when intended.  
   – Unit: –/LIT  
   – Default: ACTU  

4. ATIL (Active until construction stage)  
   – Defines the last stage for which the load remains active.  If omitted, the load persists indefinitely (“t-infinite”) through all subsequent stages.  
   – On short-time load cases (TYPE SL at the CS level), ATIL must be explicitly set equal to ICS1 (so that it acts only in the one stage).  
   – Example usage:  
     • ATIL 60  – the load is active up to and including stage 60  
   – Unit: —  
   – Default: infinite  

5. FACT (Load factor)  
   – A multiplier applied to the raw load intensity.  Commonly used to model increasing load magnitudes or to apply combination factors.  
   – If a load case is declared multiple times (to simulate ramping or staged application), each entry can carry its own FACT.  
   – Example:  
     – LC 901 ICS1 41 ATIL 60 FACT 0.40  
     – LC 901 ICS1 61 ATIL 100 FACT 1.00  
   – Unit: —  
   – Default: 1.0  

Additional Remarks  
• The input file only needs to list “additional” loads; prestress effects are inserted automatically according to TENDON…CS ICS1 definitions and appear separately in the CSM output.  
• It is permissible to repeat the same load case (same NO) with different ICS1/ATIL/FACT entries to simulate increasing load factors or intermittent short-time actions.  
• For consistent reporting and auditing, match your load case numbers directly to the construction stage numbers where each load is initiated.

See also: CS
