This table defines the CREP-related input parameters used by the AQUA/CSM system to control creep and shrinkage behaviour in concrete members. It is typically found under the CREP input block (see also DEPS) and governs how default creep curves can be modified or replaced by user-defined factors or explicit curves. Below is a detailed, field-by-field description suitable for inclusion in a RAG vector store:

1. Table Purpose and Context  
   • Purpose: To list all CREP parameters that the user may specify to alter creep/shrinkage computation, covering both “simple” (standard) creep and “real” creep analyses.  
   • Related Files and Modules:  
     – DEPS: for default creep/shrinkage parameter sets  
     – real_creep_creepparameter.dat: example of scaling default creep curves for “real” creep  
     – explicit_creep_curve.dat: compares modification methods and gives recommendations  
     – AQUA … MEXT TYP EIGE VAL3+5: alternative approach to shrinkage via material definitions  
     – AQUA … SV—DEFF: for adjusting beam cross-section effective thickness

2. Column Definitions  
   – Item: The mnemonic code used in the input deck.  
   – Description: A brief explanation of what the parameter controls.  
   – Unit: The physical unit or dimension of the parameter (if applicable).  
   – Default: The value used when the user does not override this parameter.

3. Row-by-Row Parameter Descriptions  
   • MNO  
     – Description: Material number identifier.  
     – Unit: – (unitless integer)  
     – Default: ! (mandatory entry; no built-in default)  

   • GRP  
     – Description: Element group number to which the parameters apply.  
     – Unit: – (unitless integer)  
     – Default: – (user must specify)  

   • PHI  
     – Description: Creep factor (scales the standard, simple creep curve).  
     – Unit: –  
     – Default: * (inherits from default material definition)  
     – Notes: Not permitted when performing “real” creep. For real creep, scale the default curve externally (see real_creep_creepparameter.dat).

   • EPS  
     – Description: Shrinkage coefficient (negative sign indicates shortening).  
     – Unit: –  
     – Default: * (inherits default)  
     – Notes: Allowed in “real” creep; enforced EPS replaces internally computed values, but beam-thickness variation per group is lost (only average thickness used). For more flexible shrinkage control, use AQUA’s MEXT TYP EIGE VAL3+5 approach.

   • DEFQ  
     – Description: Effective member thickness for QUAD and BRIC area elements.  
     – Unit: [m]  
     – Default: –1.40 (factor applied to quad thickness h)  
     – Notes: A negative value indicates a scaling factor (e.g. –1.40*h). If omitted, AQUA/CSM computes an average thickness over all quads in the group. Default reflects limited air contact on quad tops.

   • T0  
     – Description: Reference age (in days) for in-situ added concrete in a specific construction stage.  
     – Unit: d (days)  
     – Default: – (no default)  

   • TS  
     – Description: Alternative age parameter; values above 3 days are typically nonsensical.  
     – Unit: d (days)  
     – Default: –  

   • EXP  
     – Description: Exposition class name for explicit creep curves.  
     – Unit: d (days)  
     – Default: –  
     – Notes: See explicit_creep_curve.dat for syntax and recommended practices.

4. Cross-References and Best Practices  
   – For “real” creep: scale default curves rather than use PHI; see real_creep_creepparameter.dat.  
   – For shrinkage: EPS can override, but averaging limitations make MEXT TYP EIGE VAL3+5 preferable.  
   – DEFQ must be explicitly set for BRIC groups; quad groups default to –1.40*h unless overridden.  
   – Beam effective thickness is separately controlled via SV—DEFF.  
   – Special element types (springs, elastic boundaries, bedding, FLEX, HASE) have unique notes in the “other elements” theory section.

See also: DEPS
 CREP
 With CREP user creep and shrinkage values can be modified. PHI can only be used for the simple standard creep and not for the real creep!
 For real creep you best scale your creep values with a factor to the default creep curve, see example real_creep_creepparameter.dat.
 A compare of possibilities to modify creep curves and a recommendation is shown at the end of example file explicit_creep_curve.dat.
 EPS is also allowed in the real creep. The program then scales the internal calculated eps values to the enforced input value EPS. But then AQB will not use a variable effective thichness per beam but will only use the CSM printed average value per group. So it is better to use a simple factor to shinkage, best possible in AQUA with MEXT TYP EIGE VAL3+5, see material 3 in explicit_creep_curve.dat.
 QUAD-elements: without an input to CREP...DEFQ, the CSM computes an averaged value for the effective thickness over all QUAD elements of each group. Due to top covering of quads in nearly all circumstances (bad air contact), the default effective thickness for quad elements is set to 1.40*h.
 For BRIC elements the effective member thickness must be input for the BRIC groups.
 The effective thickness of beam cross sections can be changed in AQUA ... SV—DEFF.
 For creep of springs, elastic boundaries, Quad bedding, FLEX- and HASE- elements see re- marks in theoretical part ’other elements’.

The table shown below defines the six basic input parameters that control how the CSM module will apply additional creep, shrinkage and environmental‐condition adjustments to your model.  All six items are optional overrides to the program’s internally calculated values; if you leave a field blank, the built‐in algorithm is used instead.  No numerical units apply to any of these parameters and, by default, nothing is overridden.

Table layout  
• Column “Item”  
  – The short mnemonic used at the command line or in the input deck.  
• Column “Description”  
  – A brief English explanation of the parameter’s purpose.  
• Column “Unit”  
  – This is always “—” because all entries are dimensionless coefficients or simple indexes.  
• Column “Default”  
  – Always “–” to indicate no user-supplied override.  

Parameter details  
1. MNO (Material number)  
   • Selects a specific material definition (concrete, grout, etc.) by its internal index.  
   • If you omit MNO, the additional creep/shrinkage inputs (DPHI, DEPS) apply to all material types in the model.  
   • Use this when you want to adjust only one concrete mix or only one steel grade’s creep behavior.  

2. GRP (Group number)  
   • Filters which element groups receive the extra creep or shrinkage adjustment.  
   • If left blank, all groups are assumed.  
   • Works in combination with MNO and/or CS to target precise subsets of your structure.  

3. CS (Construction stage number)  
   • Indicates a single construction stage in which you wish to add extra creep or shrinkage.  
   • If you do not specify a CS, the program automatically applies your DPHI/DEPS additions in the stage when an element first becomes “active.”  
   • Allows modeling of special behavior—e.g. rapid early hardening or staged casting.  

4. DPHI (Delta-phi creep factor)  
   • A positive or negative adjustment to the internally computed creep coefficient (ϕ).  
   • Added on top of the default ϕ for the element(s) designated by MNO/GRP/CS.  
   • Use this to represent atypical long-term stiffness loss beyond what the code’s formula predicts.  

5. DEPS (Delta-eps shrinkage coefficient)  
   • An additive (usually negative) correction to the default shrinkage strain.  
   • Sign convention: entering “–0.0002” reduces shrinkage by 0.0002 in the specified group or stage.  
   • If you leave DEPS blank, any shrinkage‐related correction is applied once when the element first goes active.  
   • Special note: DEPS values combine with any PHIP (pre-defined shrinkage strain) inputs.  Check the CSM output print to confirm the net sum.  

6. RH (Special humidity of an element)  
   • Overrides the ambient relative humidity used in the shrinkage model for the given material or group.  
   • Useful for modeling enclosure beneath tarps or in unusually dry/wet conditions.  
   • Always expressed as a fraction between 0 and 1 (e.g. 0.70 for 70 % RH).  

Additional context  
• See “CREP” for a separate command that fully replaces the code’s creep curve rather than merely adding a delta.  
• The TBEX (T-beam philosophy on eccentrically reinforced beams) option can also affect effective stiffness (E*A) of slab elements during the creep and shrinkage analysis—consult ASE manual TBEX for details.  
• Whenever you use DEPS or DPHI without specifying MNO, GRP or CS, the software assumes “all materials, all groups, all stages” and applies your correction universally.

sections: 3.12 DEPS – Additional Creep and Shrinkage Input

content:
The table shown is the input‐parameter specification for the CSM-TBEX option in the creep and shrinkage module.  In the context of ASE’s “T-beam philosophy on eccentric beam elements,” these two items allow you to isolate part of your deck‐slab mesh—identified as a “quad slab” group—and then apply a modified E·A stiffness factor for the creep and shrinkage analysis only.  All other construction stages (e.g. G or P stages) continue to use the full isotropic quad stiffness, ensuring that slab prestressing and other effects remain correctly modeled.  Key points:  
 
• Table layout  
  – Column “Item” gives the parameter name as used on the CSM input line.  
  – Column “Description” explains what the parameter controls.  
  – Column “Unit” shows the physical or reference unit (or if it is a nondimensional index).  
  – Column “Default” shows the built-in default behavior when that item is omitted.  
 
• Item #1: QGRP  
  – Description: “Group number of quad slab. Secondary groups not allowed.”  
  – Unit: “–/LIT” means it is a simple integer or literal index referring to a user-defined group of quad elements in the model.  
  – Default: “!” (no default). In practice, this means if you want to activate a TBEX stiffness reduction you must supply QGRP; otherwise, by omission, the program assumes no quad‐slab subset and applies full stiffness everywhere.  
  – Notes:  
     • If you omit QGRP, then “without MNO or GRP input all relevant elements are considered.” That is, CSM treats every quad element as though it belonged to the same group, but since EACR also defaults to “–,” no reduction is made.  
     • Secondary group numbers are prohibited: only one contiguous or disjoint set of quad elements can be modified at a time.  
 
• Item #2: EACR  
  – Description: “Factor on the E·A stiffness of the quad slab for creep and shrinkage.”  
  – Unit: “—” indicates a nondimensional multiplier, typically between 0 and 1 (e.g. EACR=1E-5 to approximate pure beam behavior).  
  – Default: “–” (no override). When omitted, the quad slab uses its full E·A value in all stages.  
  – Notes:  
     • The reduced stiffness is only applied in the creep‐shrinkage calculation; all other load or prestress stages run with the original isotropic stiffness.  
     • You may not reduce the stiffness (i.e. set EACR<1) if your model includes transverse slab prestressing, since that would invalidate the tendon‐compression behavior.  
     • In practice, setting EACR very low (e.g. 1E-5) causes the quad slab to act almost entirely in shear, giving results that closely match a pure beam‐only model, which can help you isolate beam–slab interaction effects.  
 
Cross-references:  
 - For single-stage additional creep/shrinkage inputs, see the DEPS command (adds user‐defined increment to the internally computed values).  
 - For more background on the T-beam philosophy and its implementation, see the ASE manual section “TBEX.”  
 - For a step-by-step demonstration, consult the YouTube workshop video (search GRP for “Overview workshop YOUTUBE videos,” or go directly to https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GoT1f0aGdgs).

See also: CREP
 DEPS
 With DEPS additional creep and shrinkage values can be defined for single construction stages. E.g. for the first concrete hardening, an additional shrinkage value can be input to take into account special hardening behaviour. The program adds the defined values to the internally calculated values. Additional PHIP input is considered in advance! If no input is done for CS, the value is added in the first construction stage when an element is active for the first time! Without MNO or GRP input all relevant elements are considered. Please check the addition in the CSM output.
 TBEX – T-beam-philosophy on excentric beam elements
 TBEX
 Using the ASE TBEX T-beam-philosophy, the beam elements of the longitudinal superstructure and the quad elements of the deck slab usually get different creep and shrinkage coefficients due to a different effective thickness. This sometimes causes unexpected slight redistribution of forces between the beam elements and the quad deck slab.
 With CSM TBEX the E*A stiffness of the quad deck slab can be reduced for creep and shrink- age analysis. Then the moments and normal forces are better comparable with the results of a pure beam analysis. All other stages such as G or P run with the full isotropic E*A quad stiffness.
 To the TBEX T-beam-philosophy please also refer to ASE manual TBEX.
 There the CSM TBEX is commented out but we did run the example without slab prestress and the check print delivers nearly same stresses with/without CSM TBEX EACR 1E-5
 Of course you are not allowed to reduce E*A stiffness if you have a transverse slab prestress because otherwise the compression of the tendons cannot be carried.
 See YOUTUBE Video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GoT1f0aGdgs
 All workshop YOUTUBE videos are listed in the command GRP, search there for ’Overview workshop YOUTUBE videos’

The input table defines three key parameters used when specifying additional “actions” or load cases in a structural-design input (for example in an ACT command such as  
ACT G_2 FOR SLS,ULS SLSF 1.20 …). It serves as a reference of how to name each parameter, what it means, which units apply, and what default value is assumed if the user does not override it. Below is a breakdown of its structure and contents.

1. Table Structure  
   • Four columns:  
     – Item: The keyword as it appears in the ACT command or data file.  
     – Description: A concise explanation of the parameter’s purpose.  
     – Unit: The type of value expected (if any).  
     – Default: The value assumed when the parameter is not explicitly provided.

2. Column Definitions  
   • Item  
     – LITERALS that the parser will recognize as distinct keywords.  
   • Description  
     – Explains the role or effect of the item in the design process.  
   • Unit  
     – LIT   : A literal string (no numeric unit).  
     – “—”   : No unit; typically a pure number or factor.  
   • Default  
     – The fallback value used by the system when the user does not specify an argument.

3. Row-by-Row Details  
   A. TYPE  
     – Item: TYPE  
     – Description: “Type of the action.” This identifies the action name or code (for example, traffic, wind, temperature, etc.).  
     – Unit: LIT (literal text)  
     – Default: “!” (exclamation mark). In many data‐file syntaxes this may signal a mandatory field or placeholder.  

   B. FOR  
     – Item: FOR  
     – Description: “Design state, the action shall be used.” This determines which checks or limit states include the specified action.  
       • SLS – Serviceability limit‐state checks  
       • ULS – Ultimate limit‐state checks  
       • FAT – Exact fatigue checks using load model 3  
       • ACCI – Accidental load checks  
       • EARQ – Earthquake (seismic) checks  
       • default: CODE – The system attempts to assign FOR automatically according to the design code in use but only for recognized actions. For any other action the user must explicitly set FOR.  
     – Unit: LIT (literal text)  
     – Default: CODE  

   C. SLSF  
     – Item: SLSF  
     – Description: “Factor in serviceability limit state for dead load G_2 and G_3.” Used primarily in SLS checks under certain national standards (e.g. Australian Standard via MAXIMA/AQB). If not specified, dead loads use a factor of 1.0.  
     – Unit: — (no unit; dimensionless multiplier)  
     – Default: 1.0  

4. Usage Notes and Context  
   • These table entries form part of the syntax for ACT commands that define how secondary or special loads combine with primary loads.  
   • When multiple load types exist (e.g. temperature T, wind on traffic ZW, wind alone SW), FOR may include multiple limit states separated by commas.  
   • SLSF applies only when FOR includes SLS; it does not affect ULS or other checks.  
   • If an EARQ (earthquake) action is defined under FOR, the program will automatically generate an earthquake ULS design case (e.g. csm33_earthquake_bridge.dat).  

By following these definitions, users can construct valid ACT statements that correctly assign each additional action to the intended design checks, ensuring consistent automated combination of loads under the chosen design code.

This table defines the single input parameter used to select fatigue‐design groups (the “lambda” groups) in the LAM fatigue‐design module. It appears in section 3.17 (“LAM – Lambda Values for the Fatigue Design”) and is ultimately exposed through the GRPD keyword (e.g. “GRPD 1,2,6,12”) in DESI input decks. Downstream, those group numbers drive both AQB and BEMESS design workflows; if you generate graphical output with WINGRAF, you must switch over to using BOX instead of GRPD. An illustrative example is provided in the file csm31_design.dat under the DECO check.

Detailed breakdown of the table’s columns and row:

1. Item  
   • Label: “NO”  
   • Purpose: This is the identifier used in the input deck to trigger the group‐selection mechanism. Although rendered here as the text “NO,” in practice you supply a comma‐separated list of numeric group IDs immediately following the GRPD keyword.

2. Description  
   • Text: “Group selection for the design”  
   • Meaning: Indicates that the value you supply tells the solver which predefined fatigue‐load groups (lambda groups) to include in the fatigue design calculations.

3. Unit  
   • Entry: Dash (“–”)  
   • Interpretation: No physical unit applies. You are not entering a dimensional quantity but rather an index or label (the group number).

4. Default  
   • Entry: Dash (“-”)  
   • Interpretation: There is no implicit or hardcoded fallback group list. The user must explicitly provide one or more group numbers; failing to do so will typically trigger a missing‐parameter error in DESI.

Contextual Usage Notes  
• In your DESI input file you would write, for example:  
 GRPD 1,2,6,12  
  to include groups 1, 2, 6, and 12 in the fatigue analysis.  
• Those same group IDs automatically propagate into AQB and BEMESS modules to size and verify structural elements under fatigue loads.  
• If you later generate graphical post‐processing with WINGRAF, replace the GRPD line with an equivalent BOX line (i.e. “BOX 1,2,6,12”) to ensure the graphics driver picks up the same group selection.  
• Refer to csm31_design.dat in the DECO‐check directory for a fully worked‐out input section demonstrating syntax, placement, and interdependencies.

Recommended RAG‐Vector‐Store Metadata  
• Tag: “LAM_fatigue_group_selection”  
• Keywords: GRPD, BOX, lambda, fatigue design, AQB, BEMESS, WINGRAF  
• File reference: csm31_design.dat (DECO check)  
• Section: 3.17 LAM – Lambda Values for the Fatigue Design  
• Data types: list of integers, comma‐separated input field.

sections: 3.16 GRPD – Group selection for the design

content:
The excerpt in front of us is taken from section 3.17 of a design document and carries the heading “LAM – Lambda Values for the Fatigue Design.”  In a nutshell, this table defines seven dimensionless coefficients (λ-values) that scale the equivalent stress range for different structural materials and locations in a fatigue analysis.  All of these parameters feed into the DESI module, and downstream they will be considered in the AQB (Airworthiness Qualification of Buildings) and BEMESS (Beam Element Stress) design tasks.  (If you are generating Winggraf outputs, the analogous input should be supplied via the BOX format.  See also DESI, BOX, AUSW, and particularly the GRPD conventions—e.g. GRPD 1, 2, 6, 12—for further cross-referencing.  An example of how these entries look in practice can be found in “csm31_design.dat” under the DECO check.)

Below is a line-by-line breakdown of the table’s columns and rows:

1. Column Headings  
   • Item: the symbolic name of the λ-parameter.  
   • Description: a short phrase explaining which structural element and location the coefficient applies to.  
   • Unit: since these are multipliers, they carry no physical dimension (denoted by “—”).  
   • Default: the fallback value if no user override is supplied, either a numeric constant or a reference to another λ-parameter.

2. Row Entries  

   • LAMS  
     – Description: “Coefficient equivalent stress range reinforcements midspan.”  In other words, this λ applies to the steel reinforcing bars at the midspan of beams or slabs when assessing fatigue stress cycles.  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: 1.0  

   • LMS2  
     – Description: “Coefficient equivalent stress range reinforcements inner supports.”  This is the counterpart to LAMS but for the support zones (e.g. column‐to‐beam junctions).  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: LAMS (inherits the midspan value unless explicitly overridden)  

   • LAMT  
     – Description: “Coefficient equivalent stress range tendons midspan.”  Pertains to prestressing or post-tensioning tendons in their central span region.  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: 1.0  

   • LMT2  
     – Description: “Coefficient equivalent stress range tendons inner supports.”  Similar to LAMT, this applies to tendon stresses near internal supports.  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: LAMT  

   • LAML  
     – Description: “Coefficient equivalent stress range shear links midspan.”  Covers the fatigue of shear link elements (often used in seismic detailing) at midspan.  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: 1.0  

   • LML2  
     – Description: “Coefficient equivalent stress range shear links inner supports.”  The support‐zone equivalent for shear links.  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: LAML  

   • LAMC  
     – Description: “Coefficient equivalent stress range concrete.”  A single coefficient for the concrete material itself (covering all zones).  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: 1.0  

Usage Notes:  
– All λ-values are dimensionless scaling factors that multiply the computed stress‐range cycle amplitudes before they enter a fatigue life formula (S–N curves, Miner’s rule, etc.).  
– By default, midspan and support coefficients are set to unity, implying no modification of fatigue demand.  Users can dial in local effects—such as enhanced detail quality or stress concentration corrections—by setting values greater or less than 1.0.  
– Inner-support parameters LMS2, LMT2, and LML2 default to their respective midspan siblings to ensure consistency unless a location-specific adjustment is needed.  
– In automated data workflows, these entries are usually specified under a “LAM” keyword block; look for the same names in the csm31_design.dat file to see syntactic examples.

The table shown is the definition of the COMB input block that the CSM/MAXIMA engine uses to set up up to 29 AASHTO‐style load combinations (see AASHTO Table 3.4.1-1).  Each row in the table describes one parameter (item) you can supply; the four columns are:

  • Item  
  • Description  
  • Unit  
  • Default  

Below is a row-by-row breakdown:

1. COMB  
   – Description: Combination number (1–29).  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: –  
   This integer identifies which load combination you are defining.  

2. ACT1 through ACT12  
   – Description: “Action n” (n = 1…12).  
   – Unit: LIT  
   – Default: –  
   These fields specify the name (literal) of the nth load case or action you wish to include in this combination.  Examples of actions: “G” (dead load), “P” (prestress), “LIVE”, “TRUCK”, etc.  

3. GAM1 through GAM12  
   – Description: Safety factor for Action n.  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: –  
   Each GAMn is the partial‐safety (load factor) multiplier applied to the corresponding ACTn.  In AASHTO notation G→D, P→PS, C→CR, but here you reference your own GAMU (gamma) factors or temporary GAMT values (see GAMT context).  

4. PMIN  
   – Description: Pk, inf for tendons.  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: 1  
   When you’re modelling pre‐stressing tendons, this value sets the lower bound of the tendon prestress force Pk,inf (in your chosen units).  

5. PMAX  
   – Description: Pk, sup for tendons.  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: 1  
   Similarly, this is the upper bound of the prestress tendon force Pk,sup.  

6. TITL  
   – Description: Title of the combination.  
   – Unit: LIT24  
   – Default: –  
   This is a free‐format literal (up to 24 characters) that names or describes the load combination (e.g. “STRENGTH A1”, “DEFO SLS1”).  

How the COMB block fits into the overall workflow:

– In the first MAXIMA run (“presuperposition MAXIMA”), you superpose only the variable actions (ACT1…ACTn) without dead loads or prestress (GPC).  
– In the second presuperposition run you collect the intermediate results Y_1…Y_9 (still without GPC).  
– In subsequent runs you add in G (dead load), P (prestress), C (creep + shrinkage) with the designated GAM factors from this table, producing containers for design checks (e.g. DESI, AQB beam design).  
– The PMIN/PMAX fields allow you to bracket prestress force in the superposition.  
– The TITL field lets you filter combinations later when calling DESI CHEK (single‐beam check), DESI ULTI (ULS design), DESI SIG (SLS crack analysis), or DEFO (service‐limit deformations).  

Default values are blank (“–”) for most ACT/GAM entries, meaning you must supply them explicitly.  Only PMIN and PMAX default to 1, so if you omit them the code assumes Pk,inf = Pk,sup = 1.  

By populating this table you effectively automate the generation of all required load combinations, partial‐safety factor multiplications, and naming conventions so that downstream modules (DESI, AQB, LCCS, etc.) can pick up the correct data for ULS, SLS, crack, and deformation checks.

In the upper left corner sits the SOFiSTiK logo: a stylized wave panel in blue, accompanied by the word “SOFiSTiK” in gray. Below the header, the right‐hand side of a paragraph is visible, beginning in mid-sentence with “tionen (without text ’STRE’ and without text ’DEFO’)”. This partial line refers back to the definition of combination codes used in the software (’STRE’ for strength, ’DEFO’ for deformation‐only checks).

“The crack design in AASHTO is mainly a steel stress limitation according to equation 5.6.7-1 depending on the concrete cover, the bar diameter and the bar distance:”

Immediately below this sentence is a centered, underlined heading “SECTION 5: CONCRETE STRUCTURES”. Directly under the heading is the key crack‐control formula, typeset in a display equation:

    s  ≤  700 γₑ
           ——————   –  2 d_c        (5.6.7-1)
           β_s · f_ss

Here, “s” is the maximum crack width requirement, “γₑ” is an environmental or safety factor, “β_s” is a modifier that accounts for cover geometry, “f_ss” is the specified steel stress (yield or allowable), and “d_c” is the concrete cover to the reinforcement.

Following the formula, the text “in which:” introduces a second equation for the β_s term. That equation is presented inline but offset slightly to the right:

This defines β_s as 1 plus the ratio of clear cover “d_c” to 0.7 times the effective depth (h – d_c). To the right of each equation is its reference number in parentheses: (5.6.7-1) for the main crack‐width limit and (5.6.7-2) for β_s.

This table defines the LCCS input block (“Design of Construction Stages – additional loadcases”) for a CSM AASHTO‐based analysis.  It lists the three parameters you must supply when you want to introduce bespoke loadcases for construction‐stage design (see example file csm34_stage_design.dat).  All fields marked with Default “!” are mandatory.  

Columns  
• Item – the keyword you place in your input deck.  
• Description – what this keyword controls in the construction‐stage workflow.  
• Unit – the physical or syntactic format you must follow.  
• Default – the default value if you omit the field (here, “!” means no default – you must specify it).  

1. TYPE  
 • Description: Selects the construction‐stage type as defined in the CSM‐CS module.  Commonly used stage types include B (basic), E (excavation), F (formwork), etc.  Internally, TYPE B can be converted to G_1 if you need to map a built‐in stage to a general G‐type; consult the generated file _csmlf.dat for the full list of supported type literals.  
 • Unit: LIT (a literal string)  
 • Default: !  (You must explicitly choose a stage type.)  

2. GAMU  
 • Description: Unfavourable partial safety factor (γ₍U₎).  This factor multiplies permanent or variable loads when you want to amplify them beyond their default safety values in a given stage.  Use GAMU to override the code‐prescribed γ factors (e.g. GAMU = 1.35 for dead load in Strength A1 combinations).  If you do not supply GAMU, the system reverts to the last computed safety factor from a prior MAXI or GAMT run.  
 • Unit: [–] (dimensionless)  
 • Default: !  (Must be provided if you intend to change the unfavourable factor.)  

3. GAMF  
 • Description: Favourable partial safety factor (γ₍F₎).  This factor reduces loads or resistance when you wish to apply a less conservative multiplier (e.g. 0.9 on prestress or temperature effects).  GAMF only takes effect until the next CSM MAXI run without a GAMT override.  
 • Unit: [–] (dimensionless)  
 • Default: !  (Must be provided if you intend to change the favourable factor.)  

Usage notes  
• Place the LCCS block immediately after any DESC (definition of basic loadcases) and before COMB or DESI blocks in your .dat file.  
• If you need temporary overrides of the built‐in γ values for permanent (G), prestress (P) or creep+shrinkage (C) actions, use the GAMT block instead; GAMT remains active through all subsequent AQB designs until a new MAXI run resets to code defaults.  
• Each LCCS entry generates additional loadcases that the AQB stage‐design routines treat alongside your standard AASHTO combinations (see table 3.4.1‐1 in AASHTO).  
• Consult the YouTube video “CSM Superposition and Design Concept” (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lJxF50C7pN8) and the accompanying examples (e.g. csm31_design_aashto_inch.dat, csm34_stage_design.dat) for step-by-step guidance on how these parameters feed into the DESI and AQB design tasks.

The table shown is the basic “load‐case definition” block used by the CSM COMB routine when setting up superposition and design combinations according to AASHTO Table 3.4.1-1. In a typical .dat input file (for example csm31_design_aashto_metric.dat or csm31_design_aashto_inch.dat), this section tells MAXIMA which loadcases to include, how they are to be treated, and whether they must be recalculated or read from stored results. The four fields are:

1. NO (loadcase number)  
   – This is an integer index. Each loadcase that enters the combination gets a unique NO. It is used throughout the superposition process to refer back to that particular action’s results (e.g. axial force, moments, deformations).  
   – Unit: not applicable (just an internal reference).  
   – Default: none (you must supply a number).

2. ACT (Action)  
   – A keyword or label identifying the nature of the load. Examples might be DEAD, LIVE, WIND, THRUST, PRESTRESS, TEMPERATURE, etc. These must match the action identifiers previously declared (for instance under SOFILOAD definitions or similar action‐listing blocks).  
   – Unit: not applicable (text string).  
   – Default: none; you must list the action name exactly as defined earlier.

3. TYPE (loadcase type override)  
   – In most cases the loadcase type (e.g. quasi‐static, dynamic, temperature, creep) is inherited from the SOFILOAD definition. Only if you need a different MAXIMAL LC TYPE than the one originally assigned do you use this field. For example, you might want to force a specific combination to be treated as “accidental” or “impact” even though the standard definition says “permanent.”  
   – Unit: not applicable (text, drawn from MAXI LC types).  
   – Default: blank (the program will use the action’s standard type).

4. CALC (calculation flag)  
   – A binary switch:  
     • 1 means “compute this loadcase now.” The results (bending moments, shear, displacements, etc.) will be generated by the current MAXIMA run and then stored in memory containers Y_1 … Y_9 (or similar) for later combination.  
     • 0 means “do not recalculate; use stored results.” This is useful if you have pre‐processed certain actions (for example, from an earlier ELLA run) and want to avoid redundant computation.  
   – Unit: not applicable (numeric flag).  
   – Default: 1.

How it fits into a full COMB and DESI workflow:  
– In the first MAXIMA “presuperposition” run you list only variable‐action cases (with CALC = 1) without GPC (dead load G, prestress P, creep+shrinkage C).  
– A second run superposes those results and stores them in Y_1…Y_9.  
– Subsequent runs include GPC for strength (ULS), service (SLS), deflection (DEFO) or crack‐control checks via DESI tasks.  
– The COMB table of NO/ACT/TYPE/CALC is therefore the bridge between your raw load definitions and every downstream design check (ULS, SLS, crack control, deformations).  

By keeping this table concise and accurate you ensure that each load component is handled correctly—either recalculated or reused—through the multi‐stage superposition, design, and stage‐construction sequences defined in AASHTO procedures.

Below is a comprehensive description of the single-row table you provided, organized so it can be directly embedded in a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) vector store. This write-up explains each column’s purpose, the semantics of the “CS” item, its role in the broader CSM Construction Stage Design workflow, and pointers to related resources.

1. Table Overview  
   • Purpose  
     – Defines the key input parameter “CS” used by CSM (Construction Stage Model) routines.  
     – Serves as a lookup for downstream scripts or functions that drive stage-by-stage design of reinforced elements.  
   • Scope  
     – Used alongside LCCS (List of Construction Stages) and DECS (Detailed Element Classification Scheme).  
     – Referenced by the file csm34_stage_design.dat and by related commands in the CSM environment.  

2. Column Definitions  
   • Item  
     – The mnemonic identifier for the parameter. In this table, only “CS” exists.  
     – Aligns with command-line or macro variables in “REIN” and “CTRL” scripts.  
   • Description  
     – Human-readable explanation of what the parameter controls.  
     – Here: “Number of Construction stage to be designed.” This tells the system which stage index (1, 2, 3, …) should be processed.  
   • Unit  
     – The unit of measure for the parameter.  
     – Shown as “—” because the stage index is a dimensionless integer.  
   • Default  
     – The value assumed if no explicit input is provided.  
     – Shown as “–” (dash) indicating no implicit default: the user must supply a valid stage number.  

3. Semantics of “CS”  
   • Type: Integer  
   • Valid Range: Positive integers (1, 2, … N) corresponding to stages defined in LCCS.  
   • Effect  
     – Instructs CSM routines to compute reinforcement (REIN commands) or to control checks (CTRL commands) for the specified stage.  
     – When CS=1, only stage 1 is designed; when CS=2, stage 2 is designed, and so on.  

4. Integration in Workflow  
   • Input File csm34_stage_design.dat  
     – The staging file reads “CS” to determine which portion of the project to run.  
   • “REIN” Commands Example  
     – REIN LCR 31 RMOD ACCU $ final design  
       → Operates on cumulative reinforcement for overall structure.  
     – REIN LCR 60101,60151,60201 RMOD ACCU $ stage design CS BA 101,151,201  
       → Subset of load cases for the particular stage indicated by CS.  
     – REIN LCR 1 RMOD SING $ target reinforcement distribution 1  
       → Single-stage distribution command, often paired with CS = 1.  
   • “CTRL” Commands on Quads  
     – PROG BEMESS HEAD CTRL LCRI 31 $ final design  
     – CTRL LCRI 60101,60151,60201 $ stage design CS BA 101,151,201  
     – CTRL LCR 1 $ target reinforcement distribution 1  
   • Post-Processing  
     – Results are copied (COPY) into a master report or archive.  
     – Comments and theoretical notes live under “Theoretical Background – CSM Construction Stage Design.”  
     – A tutorial video (“CSM DESI Stage Design” on YouTube) provides step-by-step guidance.  

5. Related References  
   • LCCS: Master list of all construction stages in the project.  
   • DECS: Detailed element classification that supplements stage definitions.  
   • COPY Utility: Automates transfer of stage design outputs to central storage.  
   • Theoretical Background Document: Explains rationale behind the staging logic and reinforcement algorithms.  

6. Usage Notes  
   • Always specify “CS” explicitly in the job control or batch file.  
   • Ensure that the CS value matches an entry in LCCS; otherwise the design routine will flag an error.  
   • No default means omission is treated as user oversight. Incorporate parameter validation early in your pipeline.  

This description captures the table’s structure, each field’s role, and how the “CS” parameter flows through the CSM stage-design process. Embedding this text in your RAG store will help retrievals answer questions about staging, command syntax, and integration points with LCCS/DECS.

The table defines a single input parameter, TYPE, which controls the element‐type filtering for the REIN (reinforcement) parameter in the AQB module.  In practice, TYPE tells the program which structural elements to include or exclude when extracting or aggregating results (for example, when running SUMA to sum up beam forces by CSM actions).

Table structure  
-------------  
• Item  
   – The name of the parameter. Here there is only one item: TYPE.  
• Description  
   – A brief explanation of what TYPE does and the list of valid codes.  In this table “Elementtype” is shorthand for the kind of finite‐element entity to process.  Under it are the allowed codes and their meanings:  
     • BEAM      – beams  
     • TRUS      – trusses  
     • CABL     – cables  
     • SPRI     – springs  
     • QUAD    – quad (four‐node shell) elements  
     • NODE    – support reactions (nodal springs, pads)  
     • ALL      – selects all of the above (this is also the default)  
• Unit  
   – “LIT” indicates the parameter expects a literal string (or list of strings).  
• Default  
   – “ALL” means that, unless otherwise specified, the module will process every element type listed.

Key points on usage  
-------------------  
1.  By specifying TYPE with one or more of the codes (for example, TYPE = BEAM,CABL), you restrict the results to only those element groups.  All other element types are ignored in subsequent calculations or output.  
2.  Leaving TYPE at its default (ALL) causes every supported element type to be included.  
3.  This filter is especially useful in large models or in workflows like SUMA, where you may only care about summed forces in beams (BEAM) or want to exclude reaction elements (NODE) from your external design checks.  
4.  Since SUMA can generate thousands of loadcases when combining many construction stages and actions, narrowing the element set with TYPE can reduce output size and improve clarity.  

Context with SUMA  
-------------------  
When using SUMA (the module that “stores the summed‐up beam forces separated to the used CSM actions”), you might, for instance, wish to sum forces only in beam and truss elements across all construction stages.  By setting  
   TYPE = BEAM,TRUS  
the SUMA routine will skip cables, springs, quads, and nodal support reactions, producing a more focused dataset for external design checks.  

Summary  
--------  
This concise table documents a single but powerful parameter for controlling which element categories the REIN/AQB routines (and related processes such as SUMA) should include.  With the default of ALL, it is fully inclusive, but by listing specific codes you can precisely target the subset of structural entities relevant to your design or verification task.

The snippet you’ve provided is a simple, single-row table from the “REIN – Reinforcementparameter AQB” section of the input deck. It defines one key parameter used by the AQB (reinforcement-design) module. Below is a detailed breakdown suitable for ingestion into a RAG-style vector store:

1. Table Context  
   • Section Name: REIN – Reinforcementparameter AQB  
   • Purpose: Specifies parameters governing how reinforcement distributions are handled when using the AQB solver. This section is ignored by BEMESS.

2. Column Definitions  
   – Item  
     • Token/key used in the input file.  
   – Description  
     • Brief human-readable explanation of what the Item does.  
   – Unit  
     • Physical unit (if any). A dash (–) indicates “dimensionless” or “not applicable.”  
   – Default  
     • The value assumed when the user does not explicitly specify one.

3. Row Details  
   • Item: LCR  
     – Stands for “Load Case Reinforcement” count (or similar internal mnemonic).  
   • Description: “Number of reinforcement distribution only for AQB (not BEMESS)”  
     – Controls how many distinct reinforcement layouts (or “distributions”) are computed by the AQB routine.  
     – Ignored entirely by the BEMESS design module.  
   • Unit: –  
     – This is a pure integer count, so no physical unit applies.  
   • Default: 1  
     – If the user omits LCR from their input, the solver will assume a single reinforcement distribution.

4. How It Fits into the Workflow  
   – In a typical workflow, you may run a sequence of construction-stage load cases (CSMs) and then post-process them with SUMA to get summarized beam forces.  
   – After you’ve extracted those forces, you invoke the AQB module to generate reinforcement designs.  
   – LCR tells AQB how many separate “layouts” or “design variants” to prepare. In most simple cases the default of one is sufficient; advanced users wanting multiple design options would raise LCR > 1.

5. Example Usage  
   • In your input file (e.g., “project_aqb.dat”):  
     REIN  
       LCR  2  
     END  
   • This would instruct the AQB solver to compute two different reinforcement distribution patterns based on the same force results.

6. Implications for Vector-Store Indexing  
   • Parameter Key: “LCR”  
   • Semantic Field: “reinforcement_distribution_count”  
   • Default Value (int): 1  
   • Applicability: only when “design_module = AQB”  
   • Not applicable under “design_module = BEMESS”

By capturing these attributes—table context, column semantics, row-specific metadata, operational role, and default behavior—you ensure that a RAG‐based retrieval system can answer questions such as:  
  – “What does LCR control in AQB?”  
  – “What’s the default number of reinforcement distributions?”  
  – “Can I use LCR when running BEMESS?”

The table under review defines a compact set of input parameters used in the WING pre- and post-processing environment and in related CSM design‐check runs. It is structured in four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and covers six main items:

1. XMIN, YMIN, ZMIN  
   - Description: These three parameters together form the “BOX” input for WING, specifying the minimum global coordinates of the sub‐region or component you wish to isolate for plotting or detailed checks. In practice you might enter, for example, the footprint of a bridge superstructure or a single span of a composite girder.  
   - Unit: meters [m]  
   - Default: (no numeric default; they must be supplied when BOX is used)

2. XMAX, YMAX, ZMAX  
   - Description: Complementary to the minima above, these define the maximum global coordinates of the same region. Together, (XMIN,YMIN,ZMIN) and (XMAX,YMAX,ZMAX) carve out a rectangular prism within the overall model. This focused “BOX” can be used in automatic WING runs to restrict plots to one part of the system (e.g. only a free‐cantilever segment).  
   - Unit: meters [m]  
   - Default: (no numeric default; required when BOX mode is activated)

3. GRP  
   - Description: A list of group numbers that preselect which element groups will appear in the WING plots. If your model uses composite sections or tendons, setting GRP to AUTO (the default) instructs the CSM Design‐Check routines to include only those specialized groups. You can also manually enumerate any subset of groups to be displayed.  
   - Unit: — (not dimensioned)  
   - Default: AUTO

4. XMIN–ZMAX (first CSM run input)  
   - Description: When running the very first CSM construction‐stage analysis, you may wish to limit the computational domain via a clamped box defined by its minima (XMIN,YMIN,ZMIN) and maxima (XMAX,YMAX,ZMAX). This single, combined keyword provides the same functionality in one line. It also applies to any “CSM‐DESI” stage runs that immediately follow the initial construction stage.  
   - Unit & Default: inherited from the individual XMIN … ZMAX settings

5. BOX‐GRP (CSM-DESI only)  
   - Description: An extension of GRP for later CSM‐DESI runs. If you alter the group selection after the first stage, BOX‐GRP makes sure that the updated group list is respected in all subsequent design-check stages.  
   - Unit & Default: same as GRP (AUTO by default)

6. QCUT – QUAD cuts for WINGRAF plots  
   - Description: Defines planar “cuts” through quad elements for post-processing graphics in WINGRAF when reviewing CSM-DESI outputs. You supply one or more Y-coordinates (e.g. “Y1 Y2 …”) to generate horizontal slice planes.  
     • A lone value (Y1) gives a single horizontal cut at y=Y1.  
     • An empty QCUT line deletes any previously defined cuts and restores the standard default slicing planes.  
     • WINGRAF can also import cut‐line definitions from a SOFIPLUS database (Tools → Utility → Cut‐line). In interactive mode you can toggle these DB cuts on or off (“Edit → Cuts → Database cuts → Use DB cuts”) or delete them outright (“Delete DB cuts”), forcing WINGRAF to rely exclusively on QCUT inputs.  
   - Unit: by coordinate (same global units as X/Y/Z)  
   - Default: none (use empty QCUT to reset)

Together, these parameters give the user fine control over graphical output regions, element‐group selection and slice‐plane definitions, both in batch‐driven “automatic” runs and in interactive WINGRAF sessions.

The table below defines the four numerical parameters you can supply to the QCUT block when generating WINGRAF cut‐line plots in a CSM‐DESI run.  QCUT controls exactly where planar “cuts” through your structural model are extracted for post‐processing and visualization.  In the surrounding context, QCUT inputs override or supplement any database cuts imported from SOFIPLUS, and a blank QCUT record clears all previously defined QCUT cuts, reverting to the program’s standard set.  

Table: QCUT Input Parameters for WINGRAF Cuts  
Columns:  
• Item  
   – The keyword (X1, Y1, X2, Y2) identifying one coordinate parameter.  
• Description  
   – A brief English description of what that coordinate controls in the MOVE/DRAW sequence of the cut‐line.  
• Unit  
   – The units in which the coordinate is to be entered (meters).  The subscript “1001” refers to the unit code used internally by the CSM code.  
• Default  
   – The default value if no QCUT block is given.  Here, “–” means no implicit default; cuts must be defined explicitly or fall back to the standard, program‐provided set.  

Rows (Items):  
1. X1  
   • Description: “start point of a cut (MOVE)”  
   • Explanation: This is the X‐coordinate of the first point in the cut definition.  When you issue MOVE to position the cursor for the cut, it goes to (X1, Y1).  
   • Unit: [m] (unit code 1001)  
   • Default: none  

2. Y1  
   • Description: “start point of a cut (MOVE)”  
   • Explanation: This is the Y‐coordinate of the first point in the cut.  If you supply only Y1 (leaving X1, X2, and Y2 blank), a single horizontal cut line is generated at y = Y1, spanning the full model extent in the X‐direction.  

3. X2  
   • Description: “end point of a cut (DRAW)”  
   • Explanation: This is the X‐coordinate of the second point in the cut definition.  After MOVE to (X1, Y1), the program issues DRAW to (X2, Y2), creating a straight‐line cut at any arbitrary angle.  

4. Y2  
   • Description: “end point of a cut (DRAW)”  
   • Explanation: This is the Y‐coordinate of the second point in the cut sequence.  Combined with X2, it defines the terminal point of the cut line.  

Usage notes:  
• To delete all previously defined QCUT lines and restore the default set, supply an empty QCUT block.  
• QCUT lines combine with or replace any SOFIPLUS DB cuts, which can be toggled on/off in the interactive WINGRAF menu under Edit → Cuts → Database cuts.  
• In a CSM‐DESI run, these QCUT definitions are read after any BOX‐GRP or XMIN‐ZMAX directives, ensuring user‐defined cut planes appear in the final design‐check plots.

BOX
 To achieve better plots in the automatically generated WING run, with BOX a part of the system can be selected, e.g. only the superstructure of a bridge csm5_free_cantilever.dat.
 With GPR goups can be preselected for the graphical plots in the program WING. In case the system has tendons or composite section, on GRP AUTO in the CSM Design Checks only these groups are set.
 An input to XMIN-ZMAX is used in the first construction stage CSM run and the CSM-DESI runs.
 A new input to BOX-GRP will also be taken into account in later CSM-DESI runs.
 QCUT – QUAD cuts for WINGRAF plots
 QCUT
 WINGRAF cuts for quads in the CSM-DESI plots, see examples csm32_slab_design.dat.
 With a pure input of Y1 a horizontal cut at y=Y1 is created.
 An empty input QCUT deletes previous defined QCUT cuts. Then standard cuts are created.
 WINGRAF cuts from SOFIPLUS (Tools-Utility Cut-line) are also used in the CSM-DESI plots. In the interactive WINGRAF they can be switched off in Menue-Edit-Cuts-Database cuts-’Use DB cuts’. After deleting them in WINGRAF Menue-Edit-Cuts-Database cuts-’Delete DB cuts’ only the QCUT cuts are used.

The table under discussion is part of the SCAL/EXPO input interface for a CSM-based FEA post-processing system. It defines a set of “SCAL” parameters that control how various results (displacements, forces, moments, stresses, reinforcements, etc.) are scaled and plotted in automatically generated WING runs or written out to the CSM design. Each row corresponds to one scaling item; the columns specify (1) the keyword, (2) its meaning, (3) the physical unit, and (4) the default value when no explicit input is given.

1.  Column Definitions  
    •  Item – The SCAL keyword you include in your input deck.  
    •  Description – A brief explanation of what gets scaled or switched on/off.  
    •  Unit – The physical units used in the scaling factor. A dash (—) means “unitless.”  
    •  Default – The value assumed if you omit that SCAL card.

2.  Row-by-Row Explanation  
    •  DISP  
       – Magnification factor for displacement plots.  
       – Unitless (—).  
       – Default = 0, which suppresses plotting of displacements entirely.  
    •  BEAM  
       – Scale factor applied to beam bending moment diagrams.  
       – Units: kNm.  
       – Default = 0 (i.e. no plot).  
    •  BEAN  
       – Scale factor for beam axial (normal) forces.  
       – Units: kN.  
       – Default = 0.  
    •  LOAD  
       – Scale factor for external loads in kN.  
       – Units: kN.  
       – Default = 0.  
    •  QU_M  
       – Scale factor for QUAD element bending moments (per unit width).  
       – Units: kNm/m.  
       – Default = 0.  
    •  QU_N  
       – Scale for QUAD normal forces (per unit width).  
       – Units: kN/m.  
       – Default = 0.  
    •  QU_S  
       – Scale for QUAD element stresses.  
       – Units: N/mm².  
       – Default = 0.  
    •  AQ_S  
       – Scale for AQB (beam section) stresses generated by AQB.  
       – Units: N/mm². Reinforcement stresses are automatically multiplied by AQ_S×5.  
       – In ULS mode these stresses are scaled internally; you need not supply AQ_S.  
       – Default = – (dash) indicates that, if unset, no stresses are plotted. A value of 0 explicitly suppresses beam-section stress output.  
    •  SIGD  
       – Scale factor for concrete compressive stresses in WING plots.  
       – Units: N/mm².  
       – Default = – (dash: no plot unless overridden).  
    •  QUAS  
       – Amount of reinforcement to display at QUAD-WING cuts.  
       – Units: cm²/m.  
       – Default = 0 (i.e. no reinforcement bars shown).  
    •  DESI  
       – Flag to enable WINGRAF plots in the CSM design phase.  
       – Unitless (—).  
       – Default = 1, meaning plots are generated; setting DESI 0 turns off CSM-DESI.

3.  Contextual Notes  
    – SCAL replaces the older UNIT input cards but supports identical functionality.  
    – You can preset most plot scalings to non-zero values if you want consistent legend scales across multiple load cases.  
    – SCAL DISP 0 suppresses the WING-run entirely in the resulting _csm file.  
    – SCAL AQ_S 0 deactivates AQB beam-section stress plots.  
    – SCAL DESI 0 switches off the detailed CSM-DESI design checks and associated graphics.

The table shown under the “EXPO” command defines the four keywords you can use to control what gets written into the CSM export file (…_cse.dat).  EXPO does not itself perform any structural checks or plots; its sole purpose is to gather whatever CSM input data you specify and dump it into an external file for use by downstream processes or archives.  Here is a detailed breakdown of each table entry:

1. Item = BEAM  
   • Description: “Beam element number”  
   • Unit: none (“–”)  
   • Default: “!”  
   Explanation:  
   – BEAM expects a single integer or a list of integers identifying which beam elements from the current model you wish to export.  
   – If you omit BEAM, the default “!” instructs EXPO to export all beam elements.  You can also give multiple BEAM cards (for example “BEAM 12” on the first line and “BEAM 17” on the next) to pick out a custom subset.

2. Item = X  
   • Description: “Beam ordinate”  
   • Unit: m  
   • Default: 0  
   Explanation:  
   – X sets the local coordinate along the beam’s longitudinal axis, measured in meters from the element’s start node.  
   – A default of 0 means EXPO will extract data at the very start section of each selected beam.  If you need outputs at intermediate or end sections, you can override X (e.g. X = 3.50 for a 3.5 m span).

3. Item = Y  
   • Description: “Y‐coordinate for quad selection”  
   • Unit: [m]  
   • Default: – (not set)  
   Explanation:  
   – When you are exporting data for plate‐ or shell‐type (quad) elements, Y gives one in‐plane coordinate of the location where you want the numerical (or plotted) results.  
   – No default is provided—specify both Y and Z whenever you want to export quad results at a particular point.  Internally this aligns with the BEMESS runs that generate detailed quad stress/output tables.

4. Item = Z  
   • Description: “quad selection”  
   • Unit: [m]  
   • Default: – (not set)  
   Explanation:  
   – Z is the second in‐plane coordinate for quad (plate/shell) element export.  Together with Y it fully locates the sampling point in the element’s local coordinate system.  
   – Like Y, it must be provided explicitly if you want quad data.  Leaving Z blank (and Y blank) means no quad selection points will be exported.

How this ties into the broader workflow:  
– If you want to “turn off” quad or beam‐section stress exports entirely, you can instead use the SCAL command (e.g. “SCAL AQ_S 0” disables beam‐section stresses, “SCAL DISP 0” suppresses WING‐run plots, “SCAL DESI 0” skips CSM‐DESI output).  
– For stress‐viewing within CSM you would normally use SELE to trigger a stress analysis for beams (via AQB) or quads (via XY Z). EXPO simply duplicates the necessary input definitions—BEAM, X, Y, Z—so that an external file contains exactly the same selection criteria without reinterpreting them.  
– Combining SELE (for on‐screen or WINGRAF plots) with EXPO (for export) gives you maximum flexibility: e.g. “SELE 10, X=1.75” to visualize stresses at midspan in the GUI and “EXPO BEAM=10 X=1.75” to dump the same data points into …_cse.dat for reporting or further processing.

SCAL
 SCAL replaces the old CSM input UNIT with same funktion!
 To achieve better plots in the automatically generated WING run, some scalings can be preset with SCAL.
 With SCAL DISP 0 the WING-run in the _csm file can be deactivated, with SCAL AQ_S 0 the beam section stresses can be deactivated.
 The CSM-DESI can be switched off with SCAL DESI 0.
 3.28 SELE – Selection Stress View
 SELE
 Beam selecion:
 With SELE beam x via AQB a stress analysis is generated for this beam section.With ROG RESULTS a stress plot follows. Please use AQUA stress points to print stresses on top and bottom of your beam.
 Quad selecion:
 In a quad design you can select a quad with SELE X,Y,Z. Then you get stress plots and numerical output for this quad in the BEMESS runs. For further checks on quad design see also example voided_slab.dat
 WINGRAF cuts for quads can be defined with QCUT.
 For BEAM x it is possible to input several beam numbers, e.g. with two records SELE, for a more detailed result printout.
 Per default only the start of a beam is printed or designed in the check design (x=0). For exact shear design it may be necessary to select multiple beam sections in a beam, because only then AQB can exact design haunches and flange connections. Then for the selected beam please input x=0 and x=3.50[m] (example for a 3.50m long beam).
 3.29 EXPO – Export
 EXPO
 Item Description Unit Default
 Exports the relevant CSM input to file ..._cse.dat.

The table shown defines the input parameters for the EQLC (Equation‐Load‐Case) command, which is used in CSM’s force‐ and shape‐optimization workflows to manipulate a set of uniform (scalable) load cases and permanent loads so as to achieve prescribed stress or deformation targets. Below is a detailed, field‐by‐field description of each column and how it fits into the broader optimization context.  

1. Columns  
   • Item: The keyword or identifier used in the EQLC command.  
   • Description: A brief explanation of what that keyword controls or represents—often including usage notes or references to example data files.  
   • Unit: Indicates the expected data type or unit. “LIT” means a literal string; “–” means unitless or not applicable.  
   • Default: The value assumed when the keyword is omitted.

2. Row Definitions  

• NO  
  – Description: Specifies which load case number is being defined or, if set to the literal CONT, tells CSM “continue the optimization from the previous stage.” This is particularly relevant for nonlinear analyses—see csm20_opti_intro_finalstage.dat for an end‐stage continuation example.  
  – Unit: “–/LIT” means you can enter either a numeric load‐case index or the literal CONT.  
  – Default: “!” indicates that NO is a required entry; no default load‐case number is assumed.

• TYPE  
  – Description: Defines how CSM treats the load case in the optimization. There are three valid options:  
    • G: “permanent” or “target” load case—usually the permanent loads or a specific target stage load case (e.g. target construction‐stage CS).  
    • FREE: a uniformly scalable load case whose factor is adjusted by the optimizer.  
    • F: a “following” load case that is tied to the same factor as a preceding FREE case—useful when two load cases must scale identically (for example, wind loads on symmetrical spans).  
  – Unit: LIT (literal).  
  – Default: FREE (if omitted, CSM treats the load case as a uniform, optimizable load case).

• FMIN  
  – Description: The minimum absolute factor that may be applied to this load case. For example, set FMIN = 0 if ballast or negative pressure is physically impossible.  
  – Unit: –.  
  – Default: “–” (no lower bound unless you explicitly define one).

• FMAX  
  – Description: The maximum absolute factor allowed. If you need to limit how much a load can grow during optimization (to prevent runaway amplification), specify FMAX here. The manual recommends using the EQIT command’s FMAX feature for smoother damping of factor changes.  
  – Unit: –.  
  – Default: “–” (unbounded unless defined).

• USE  
  – Description: When a load case has only an indirect effect on your target—for instance, when LC-NO is not part of the direct equation chain but influences equilibrium—you can tell EQLC to “USE” a different load case to stand in for its effect. In practice, this lets you account for secondary or coupling effects without forcing the optimizer to treat the indirect case as a primary variable.  
  – Unit: –.  
  – Default: “–” (no substitution unless specified).

3. Contextual Notes and Best Practices  
- EQLC is often used alongside EQUU, EQPP and EQBE when targeting a particular construction stage or deformation state. In stage‐by‐stage analyses (e.g. 5000-CS scalable load cases), be sure to identify the target load case in TYPE = G; this automatically propagates into EQUU…EQBE as the “CS target.”  
- For precambering in linear systems, use UEBE with MODE LINE. Because in a linear regime the deformation does not alter force distribution, you can simply adjust starting displacements without a full reanalysis (see csm23_cable_stay_optimisation_2.dat). Only for nonlinear systems must you iterate (see csm29_precamber_nonl.dat).  
- The main goal of all equation‐based optimization in CSM is to reach an optimal internal‐force state—e.g. uniform bending moment in a beam or zero bending in a cable‐stayed pylon. Displacement targets are usually avoided in the EQLC/EQUU workflow.  
- For worked examples, refer to the workshop videos (search “Overview workshop YOUTUBE videos” via GRP) and specific demos like the “CSM force optimization nonlinear cable stayed bridge” (https://youtu.be/W2GqbTaRSsE).

The input table organizes a series of worked examples illustrating how to apply the Equation‐based load‐case optimization (CSM) feature in a structural analysis environment. It is laid out in two columns:

1. Examples to optimization  
2. Input file  

Below is a detailed description of its structure and contents:

Column 1: “Examples to optimization”  
– This column lists nine distinct example scenarios, each representing a particular use case for force or deformation optimization.  
– The scenarios progress from simple, linear‐system tasks up through more complex nonlinear and staged analyses, as well as special topics such as creep effects and real‐world suspension bridge behavior.  
– The final entry points users to a consolidated overview of all examples.

Column 2: “Input file”  
– For each scenario in column 1, this column gives the filename of the corresponding .dat input file.  
– All filenames share the prefix “csm” (for “Cable‐Structure Modeling” or “Construction Stage Modeling”), followed by a two‐digit number indicating the example index, and a descriptive suffix.  
– These .dat files can be loaded directly into the analysis program to reproduce the example, study the setup, or adapt it to new projects.

Row-by-row breakdown:

1. Linear precamber  
   – Input file: csm26_precamber_spanbyspan.dat  
   – Demonstrates how to compute and impose a span-by-span linear precamber in a multi-span beam using Equation techniques in a purely linear elastic analysis.

2. Opti. final system linear  
   – Input file: csm21_equation_cable_stayed.dat  
   – Shows optimization of the final system (e.g. cable‐stayed bridge) under linear assumptions, driving internal forces into a desired pattern.

3. Opti. final system nonlinear  
   – Input file: csm20_opti_intro_finalstage.dat  
   – Extends the previous example into a geometrically or materially nonlinear regime, requiring iterative solution steps.

4. Opti. with stages nonlinear  
   – Input file: csm20_opti_intro_staged_analysis.dat  
   – Illustrates nonlinear optimization across multiple construction stages, controlling force distribution as the structure is built up.

5. Opti. with stage linear  
   – Input file: csm23_cable_stay_optimisation_2.dat  
   – Returns to a linear‐stage analysis, showing how to define target force states based on prior construction stages to optimize cable tensions.

6. Optimization incl. creep  
   – Input file: csm24_equation_iteration_creep.dat  
   – Incorporates time‐dependent creep effects into the Equation method, iteratively adjusting preloads or deformations to account for long‐term deformations.

7. Cable removal  
   – Input file: csm25_equation_cable_removal.dat  
   – Focuses on force redistribution when a cable (or set of cables) is removed from a prestressed or cable‐stayed system, optimizing for new equilibrium.

8. Suspension bridge real  
   – Input file: csm27_suspension_w_nonlopti.dat  
   – Presents a real‐world suspension‐bridge example, combining nonlinear static analysis with Equation‐based force optimization.

9. Introduction TH3 optimization  
   – Input file: csm29_precamber_nonl.dat  
   – Serves as an introductory tutorial for nonlinear precamber optimization (often referenced in the Theoretical Background – Shape and force optimization chapter).

10. -> Example overviews  
   – Input file: -> Summary of example overviews  
   – A pointer to a consolidated summary or index file, listing all workshop videos, example descriptions, and cross‐references (invoked in the GRP command).

How this table fits into the broader context:  
– It complements the detailed description of the EQLC feature (“Equation Load Cases,” see keyword EQLC) which allows users to specify target deformation or stress states and have the software compute the load‐case superposition factors automatically (including permanent loads).  
– Prior sections reference related commands and modules (EQUU, EQPP, EQBE) and link to YouTube walkthroughs for both general overviews and specialized tutorials (e.g. nonlinear cable‐stayed bridge optimization).  
– The table is meant to be your quick‐start index: load the .dat file that corresponds to your preferred demonstration, run it in the analysis environment, and follow the embedded commentary to see how target force states are defined, how the system converges, and how to extract optimized prestress, camber or cable tensions.

See also: EQUU, EQPP, EQBE
 EQLC
 With this feature, for a set of uniform load cases a set of desired deformation or stress states can be computed. The CSM calculates the load case factors that will satisfy the restrictions - together with the permanent loads.
 See also YOUTUBE Video: https://youtu.be/vRyBkK6kvvo

Below is a detailed description of each column and row entry in the provided input table, together with contextual notes on how these fields are used when defining displacement or rotation equations (EQUU) in a RAG-based vector database. This write-up also highlights the special “ADD” usage and cross-references related equation types (EQLC, EQPP, EQBE, EQIT).

1.  Table Columns  
    •  Item  
       –  The keyword or code identifying the parameter in an EQUU (or related) command line.  
    •  Description  
       –  A brief English description of the parameter’s role.  
    •  Unit  
       –  The physical unit in which the parameter is measured. A dash (–) means dimensionless.  
    •  Default  
       –  The value assumed if the field is omitted. An exclamation mark (!) indicates a required field.

2.  Row Entries  
    1.  NO (Node number)  
        –  Unit: –  
        –  Default: ! (mandatory)  
        –  Specifies the unique ID of the node to which the constraint or displacement applies.  

    2.  UX, UY, UZ (Desired translational displacements)  
        –  Unit: m (meters)  
        –  Default: – (zero unless explicitly set)  
        –  Defines the target displacement along the global X, Y or Z axis, respectively.  

    3.  PHIX, PHIY, PHIZ (Desired rotational displacements)  
        –  Unit: RAD (radians)  
        –  Default: –  
        –  Prescribes a rotation about the corresponding global axis.  

    4.  CS (Construction stage number)  
        –  Unit: –  
        –  Default: –  
        –  Associates the condition with a specific construction or analysis stage, enabling staged loading or boundary-condition application.  

    5.  ADD (Addition factor to the previous condition)  
        –  Unit: –  
        –  Default: –  
        –  Used to link multiple node equations into a single constraint. When ADD appears by itself (with no UX/UY/UZ/PHI field), it defines a multiplier in a linear relationship between the current node’s displacement and that of the previously listed node(s).  

    6.  TOL (Tolerance)  
        –  Unit: –  
        –  Default: –  
        –  Acceptable numeric tolerance for satisfying the imposed displacement or equation. Same physical dimension as the target.  

    7.  DRX, DRY, DRZ (Direction‐vector tokens)  
        –  Unit: –  
        –  Default: –  
        –  When present, these flags allow you to define a local direction vector along which the displacement (DRX, DRY) or combined direction (DRZ) applies. For example,  
           •  “DRX 1 DRY 0 DRZ 1” would resolve into a direction lying in the X–Z plane (45° between X and Z).  

3.  Special “ADD” Usage Example  
   –  Without ADD:  
      •  EQUU 312 UZ 0.115  
         → Node 312 is fixed at 0.115 m displacement in Z.  
   –  With ADD (linking nodes):  
      •  EQUU 18 UZ 0.0  
      •  EQUU 19 ADD –1  
         → Imposes the equation UZ(18) – 1.0·UZ(19) = 0.0, so the two nodes move identically in Z.  
      •  In this pattern the first line establishes the result variable (UZ) rather than a final displacement.  

4.  Cross-References  
   •  EQLC/EQPP/EQBE/EQIT – other equation types that follow a similar syntax for imposing load, phase‐coupling, boundary or temperature constraints.  
   •  Example data file: “csm30_f_precamber_equu.dat” demonstrates advanced use of EQUU with staged construction (CS), linking (ADD) and tolerances (TOL).  

By indexing each entry in a RAG vector store with these field definitions, downstream applications (post-processing, optimization, constraint tracking) can automatically parse which nodes are constrained, how they are linked by linear equations, what units apply, and how tolerances or construction stages influence the final assembly.

See also: EQLC, EQPP, EQBE, EQIT
 EQUU
 The normal usage does not contain an ADD, e..g. EQUU 312 uz 0.115: Node 312 shall get a displacement of 115[mm].
 Using ADD, only the node number and ADD must be input in the ADD line - usage e.g.:
 EQUU 18 uz 0
 EQUU 19 ADD -1 $ main usage is ADD -1
 requires that the nodes 18+19 shall get the same displacement: uz(18)=uz(19)
 Equation uz(18)-1.0*uz(19)=0.0
 In the first line [EQUU 18 uz 0] uz now defines the result of the equation, not the final displace- ment. Examlpe see optimize - csm30_f_precamber_equu.dat.

Below is a comprehensive, self-contained description of the input table, suitable for ingestion into a RAG-powered vector store. It explains each column and entry, highlights units and defaults, and points out related commands for further reference.

1. Table Purpose  
   This table defines the parameters used to specify a target reaction force (and/or moment) at a particular node in a structural analysis model. It is typically invoked via commands such as EQLC, EQUU, EQBE, EQIT or EQPP (see “See also” below).

2. Column Definitions  
   • Item  
     – The mnemonic code for each parameter. These codes appear directly in input decks or command lines.  
   • Description  
     – A brief explanation of what each parameter controls.  
   • Unit  
     – The physical units in which the parameter must be specified. If no units are shown (“–”), the value is dimensionless or inherits units from context.  
   • Default  
     – The assumed value if the parameter is omitted from the input. A dash (“–”) means no default is applied (the user must supply a value). An exclamation mark (“!”) indicates a mandatory field.

3. Row-by-Row Breakdown  
   1) NO (Node number)  
      • Description: Identifies the node at which the reaction target is enforced.  
      • Unit: – (dimensionless integer index)  
      • Default: ! (mandatory—must always be specified)  

   2) PX, PY, PZ, MX, MY, MZ (Desired reaction force/moment)  
      • Description: Six components of the target reaction vector.  
         – PX, PY, PZ specify axial forces along X, Y, Z.  
         – MX, MY, MZ specify bending or torsional moments about X, Y, Z.  
      • Unit: kN for forces (PX, PY, PZ) and kNm for moments (MX, MY, MZ).  
      • Default: – (any or all may be omitted if zero or not constrained)  

   3) CS (Construction stage number)  
      • Description: Associates this reaction condition with a specific construction or analysis stage, enabling stage-wise application of loads.  
      • Unit: – (stage index)  
      • Default: – (if omitted, applies to the global or default stage)  

   4) ADD (Addition factor to the previous condition)  
      • Description: When multiple reaction conditions are defined at the same node, ADD scales or adds this set of forces to the prior one rather than replacing it.  
      • Unit: – (dimensionless multiplier)  
      • Default: – (treated as direct replacement if omitted)  
      • Note: For detailed behavior, see the EQUU command’s ADD functionality.  

   5) TOL (Tolerance)  
      • Description: Permissible deviation from the target reaction value during iterative solution. The solver will drive the residual reaction to within ±TOL of the specified target.  
      • Unit: Matches the associated reaction component (kN or kNm).  
      • Default: – (a global tolerance or solver default is used if not provided)  

4. Usage Notes  
   – At least one of PX, PY, PZ, MX, MY, MZ must be nonzero to define an active reaction specification.  
   – The node number (NO) is always required.  
   – CS allows you to activate or deactivate reaction constraints as the structure is built or loaded in phases.  
   – The ADD flag is primarily useful in load combinations or staged load cases; for pure replacement behavior, simply omit ADD.  
   – TOL can be tightened for high-precision control of reaction forces, at the cost of additional iterations.

5. Cross-References (See also)  
   – EQLC: Defines equivalent nodal loads in a load case.  
   – EQUU: Governs user-defined reaction targets—includes detailed ADD semantics.  
   – EQBE, EQIT: Other variants for boundary-element or iterative reaction enforcement.  
   – EQPP: Post-processing reaction extraction.  
   – For ADD specifics, refer to the EQUU command documentation.
