The table is the parameter‐list for the EQBE (equivalent beam-force) entry.  It defines all possible keywords (the “Item” column), explains their meaning, shows the required units and gives any built-in defaults.  You will typically see this used in combination with related commands (EQLC, EQUU, EQPP, EQIT), and the same fields appear in those entries as well.

1. NO  
   – Element number (integer).  
   – Unit: none.  
   – Default: “!” (must be supplied by the user unless inherited).

2. X  
   – Beam ordinate (the local position along the beam where the target force or moment is applied).  
   – Unit: meters (m).  
   – Default: 0.0

3. N, VY, VZ, MT, MY, MZ  
   – Desired element forces or moments in the six basic beam‐force components:  
     • N = axial force  
     • VY, VZ = shear forces about local Y and Z  
     • MT = torsional moment  
     • MY, MZ = bending moments about local Y and Z  
   – Unit: kN for forces, kN·m for moments.  
   – Default: “–/LIT” (i.e. blank unless the literal FROM is used to pull a value from a loadcase, see LC below).

4. DSIG  
   – Delta-sigma (σ_bottom – σ_top) for a composite section, i.e. the difference between bottom and top fibre stresses.  
   – Unit: N/mm².  
   – No built-in default (must be specified if you’re controlling stress).

5. MNO  
   – Material number (in a composite cross-section) to which the DSIG request applies.  
   – Unit: none (integer index).  
   – No default.

6. ETYP  
   – Element type to which the target condition is assigned.  One of:  
     • BEAM – beam elements (default)  
     • CABL – cable elements  
     • TRUS – truss elements  
     • SPRI – spring elements  
   – Unit: literal.  
   – Default: BEAM  
   – Note: if ETYP = SPRI and you wish to apply a torsional‐moment target, you must use MT; for cables or trusses a normal‐force (N) restriction is valid.

7. CS  
   – Construction stage number (used in staged‐construction analysis).  
   – Unit: none.  
   – Default: “–” (applies to all stages unless specified).

8. ADD  
   – Addition factor to the previous condition.  Use this to incrementally add to an earlier EQBE or related entry.  
   – Unit: none.  
   – Default: “–” (no additive effect).

9. TOL  
   – Tolerance on the target value (same units as the target).  Controls convergence when iterating to achieve the force or stress.  
   – Unit: same as N, VY, etc., or DSIG.  
   – Default: “–” (use global default or none).

10. LC  
    – Load‐case specifier.  If you set any force or moment keyword to “FROM,” this field selects the source loadcase:  
      e.g.  
        FORCE ... ETYP CABL N FROM LC 1001  
      will read the axial force from loadcase 1001.  
    – Unit: loadcase number (integer).  
    – Default: “–.”

Additional notes:  
• To define a composite‐section stress requirement, combine DSIG and MNO as in  
    EQBE DSIG 50 MNO 5  
  which enforces a Δσ = 50 N/mm² in material #5.  
• For cumulative or sequential loading, see also the ADD field or the companion EQUU command.  
• The table’s structure is mirrored in EQLC, EQUU, EQPP and EQIT.

See also: EQLC, EQUU, EQPP, EQIT
 EQBE
 e.g. EQBE ... ETYP CABL N FROM LC 1001
 Also for cables and truss- and spring elements a normal force restriction can be defined. A spring torsional moment must be input with ”MT” and ETYP SPRI.
 An EQBE DSIG 50 MNO 5 defines a target of delta-sigma = 50 N/mm2. That represents a specific moment in the partial section with material 5.
 ADD see EQUU

The table below summarizes the three core EQIT keywords governing how many times and in what manner the construction-stage analysis is iterated to account for nonlinear effects such as creep and shrinkage. Units and defaults are all “–” because these parameters are pure control flags rather than physical quantities.

Item      | Description                                                        | Unit | Default  
--------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---- | -------  
ITER      | Number of iterations                                               | –    | –       
FMAX      | Iteration parameter                                                | –    | –       
          | – used like “ASE – SYST … FMAX”                                     |      |         
          | – to tame oscillations, e.g. set to 0.8                              |      |         
COPY      | Copies intermediate iteration loadcases for verification checkpoints | –  | –       

Detailed Description

1. ITER (Number of iterations)  
   • This integer flag tells the solver how many repeated passes through the construction-stage sequence are to be performed. Each pass adjusts the load-case scale factors to drive the internal forces toward the target “final stage” values when accounting for time-dependent effects.  
   • If omitted, no automatic iteration occurs—only the base construction stage loadcases will be processed.  
   • Typical usage:  
       EQIT 5  
     would invoke five sequential construction-stage runs, each starting from the output of the previous iteration.  

2. FMAX (Iteration parameter)  
   • This real-valued coefficient controls the step size or acceleration scheme used to update the load-case multipliers during each EQIT iteration.  
   • Positive values (the default mode) invoke the Crisfield acceleration typically found in ASE analysis. A value of, for instance, FMAX 1.5 allows the load-case factors to grow by up to 50 % per iteration, speeding convergence.  
   • Negative values switch to the older regula-falsi (false-position) scheme. For example FMAX –0.7 would cap the update to 70 % of the last computed increment but follow a more conservative mix of secant-based steps.  
   • On convergence difficulties or oscillatory behavior, users are advised to lower FMAX to values such as 0.8 or even below unity.  

3. COPY (Intermediate-case copier)  
   • When specified, the COPY flag instructs the solver to clone the current “highest target” loadcase after each iteration into a user-defined slot. This is useful for post-processing checks or exporting intermediate force states.  
   • Syntax example:  
       EQIT 5 COPY 80000  
     With CS-max = 701, the base target loadcase is 4701. The sequence of saved cases becomes:  
       – LC 80000 = initial LC 4701 (pre-iteration)  
       – LC 80001 = post-1st iteration result of LC 4701  
       – …  
       – LC 80005 = post-5th iteration result of LC 4701  
   • These snapshots allow comparison of stress or displacement evolution over the iteration loop.  

Related Keywords and Workflow  
• EQBE, EQUU, EQPP – define upper/lower bounds and stopping tolerances on internal-force or displacement targets for EQIT convergence.  
• CAMBER…MODE EQIT – if force convergence is reached, an extra pass will run the full construction sequence with the final multipliers to refine the precamber shape.  
• KINK – can be combined to insert geometric “kinks” in a construction stage, for instance to correct on-site deformations. An empty KINK input or a new CSM stage clears any previously stored kink definitions.  
• See example files csm24_equation_iteration_creep.dat, csm29_precamber_nonl.dat and csm30_c_precamber_site.dat for detailed recipes.

The image is a pair of side-view sketches (in green and red) of a two-span cable-stayed bridge model, illustrating the “gap‐closing” problem that arises when foundations settle unevenly and how a KINK segment can be used to remedy it. Below is a detailed breakdown of what each sketch shows and how it ties into the surrounding context (EQIT iteration, nonlinear precamber, KINK input).

1. General Layout  
 – The structure consists of two symmetric cable-stayed spans meeting at a central pylon zone. Each half-span is supported by a set of inclined stays fanning out from the pylon head to discrete connection points (nodes) along the deck.  
– All structural elements (deck segments, stay cables, pylons) are drawn in light green lines. Support locations at the ends of the deck are marked by red symbols:  
   • Left-end support: a red filled triangle (roller or pinned support).  
   • Right-end support: a red filled square (fixed or guided support).

2. Left Sketch: Asymmetric Settlement Gap  
 – The deck appears to slope gently downward from the central pylons toward each abutment, but the slope toward the left support is steeper, leaving a visible vertical gap between the last deck node and the red triangle support. This gap indicates that the left foundation has settled less (or the deck has moved downward more) relative to the right.  
– Cables on the left span are slightly longer or more taut, reflecting the unbalanced geometry. The red triangle support sits below the deck’s end node, with no connection drawn—this highlights the “open gap” condition.  
– The right span in this sketch meets the right support cleanly (deck node touches the red square), showing that only the left side exhibits the settlement-induced discontinuity.

3. Right Sketch: KINK Segment Introduced  
 – In the second drawing, the deck profile on the left span now lines up with its roller support, indicating that the gap has been closed. However, a small local “kink” appears just to the right of the left pylon: the deck segment has an intentional angular bend.  
– This kink is the result of inserting a KINK segment into the construction stage model (.cdb) to compensate for the unsymmetric settlement (as described in csm30_e_precamber_kink.dat). By adding that extra segment, the finite‐element model “absorbs” the differential movement without requiring unrealistic cable force changes.  
– All stays remain green and retain their original anchorage points at the pylons, but the deck geometry is now piecewise straight rather than one continuous line. The right span still meets its abutment squarely.

4. Connection to Nonlinear Iteration (EQIT) Context  
 – In practice, one would first try to close the gap through iterative adjustment of load-case factors with EQIT (using Crisfield acceleration or regula‐falsi for convergence). You can set tolerances with EQBE, EQUU or EQPP to stop once forces match target values.  
– If pure iteration cannot fully correct the deck elevation mismatch (because the settlement is too asymmetric), the KINK input offers a deterministic fix: it introduces an extra segment whose orientation or length compensates for the residual displacement.  
– The combination of EQIT (to balance cable forces and construction-stage loads) and a final KINK segment (to close geometric gaps) yields a precise precamber result, as documented in the “Theoretical Background – Nonlinear precamber analysis.”

5. Caption and Source  
 – The figure is labeled “Figure 3.4: csm30…dat: Problem on closing the gap due to unsymmetric settlement.” It visually contrasts the initial settlement‐induced gap scenario (left) with the post-KINK corrective geometry (right).  
– This example lives in the broader workflow of CSM construction‐stage analysis, where nonlinear effects (creep, shrinkage, settlement) are handled through iterative runs (EQIT) and, if needed, kinks to fine-tune final alignment.

The table shown defines the syntax and default values for the KINK block in a CSM (construction stage model) input. KINK is a specialized command used when you need to introduce a local “kink” or angular offset in a selected group of elements during a particular construction stage—most often to correct site‐measured deformations or to fine-tune precamber. An empty KINK card (or any subsequent new CSM stage input) clears previously stored kinks from the database.

Columns  
•  Item: the keyword or parameter name.  
•  Description: a brief explanation of what the parameter controls.  
•  Unit: the measurement unit (if applicable).  
•  Default: what value is assumed when none is provided.

Rows

1. CS  
   – Description: Construction stage index.  
   – Unit: none.  
   – Default: “!” indicates this is a required field.  
   – Notes: CS must correspond to one of the numbered stages defined elsewhere in your CSM input. This is where the kink will be applied.

2. GRP  
   – Description: Group number.  
   – Unit: none.  
   – Default: “!” (required).  
   – Notes: Specifies which group of elements (defined via GRP commands) receives the kink. The group must already exist.

3. DXX  
   – Description: Rotation about the global X-axis (tilt around longitudinal axis).  
   – Unit: milliradians (mrad), using the internal [mrad]_1004 unit code.  
   – Default: 0.  
   – Notes: Positive DXX rotates the entire group about X; use small values (typically a few mrad) to correct camber or twisting.

4. DYY  
   – Description: Rotation about the global Y-axis (tilt in the transverse vertical plane).  
   – Unit: [mrad]_1004.  
   – Default: 0.  
   – Notes: Adjusts vertical camber or lateral bending offset.

5. DZZ  
   – Description: Rotation about the global Z-axis (in‐plane twist).  
   – Unit: [mrad]_1004.  
   – Default: 0.  
   – Notes: Applies a planar rotation, used less often but available for complex deformation corrections.

Typical Usage Example  
— To introduce a 2 mrad downward tilt about Y in group 12 during stage 5:  
   KINK  
     CS   5  
     GRP  12  
     DYY  2.0  

After this card is read, the solver will insert a local hinge that enforces the specified rotations on all elements in GRP 12 at the start of stage 5. If you later decide to remove or redefine kinks, simply supply an empty “KINK” input or move on to the next stage without including DXX/DYY/DZZ parameters.

Contextual Notes  
– KINK is often used together with advanced precamber procedures (see “Theoretical Background – Nonlinear precamber analysis”).  
– For iterative internal force adjustment (e.g. for creep/shrinkage), you would combine KINK with EQIT (equation iteration) entries.  
– Example files: csm30_e_precamber_kink.dat shows KINK in action on a cable-stayed bridge model.  
– Whenever force convergence is achieved via EQIT, an extra run of the construction sequence helps capture precise camber (see csm29_precamber_nonl.dat).

By following this table, one ensures that kinks are applied rigorously and reproducibly, greatly aiding in field-driven corrections and advanced construction-stage analyses.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter breakdown of the input table used by the CABL function (cable anchorage angle check).  This table defines the range of loadcases to be processed and the “type” of angle results to report.  Units and defaults are noted, and each entry is tied back to how CABL uses it when computing nodal rotations at cable anchorages.

1.  LC1  
   • Description  
     – The first (lowest) loadcase number in the range to be included in the angle check.  
     – For the very first input line, LC1 also defines the permanent (reference) state against which all other cases are compared.  In subsequent lines you may repeat the permanent LC if you wish to isolate multiple case ranges.  
   • Unit: — (loadcase indices are integer identifiers, no physical unit)  
   • Default: “–” (must be supplied by the user)

2.  LC2  
   • Description  
     – The last (highest) loadcase number in the set.  CABL will process LC1, LC1+1, … up through LC2.  
     – All loadcases in this inclusive range are used to compute rotation‐difference extrema (min/max) in the main plane.  
   • Unit: — (integer index)  
   • Default: “–” (must be supplied by the user)

3.  TYPE  
   • Description  
     – Selects how CABL builds the rotational result for each loadcase in the LC1→LC2 range:  
       • FULL: Compute the absolute angle change daA/daE including dead-load in global z plus prestress effects.  In other words, the full rotation at anchor nodes A and E.  
       • DIFF: Compute only the differential change relative to the permanent (reference) loadcase.  Dead-load and prestress are assumed present in the reference state, so output is simply the incremental rotation for each LC.  
     – The difference form is often used when only variation about the baseline geometry is of interest.  
   • Unit: LIT (literal string “FULL” or “DIFF”)  
   • Default: FULL  

How these inputs affect CABL’s calculations  
– CABL reads each input line in sequence.  The first LC1 defines the permanent state.  For each subsequent LC1→LC2 and TYPE, the code:  
  • Extracts cable end tangents from ASE-TH3 if available (nonlinear sagging, wind, etc.), or else assumes a flat cable.  
  • Computes raw end‐tangent inclinations αA, αE = ATAN(±h/(l−xy) + a1 ∓ a2E) in the global “main plane.”  
  • Subtracts the superstructure/pylon anchorage rotation a3 at nodes A and E to isolate cable‐only rotation:  
      daA =  +a1 − a2E − a3A  
      daE =  +a1 + a2E − a3E  
  • Depending on TYPE, either presents these da-values directly (FULL) or subtracts the permanent‐state da’s and reports only the difference (DIFF).  
  • Records the minimum and maximum daA/daE across all cases in the range LC1…LC2.  

Default behavior (TYPE=FULL) includes all dead loads and prestress in each case; switching to DIFF yields a cleaner view of variations around the baseline. This table therefore lets you tailor the angle‐check run to any contiguous block of loadcases and choose whether you want absolute or incremental rotations at the cable anchorages.

CABL
 This function has not much to do with the CSM itself. But it may help do design rotation angles at cable anchorages.
 For cables see also YOUTUBE Video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PmAeevUeJcU
 All existing loadcases from LC1 to LC2 are used. Multiple input lines are allowed. LC1 of the first input line defines the permanent state (in following lines the permanent LC may occur again).
 Example see: csm21_cable_anchorage_angle.dat and csm21_cable_anchorage_angle_3d.dat

 The real end tangent inclination for a cable in a loadcase in the main plane is: (in the above figure global z falls from A to E - so -h must be inserted:)

In the second part you’ll find a formatted table showing how the transverse rotations (t-direction) and main-plane rotations (u-direction) would be combined for the three “parts” of cable 14001, as if extracted from csm21_cable_anchorage_angle_3d.dat under a transverse wind case.  All angle units are in degrees (°).

Part 1: Detailed Description of the Image  
1. Overall View  
   • You are looking at a 3D model of a stay-cable and girder arrangement, shown in perspective.  The girder (blue) spans horizontally, supported at its ends by red bearing blocks.  A vertical mast or pylon rises upward at the center, splitting the girder into two cantilever spans.  
   • The cable runs from the top node A on the pylon down to node E on the girder.  Two thin “hanger” elements (light blue lines) connect intermediate points on the cable to the girder.

3. Local Cable Coordinate System (ss-t-u)  
   • The local longitudinal axis ss (black arrow) runs along the cable from top node A down toward node E.  It is drawn slightly off the girder to illustrate direction.  
   • The local normal axis u (black arrow) is defined as the direction perpendicular to ss, projected as much as possible into global Z.  In this view it points back and slightly upward.  
   • The local transverse axis t (black arrow) completes the orthogonal triad: t is perpendicular to both ss and u.  Here it projects mostly in the left-to-right direction relative to the girder.

4. Sign Conventions and Hanger Details  
   • The caption at the bottom (“3.6: cable coordinate system for SYST GDIR NEGZ and hanger start node A = upper node”) indicates that the hanger elements begin at A (upper) and terminate at E (lower).

5. Key Points Referenced in the Accompanying Text

The input table defines seven key parameters for the MEX command in the CSM (Cross-Sectional Stress Model) environment. MEX generates a modified load case by copying an existing one (LC) and, if a beam or quad element is under net compression, adds an eccentricity-driven bending moment to ensure the section is checked under worst-case combined loading. Below is a detailed description of each table entry:

1. LC  
   • Description: Specifies the original load case number to copy. MEX takes this load case as the baseline.  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: mandatory (no default; must be supplied with “!”)  
   • Notes: This is the primary reference. If LC is omitted or invalid, MEX cannot proceed.

2. DIFF  
   • Description: Defines the number (offset) of the newly created load case. MEX writes results into this new case.  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: mandatory (no default; must be supplied with “!”)  
   • Notes: Using DIFF avoids overwriting the original load case. DIFF must differ from LC.

3. EX_Z  
   • Description: Eccentricity applied to the beam normal force or quad normal force in the local z-direction.  
   • Unit: millimeters [mm]  
   • Default: 0  
   • Notes: A positive value shifts the line of action in +z; negative values shift toward –z. You must specify an eccentricity if you want to amplify bending in z.

4. EX_Y  
   • Description: Eccentricity of the beam normal force in the local y-direction.  
   • Unit: millimeters [mm]  
   • Default: 0  
   • Notes: Analogous to EX_Z but in the y-axis. Used to generate moment My = N × ex_y.

5. EX_R  
   • Description: Additional beam eccentricity along the principal bending axis (“skew main moment”). Acts on top of EX_Z and EX_Y.  
   • Unit: millimeters [mm]  
   • Default: 0  
   • Notes: Calculates a resultant eccentricity vector whose magnitude equals ex_r. If the normal force N is compressive (negative), MEX computes ΔM = |N| × ex_r and resolves it into ΔMy and ΔMz proportional to the pre-existing My and Mz components. When My and Mz are zero, ex_r splits equally between y and z.

6. EX_Q  
   • Description: Eccentricity applied to quad (plate or shell) elements. In quads, MEX uses ex_q for both principal normal directions.  
   • Unit: millimeters [mm]  
   • Default: 0  
   • Notes: Quad elements have two orthogonal principal directions. EX_Q displaces the normal force line equally into both, simulating combined bending under compression.

7. GRP  
   • Description: Group number filter. When omitted, MEX applies the specified eccentricities to all element groups.  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: all groups (denoted by “–”)  
   • Notes: To vary eccentricities by group, repeat MEX lines with GRP n. For example, you can assign ex_z=80 mm/ex_y=50 mm to group 4 and ex_z=20 mm/ex_y=20 mm to group 6, leaving other groups unaffected or at default.

Usage pattern:  
+PROG CSM  
HEAD MEX lc 15 diff 100000 ex_z 60[mm] ex_y 30[mm] end  

In this example, if N=–1000 kN, My=300 kNm, Mz=–400 kNm, then the skew main moment magnitude is 500 kNm. With ex_r=60 mm, ΔM=0.060 m×1000 kN = 60 kNm. The additional moments resolve to ΔMy=36 kNm and ΔMz=48 kNm, leading to revised My=336 kNm and Mz=–448 kNm.

MEX
 This function has not much to do with the CSM itself. But it may help do design compression members.
 MEX makes a copy of a loadcase and increases the bending moments in beams and quads if the normalforce is compression. In Quads this is done in the two main normal force directions using only ex_q
 example:
 +PROG CSM
 HEAD MEX lc 15 diff 100000 ex_z 60[mm] ex_y 30[mm] end
 EX_R 60[mm] will give e.g. for N=-1000kN and MY=300kNm and MZ=-400kNm -> skew main moment = 500kNm: delta-M= 0.060*1000 = 60kNm in direction of the skew main moment: delta-MY= 60kNm*300/500 = 36kNm -> MY= 300+36 = 336kNm delta-MZ= 60kNm*400/500 = 48kNm -> MZ= -400-48 = -448kNm On MY=0 and MZ=0 , EX_R is applied for both directions.
 If you want to vary the excentricities per group you can input following lines without LC and DIFF, example:
 MEX lc 15 diff 100000 ex\_z 60[mm] ex\_y 30[mm] $ default all groups MEX lc - diff - ex\_z 80[mm] ex\_y 50[mm] GRP 4 MEX lc - diff - ex\_z 20[mm] ex\_y 20[mm] GRP 6

The table defines the input parameters for the BOND‐related command in the CSM program. It comprises four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and three parameter rows: LC, SIGN and END. Below is a detailed breakdown suitable for indexing in a RAG vector store:

1. Column Definitions  
   • Item  
     – The name of the input parameter recognized by the CSM preprocessor under the BOND (and related) functionality.  
   • Description  
     – A brief explanation of what the parameter controls or how it modifies the bond‐force calculation. This ties directly into the text’s discussion of “bond force” jumps between adjacent steel beams in a composite system.  
   • Unit  
     – The expected unit or notation for the parameter value. If a dash (–) appears, the parameter is dimensionless or uses an internal literal type (LIT).  
   • Default  
     – The value assumed if the user does not override the parameter on the command line or in the input file.

2. Parameter Rows  
   A. LC (Load Case)  
     – Description: Specifies which load case(s) the BOND command should process. Internally MAXI logic will treat this LC as encompassing all CSM‐MAXI normal‐force loadcases. In practice you choose a load case number (e.g. 4015) to capture the maximal normal‐force differences between adjacent beams and thereby compute bond forces automatically.  
     – Unit: “– / LIT” indicates that LC can be given as a literal integer (the load case identifier).  
     – Default: “!” denotes that this parameter is mandatory. An exclamation point signals that the user must supply a load case id; there is no automatic default case.  

   B. SIGN  
     – Description: Governs the sign convention for bond forces.  
         • If SIGN = 0, the output bond force is forced to be non‐negative (absolute value). Every jump in beam normal force is reported as a positive scalar, ignoring sign.  
         • If SIGN = 1, the sign of the jump (tension versus compression transfer) is preserved in the output.  
     – Unit: “–” indicates a dimensionless selector flag.  
     – Default: 1 (signed mode). This means by default the user sees positive or negative bond‐force values corresponding to the direction of force transfer.  

   C. END  
     – Description: Determines at which beam chain locations the bond‐force results are stored. There are three options:  
         0 = Do not store bond‐force values at the chain ends (for instance, if the end is fully restrained in an abutment wall, bond does not develop there).  
         1 = Store the computed bond force at beam chain ends only.  
         2 = In addition to chain ends, also store bond‐force values at junction points where beams intersect or splice.  
     – Unit: “–” (dimensionless choice flag).  
     – Default: 1 (store at ends but not at junctions).  

3. How This Table Fits Into the Larger Context  
   • The BOND command eliminates the need to manually define spring connectors to extract bond shear between slab and girder. Instead, it directly reads the jump in normal forces between adjacent beam elements in a “real‐system” composite model (slab and steel beam defined separately).  
   • LC drives which load‐case scenario is evaluated (e.g. MAX‐MIN‐N loadcase to ensure the largest midspan normal force). SIGN allows designers to distinguish between tensile and compressive bond. END determines the spatial coverage of the reported bond results.  
   • In practice, a user would invoke BOND in the CSM input deck as follows:  
       +PROG CSM  
       HEAD BOND LC 4015 SIGN 1 END 2  
       end  
   • This table ensures that the preprocessor can validate user input, apply defaults where appropriate, and integrate bond‐force extraction seamlessly into subsequent design checks (for shear in dowels or welds).

The table shown defines the full set of input parameters required by the CSM “TEMP” command (temperature loading) when working with TBEX T-Beams or a beam-quad real-system.  It is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and ten logical entries (some of which expand into sub-items).  Below is a row-by-row breakdown:

1.  Item: LC  
    • Description: Load case  
    • Unit: —  
    • Default: “!” (mandatory user input)  
    → Identifies the unique load case number under which the temperature field will be stored.

2.  Item: TN  
    • Description: Constant temperature increase  
    • Unit: [degree]₁₂₁₅  
    • Default: 0  
    → A uniform temperature offset (in °) applied to the entire section at the reference plane (global z = 0 in ZVAR, or nodal centroid plane in SLAB).

3.  Item: DT  
    • Description: Temperature gradient (local z, positive=bottom warm)  
    • Unit: [degree]₁₂₁₅  
    • Default: 0  
    → Linear change of temperature per unit length in the local z-direction; positive values imply the bottom fiber is hotter than the top.

4.  Item: HM  
    • Description: Average height of main girder (DT per meter is calculated with this height)  
    • Unit: [mm]₁₀₁₁  
    • Default: “!”  
    → Defines the full height (quad + beam) over which the global gradient DT is normalized.

5.  Item: SM  
    • Description: Average eccentricity main girder below nodal plane  
    • Unit: [mm]₁₀₁₁  
    • Default: “!”  
    → Vertical offset of the zero-strain plane (no longitudinal elongation) measured from the element’s nodal plane.  

6.  Item: GRP  
    • Description: Beam- and Quad-elements from group GRP up to TO get this temperature loading  
    • Unit: —  
    • Default: –  
    → Starting element group index: all beam- and slab-(quad) elements with group IDs in [GRP, TO] will receive the defined TN/DT field.

7.  Item: TO  
    • Description: (see GRP)  
    • Unit: —  
    • Default: –  
    → End group index inclusive for the temperature assignment.

8.  Item: GRPM  
    • Description: Group number of main girders (only necessary in case of haunched main girders)  
    • Unit: —  
    • Default: –  
    → When girders vary in depth (haunched), this group ID marks the first of the main-girder groups whose DT gradient is to be scaled individually.

9.  Item: TOM  
    • Description: GRPM to TOM are treated as haunched main girders (the DT is applied over their individual height)  
    • Unit: —  
    • Default: –  
    → Defines the last group index of haunched girders; those in [GRPM, TOM] each get a custom DT/h.

10. Item: MODE  
    • Description: Analysis mode  
    • Unit: LIT  
    • Default: SLAB  
    → Two possible settings:  
      – SLAB: Grillage (beam-quad) model. The slab (quad elements) always shares the same top-surface temperature, regardless of any longitudinal incline of the bridge. Local z-axes must point downwards.  
      – ZVAR: Full 3D shell model. Temperature at global z = 0 equals TN; DT is applied per meter in the global gravity direction. Local z-axes may point sideways for web quads.

11. Item: TITL  
    • Description: Title of the loadcase  
    • Unit: LIT24  
    • Default: –  
    → Optional text label (up to 24 characters) describing the temperature scenario (e.g. “Summer Hot Top”).

In practice, a complete TEMP command might look like:

+PROG CSM  
HEAD TEMP LC 90 TN +27.0 DT –12.3 HM 1800 SM 656 GRP 1 TO 6 MODE SLAB TITL “SummerTopHot”  
END

This instructs CSM to generate a temperature field for load case 90, imposing +27 °C at the reference plane, a bottom-warmer gradient of 12.3 °C/m over a 1.80 m section height, with zero‐strain at 0.656 m below the slab nodal plane, applied to element groups 1 through 6, using the SLAB grillage approach and labeling it “SummerTopHot.”

The picture is a horizontal cross-section and accompanying temperature-gradient diagram for a composite T-beam with a total depth of approximately 1.80 m and a top flange width of 6.00 m. The left-hand portion of the drawing shows the actual T-section in solid hatching. A thick concrete slab forms the flange at the top, and a deeper, narrower web (stem) extends downward from its middle. The slab is drawn as a long, thin rectangle 6 000 mm in length (annotated along its upper edge) and about 150–200 mm in thickness; below it, centered laterally, is the web approx. 1 600 mm tall and about 900–1 000 mm wide. Two small circular symbols appear embedded in the web: one near the mid-depth (likely denoting a shear connector or reinforcing bar) and another smaller dot at the very bottom face. Dimension lines along the left side of the section confirm the overall beam depth of “1800” (presumably millimeters). All concrete elements are hatched at a 45° angle with uniform spacing.

To the right of the T-section is a schematic temperature profile drawn as a straight sloping line through a series of thin horizontal tick marks, representing layers of the beam depth. A circle labeled “O” marks the zero-strain or neutral-temperature plane. Above that point, the line segment is colored blue and slopes upward toward the top face, indicating a positive temperature increase (tension on the hot side); below it the line is colored red and slopes downward toward the bottom face, indicating a negative temperature relative to that neutral plane. The neutrality point lies approximately 0.656 m below the top of the section, consistent with the centroid location of the composite section. From that neutral line the blue segment rises to the top of the slab with a total change of +X°C (proportional to the specified +7°C over the full 1.80 m height), while the red segment extends down to the bottom of the web with the complementary negative change.

Beneath the drawing is the figure caption “Figure 3.8: dt = +7 degree on a 1.80 m height t-beam,” indicating that a net temperature difference of +7 °C is applied between extreme fibers. The overall layout is intended to show how a linear temperature gradient can be imposed on a composite concrete-steel T-beam in a “real system” model, fixing zero longitudinal strain at the beam’s centroid depth (SM = 0.656 m) so that curvature induced by thermal loading is correctly represented. The diagram highlights the ease with which the CSM “TEMP” command can create such a gradient without resorting to complicated element-by-element temperature assignments.

The image is a computer‐generated, three‐dimensional view of a finite‐element model for a composite steel‐concrete bridge superstructure under a specific temperature‐induced loading case (loadcase 999, “Summer posdt TN+wm*dT (top=hot)”). Key features include:  
1. Geometry and Global Shape  
 • A continuous, slightly curved bridge segment spans across three support piers.

1. Upper subfigure (“quad 20 cm BELO”):

     • Below it hangs a blue rectangular steel beam section 80 cm tall, labeled “beam 80 cm.”

2. Lower subfigure (“quad 20 cm ABOV”):

General notes implied by the drawing and surrounding text:

   - “SM” denotes the height of the zero‐elongation plane relative to a reference level (the datum).

content:
BOND
 This function has not much to do with the CSM itself. But it may help do design compression members.
 ‚Real system’ means that for the concrete slab and for the steel beam separate elements are used. The beam section only represents the steel girder and is hanging eccentrically below the slab.
 A positive bending of the total system delivers a tension normal force in the beam. Near the supports the normal force in the beam decreases from one beam to the next. This jump in the beam force represents the bond force.
 With the command BOND this jump in the normal force between two beams is stored as bond force and it is no longer necessary to define complicated spring connectors to extract the bond force. After BOND, WINGRAF offers design-beams-stress of the material-Shear in dow- els/welds
 A little bit critical is the use of Maxima oder Ella load cases as usually different basic load cases are used on two neighboring beams. So you should not use the Maxima load cases Max-Min-VZ as the sign of the shear force jumps inside the span.
 We recommend to use the Maxima load case Max-Min-N. This load case contains the max- imum normal force in mid span and it is guaranteed that this normal force is transferred via the beam jumps as bond force up to the support. Only the distribution maybe shifted a little bit to the supports. We recommend an additional shift of the maximum bond force into the direction of midspan. It may also be senseful to calculate the maximum traffic combination for the maximum bending moment in midspan as a separate ASE loadcase and then also take into account the bond force of this separate loadcase.
 Usage: Example see: steel_composite_real.dat
 +PROG CSM HEAD BOND LC 4015 end
 TEMP – Temperature input on TBEX T-Beams
 TEMP
 This function has not much to do with the CSM itself. But it is very useful for a temperature input on TBEX T-Beams.

Usage: Example see: steel_composite_real.dat. +PROG CSM HEAD BOND LC 4015 end. TEMP – Temperature input on TBEX T-Beams. TEMP. This function has not much to do with the CSM itself. But it is very useful for a temperature input on TBEX T-Beams..
 A statically determined supported bridge superstructure shall not get internal restraint stresses. All elements shall get a constant curvature - and at the same time in the cross direction (double curvature)!
 You best fix the curvature for the most important element, usually the superstructure beams e.g. with a heigth of 1.80 m.
 If we want to apply e.g. a dT/h of +7°C we have to apply 7°/1.80m (DT=7 , HM=1.80[m]). In the height of the center of gravity of the main girder at SM=0.656 m no longitudinal strain shall occur, dt shall be 0.0 there.
 This leads to a surface temperature of -0.656m*7°/1.80m = -2.53°
 To get the same curvature in the 0.45m thick slab we must apply only 1.75°/0.45m (=7°/1.80m). E.g. a 0.25m thick slab may only get 1.00°/0.25m.
 To get the same longitudinal elongation on the top of the bridge we get:
 top of main beam
 -2.53°C bottom +4.47°C = beam
 top 0.45m slab -2.53°C bottom -0.78°C = quad loading top 0.25m slab -2.53°C bottom -1.53°C = quad loading
 Such a temperature on a haunched quad can be input in absolute temperatures with QUAD TYPE ’T’. But this is quit complicated and so we implemented this feature in CSM to define such a temperature field, e.g. for summer posdt TN+wm*dT (top=hot):
 TEMP LC 90 TN +27.0*1.00 DT -12.3*0.75 HM 1.80[m] SM 0.656[m] GRP 1 TO 6

The input table is a concise, four-column specification of two related parameters—OPT and VAL—that control the scope and detail of output in a creep-analysis reporting tool (e.g. in combination with ECHO, CREP, RCRE commands). Below is a structured breakdown of its contents and context:

1. Overall Structure  
   • Columns  
     – Item: the keyword to be specified by the user.  
     – Description: a text summary of what the keyword does or accepts.  
     – Unit: the expected data type or literal category (here, LIT for “literal”).  
     – Default: the value assumed if the user omits the keyword.  

2. Row 1: OPT  
   • Purpose  
     – Determines which subsets of data are printed in the creep-parameter output.  
     – Works in tandem with “ECHO RCRE” and “CTRL CREP RCRE” to switch on or off specific parts of the listing (for instance, later-acting load parts’ creep factors).  
   • Allowed Literals (unit = LIT)  
     – CS: Construction stages  
     – GRP: Groups  
     – LC: Load cases  
     – CREP: Creep parameters (with optional specification of output-line width)  
     – RCRE: Partial creep factors  
     – OPTI: EXTR output for Target-LC components  
     – EXPO: (typically for exposure or similar domain-specific data)  
     – FULL: All of the above options combined  
   • Default Value = FULL  
     – If OPT is omitted, the system prints the entire suite of tables for CS, GRP, LC, CREP, RCRE, OPTI, and EXPO.  

3. Row 2: VAL  
   • Purpose  
     – Controls the verbosity or “extent” of the output itself.  
     – Affects whether calculations are performed and how much detail is printed.  
   • Allowed Literals (unit = LIT)  
     – OFF: No calculation or output at all  
     – NO: Skip output (calculations may still run)  
     – YES: Standard, regular output  
     – FULL: Extensive output, showing additional intermediate results  
     – EXTR: Extreme output, with the highest level of detail  
   • Default Value = YES  
     – By default, users receive the standard set of results without overwhelming detail.  

4. Contextual Usage Notes  
   • Wide-Table Output  
     – When many construction stages or load cases exist, the table can become very wide. You may use “ECHO CREP <width>” (for example, ECHO CREP 245) to increase column count in the listing.  
     – Caution: For printer reports on large paper formats, do not set the width above 150, or columns may be truncated or become unreadable.  
   • Viewing and Archiving  
     – For best results, view the wide table via TEDDY, opening the generated .erg or .lst file.  
     – To store the .lst file in an SSD task, include at the end of your program:  
         PROG TEXTILE  
         HEAD  
         …  
         END  
         +sys copy $(name).lst file.lst  

This table thus gives users precise control over which creep-related data are output and how verbose that output will be, while integrating smoothly with existing ECHO/CREP/RCRE report-generation workflows.

ECHO
 With ECHO RCRE FULL/NO a listing of creep values of later acting load parts can be switched on/off in case of CTRL CREP RCRE.
 The output of the creep parameters in a wide table shows the development of the construction stages in a good overview. If you have many stages, you can increase the width of this table with ECHO CREP 245. Using report e.g. with greater paper format, please do not input ECHO CREP greater than 150 because otherwise not all columns are visible!
 To view such a wide table please use TEDDY and view the result file .erg or .lst. In an SSD-Task you can store the .lst file with a +sys copy into a file file.lst:
 PROG TEXTILE
 HEAD
 ...
 END
 +sys copy $(name).lst file.lst

The input files which are explained here are to be found in the installation directory SOFiSTiK in the subdirectory csm.dat\english. You will find an overview there in file
 overview_csm_examples_english.pdf
 Alternatively you will find the examples via the TEDDY menu HELP > EXAMPLES sorted by program name and language.
 For additional help like tutorials, tutorial movies and practical examples please refer to the SOFiSTiK Infoportal (www.sofistik.com/Infoportal).

The image presents a finite-element–style deflection plot of a four-span continuous bridge, drawn in a series of closely spaced rectangular deck elements. The graphic is captioned “Figure 4.1: 4-span Bridge” and shows the completed structure under self-weight and perhaps staged construction loads. A simplified description follows:

1. Geometry and Supports  
• The deck is divided into four spans of roughly equal length. You can see five vertical support locations: two end abutments (at the far left and far right), plus three intermediate piers.  
• At each support, a small red triangular symbol indicates a pinned or fixed reaction point. The end supports at the left and right extremities also show red markers, suggesting abutment conditions.  

2. Mesh and Coloring  
• The bridge deck is modeled by a fine mesh of long, narrow beam or slab elements running longitudinally. Each element is color-filled to reflect vertical deflection.  
• Coloring follows a blue-to-red spectrum: deep blue areas imply upward or least downward movement (negative deflection in hogging regions), green represents moderate deflection, and yellow through red highlights maximum sagging under applied loads.  

3. Deflected Shape and Precamber Implications  
• Within each interior span, the deck sags under its own weight, reaching peak downward displacement in the midspan zones. These regions glow in warm tones (yellow to orange).  
• Near the three interior piers, the deck goes into hogging curvature (slight upward deflection) displayed in cooler hues (blue to teal). This hogging moment signature is typical of continuous multispan construction under dead load.  
• The end spans exhibit asymmetry: the rightmost span shows a more pronounced sag (reddish tint) than the left, possibly reflecting uneven loading stages or a sequence of cantilever construction that left more load unsupported temporarily.  

4. Construction Staging and Theoretical Context  
• The accompanying theoretical principles on “pre-camber” describe how designers introduce an initial upward camber during fabrication. This ensures that once all spans are cast and dead loads applied, the deck settles into near-level geometry.  
• A span-by-span precamber table (for example, csm26_precamber_spanbyspan.dat) would list the incremental camber offsets needed at each support as each span is cast, so the final completed bridge aligns flat under service loads.  

Overall, Figure 4.1 offers both a clear visual of live structural behavior after staged construction and a verification tool for designers to compare measured deflections against the theoretically computed precamber values.
A 4-span bridge is build in construction stages. A detailed description is found in theoretical principles - precamber - see also example csm26_precamber_spanbyspan.dat

The image is a finite-element‐style rendering of two simply supported concrete girders that have been placed end-to-end and then rigidly connected at midspan. It is labeled “Figure 4.2: Two Span Girder Creeping.” The long, horizontal beam is shown in isometric view, discretized into a regular mesh of rectangular elements. A cool-to-slightly-warmer blue color gradient runs continuously along the length of the beam, indicating the distribution of bending‐moment demand or possibly cumulative deflection; the left half of the beam is drawn in darker navy-blue tones, while the right half transitions through lighter blues and cyan.

At the very center of the model, a bright orange hexagonal outline surrounds the joint between the two originally separate girder segments. Superimposed on that hexagon is a green, curved‐arrow symbol that points downward (mirroring the convention for a hinge or moment release). Similar green arrow symbols are also placed just inside each support location at the beam ends: these indicate reaction supports that restrain vertical displacement but allow rotation. The green arrows are schematic markers showing the activation of a beam hinge or release.

The entire assemblage floats against a pale, sky-blue background, highlighting the structural elements without any extraneous context. The slight sag of the beam at midspan hints at a deformed shape under load, although the emphasis is on the color‐mapped bending‐moment variation rather than on explicit displacement exaggeration.

Context supplied with the figure explains that, in construction practice, two single girders (“single span distributions”) are first installed independently; they are then connected in the field. Over time, creep and shrinkage in the concrete cause the bending‐moment profile to evolve from the original single‐span pattern into a two‐span pattern, with negative moments developing over the newly formed interior support (the joint). The green hinge symbol and orange hexagon mark that connection, which is automatically “activated” and “fixed” in the structural model by the CSM…GRP…HING input command (with further details referenced in the ASE…GRP…HING documentation).

Key visual details:
• Beam Geometry and Meshing: A long, straight element divided into many small, rectangular finite elements, indicating a refined discretization.  
• Color Mapping: A continuous blue gradient—darker at the supports and lighter toward midspan—used to visualize moment magnitudes or creep‐induced redistribution.  
• Hinge/Connection Marker: A bright orange hexagon surrounding the midpoint joint, overlaid by a green curved arrow to denote the newly activated hinge release.  
• Support Symbols: Identical green arrows at both ends, signifying pinned supports that allow rotation but prevent vertical translation.  
• Background: A uniform light-blue backdrop providing clear contrast, so the beam and symbolic markers stand out crisply.  

Overall, the figure conveys the automatic generation and fixation of an interior beam hinge in response to long-term effects (creep and shrinkage) that convert a simply supported pair of girders into a continuous two-span system.

Two single girders are put in place and then connected. Due to creep and shrinkage the bending moment will change from a single span distribution to a twospan distribution.
 The activation and fixing of the beam hinge runs automatically with the CSM...GRP...HING input - please refer to ASE...GRP...HING.

The image presents a three-dimensional finite-element model of a precast-girder bridge over two spans, topped by a cast-in-situ concrete deck. Rendered against a pale blue background, the visualization superimposes the original (undeformed) girder line in black and the deformed shape in light blue, highlighting the deflection profile under applied loads and prestress. Eleven precast girders lie parallel to each other along the bridge length. Each girder is depicted in a subdued charcoal gray for its steel or prestressed concrete stem, with regularly spaced transverse cross-beams or diaphragms shown in solid blue. These transverse elements define the CSM…GRP groups in the finite-element input, controlling which support springs (modeled at the diaphragm locations) are active or released during successive construction stages.

At the midpoint of each span and at the abutments, the support conditions are represented by spring symbols or small green “cups.” These green elements correspond to springs that have been switched on in the current construction stage, as directed by the CSM…GRP and AQUA…SECT…CS input cards. The green color denotes that those spring supports are currently engaged, providing a varying cross-section stiffness to the structure. Adjacent springs rendered in a more neutral blue indicate supports that are currently inactive or released.

Above the girders rests a continuous deck slab, depicted in translucent sky blue. This slab is modeled as a prestressed finite element surface, representing the cast-in-situ concrete that ties the precast units into a composite section. The definition of the composite cross-section is handled by the AQUA…SECT…CS technique, which allows the deck and girder profiles to share bending and shear stiffness dynamically. The result is a single composite bridge section whose effective stiffness changes as individual girders and springs are activated or deactivated in different construction stages.

Short connection beams of matching light-blue color bridge the gap between adjacent girders at overhangs, symbolizing the field-cast continuity diaphragms that transform single-span units into a two-span system. These connectors ensure load distribution across spans, and their presence emerges mid-model to mirror the actual construction sequence: precast girder erection, temporary support release, deck casting, and final prestress transfer. 

The underlying purpose of this model is to generate sectional stress plots—produced at the end of the “csm3…_csm.dat” analysis run—which reveal how bending moments, shear forces, and axial stresses evolve across the composite section during each stage. Figure 4.3 thus encapsulates not only the geometric layout of a precast-girder bridge with a cast-in-situ deck but also the sophisticated activation logic of support springs and composite section stiffness that underpins realistic finite-element simulation of staged construction.

The model is a long, slender rectangular slab, discretized along its length into a series of identical, dark-blue quadrilateral panels on the top face. The image presents a three-dimensional structural model of a small test bridge erected by the classical free-cantilever method using a moving form traveler. Key elements and observations are as follows:

1. Overall Geometry  
- The bridge model comprises a single pier (column) rising from a square foundation block, supporting a series of rectangular deck segments that extend symmetrically on either side in a balanced free-cantilever configuration.  
- Only one span (half-span on each side of the pier) is shown: six contiguous precast or cast-in-place deck segments build out from the pier to the cantilever tip.  

2. Support and Foundation  
- At the very bottom is a conspicuous red cube representing the foundation or footing block, indicating the location of fixed or pinned support to the ground.  
- Above this red foundation sits a pale-blue rectangular pier shaft. Its solid color distinguishes the permanent vertical support from the superstructure segments.  

3. Deck Segments and Cantilever Construction  
- The deck is modeled as a series of finite elements or discrete segments. Starting at the pier, each segment is colored in a gradient from deep navy blue (closest to the pier) through medium blues toward cyan at the outermost segment.  
- This color progression may encode values such as bending moment magnitudes, relative stiffness, or simply segment numbering from 1 (pier) to 6 (tip).  
- The rectangular shape of each segment, with uniform thickness, suggests typical box-girder or slab elements used in cantilever erection.  

4. Free-Cantilever Erection and Form Traveler Load  
- The absence of falsework beneath the cantilevered deck illustrates the “free-cantilever” erection principle—each new segment is cast or placed at the tip and then counterbalanced on the opposite side of the pier.  
- Although the moving form traveler apparatus itself is not explicitly rendered, its temporary loads are implied at the tip segment. The lightest shade of cyan on the outermost element suggests the presence of the form traveler’s weight plus fresh concrete load at that stage of construction.  

5. Structural Analysis Context  
- The model’s color mapping and discrete segmentation align with a structural analysis workflow in which temporary loads (form traveler, fresh concrete, construction sequence) are applied incrementally.  
- This visualization helps engineers check stresses, deflections, and required prestressing sequences at each stage of cantilever erection before the continuity span is closed.  

6. Figure Annotation

The image is a low–resolution, computer‐generated rendering titled “Figure 4.6: Free Cantilever Erection – Big Bridge.” It consists of two side‐by‐side, isometric views of a single‐span cantilever bridge being built by the free‐cantilever method. A simplified pier, its footing, and the incrementally cast deck segments are shown against a plain light-blue background. 

1. General Geometry  
   - Both subfigures depict a vertical pier (black) rising from a square footing block (solid red).  
   - Extending symmetrically from the top of the pier are a series of rectangular deck segments. Each segment is rendered as a slender box; these are “added” one by one on alternating sides of the pier.  
   - The deck segments form two opposing cantilevers, which at their extremities join to complete the full span once erection is finished.  

2. Color‐Coded Force Distribution  
   - The deck segments are color–graded from deep red (adjacent to the pier) through shades of orange and yellow to bright green (near the free ends).  
   - This gradient visually encodes the magnitude of restraint forces or bending moments developing during erection: highest at the support (red) and tapering off toward the tip (green).  
   - As additional segments are cast, the diagram updates the color map to reflect the evolving distribution of internal forces.  

3. Left‐Hand View (Early/Early‐Intermediate Stage)  
   - On the far left, the cantilever arms are relatively short. Only a handful of segments (approximately five to six per side) are in place.  
   - The red‐orange banding is concentrated in the two or three segments closest to the pier, indicating peak restraint. Down the span, colors transition through yellow into the green range for the newest segments.  
   - The symmetry of the two arms suggests that alternating segment casting has been carefully balanced to minimize unbalanced moments on the pier.  

4. Right‐Hand View (Later Stage)  
   - Here the arms are notably longer—nearly double the number of segments compared to the left view.  
   - Red and deep orange zones have crept farther outboard, reflecting the increased lever arm and accumulated stiffness of the growing cantilever.  
   - The dynamic color shift highlights how restraint demands evolve as the structure lengthens, underscoring the need for realistic force prediction at each step.  

5. Contextual Note on Restraint‐Force Analysis  
   - During stepwise erection of prestressed or cast‐in‐place structures, restraint forces (moments, shears, axial reactions) develop as each new segment is added.  
   - The rendering implicitly demonstrates how the Constraint Stiffness Method (CSM) can simulate these forces in a realistic manner, capturing whether the pier, deck, and temporary supports remain within acceptable stress limits.  

Overall, the figure provides a clear, color‐coded visualization of the incremental development of internal restraint forces in a free‐cantilever bridge during construction. It underscores both the geometric sequence of casting and the shifting force patterns, illustrating why an accurate analysis method such as the CSM is essential for safe, balanced erection.

The image presents a three-dimensional, computer-generated model of a multi-storey, reinforced‐concrete (or composite) building under incremental erection. Shown against a uniform light-blue background, the structure rises in nine distinct floor levels above a ground slab. Each level is composed of a square grid of dark-gray floor panels—depicted as slightly raised, tile-like plates with thin white edging. The repetition of these floor plates emphasizes the building’s modular construction and makes clear the staged, floor-by-floor assembly process.

Supporting each slab are slender, bright-red columns. These red vertical elements are uniform in cross-section and extend continuously through successive floors where the concrete has been cast, but on levels not yet completed they protrude above the slab below—visually marking the progression of the erection sequence. At the very top of the model, one central red column stretches further upwards, indicating either a temporary support or the next level of construction in preparation.

In addition to the columns, two rigid vertical walls—likely shear walls or cores—are highlighted in pastel colors. On the building’s left face runs a peach-colored wall plate, while on the rear or opposite side sits a light-gray wall. These planar elements span multiple storeys and are integrated with each floor slab, suggesting their role in carrying lateral (wind or seismic) loads and contributing to overall stiffness. Their contrasting hues set them apart from the darker floor slabs and the red columns, underscoring their structural importance.

Viewed in semi-axonometric perspective, the model reveals floor edges exposed on three sides, allowing a clear sightline through the grid of panels and column locations. The systematic arrangement of panels and supports conveys a highly regular, orthogonal structural grid. Differences in column extension from floor to floor illustrate the stepwise nature of the build: lower levels are fully supported and constrained, while upper levels are in the process of being tied into the emerging frame.

By capturing each stage of slab casting and column extension, the image implicitly points to the development of restraint forces as new elements are connected to previously hardened concrete. Such forces—arising from differential shrinkage, temperature changes, and sequential loading—can lead to internal stresses if not properly anticipated. The accompanying note suggests that these evolving restraint effects are best captured by a realistic, stepwise analysis using the Component Structural Modelling (CSM) approach. In CSM, each newly erected slab, wall, and column is introduced into the finite‐element model in the order of construction, enabling the engineer to resolve the instantaneous redistribution of loads and stiffness and to quantify the restraint forces that develop throughout the build.
Also during the stepwise erection of a building, restraint forces appear. They can be analyzed in a realistic way with the CSM.
